experiment_title: Renal Stone Risk During Space Flight:  Assessment and Countermeasure Validation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this study was to assess the renal stone-forming potential of humans as a function of mission duration and to determine how long after space flight the increased risk exists. In addition to the analyses of mineral components, this study was designed to determine levels of the naturally occurring urinary protein inhibitors of calcium crystallization. This investigation provides a direct understanding of and overcoming human limitations in space that may affect crew health and potentially mission success. If a crewmember were to develop a kidney stone, only supportive action is possible at this time. Medical support would involve pain relief through on-board medication with the hope that the crewmember would pass the stone over time. The afflicted crewmember may not be able to perform his/her duties or, more significant, cause the mission to be aborted and return to Earth.

Previous data have demonstrated that human exposure to the microgravity environment of space increases the risk of renal stone development during and immediately after space flight. In-flight assessment has shown a greater risk of calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate and sodium urate stones. Postflight changes to the urinary chemical composition increase the risk of uric acid and calcium oxalate stone formation.

Astronauts in the U.S. program have experienced multiple postflight stone events (2 crewmembers had 2 postflight stones). The length of time for appearance of symptomatic stone formation ranged from 9-120 months. Six of these postflight stones have occurred since 1994 and have taken place concurrently with the beginning of the extended shuttle missions of greater than 12 days in space. Discussions with Russian medical science investigators have noted multiple stone events among cosmonauts, with one in-flight renal stone episode nearly causing the crewmember to abort the mission. These epidemiologic data may suggest that that risk of stone formation may extend beyond the testing period implemented during this investigation in some crewmembers.

APPROACH:
Potassium citrate (K-cit), a proven Earth-based therapy to minimize calcium-containing renal stone development, was tested during space flight as a countermeasure to reduce the risk of renal stone formation. Preflight baseline data collection sessions were performed at approximately L-180, L-60 and L-45 days. Two 10 mEq potassium citrate tablets (total dose 20 mEq) or placebo were ingested daily with the evening meal beginning three days before launch, all days during flight, and following landing through R+14. Urine was collected before, during, and after flight. Food, fluid, exercise, and medications were monitored before and during the urine collection period in order to assess environmental influences other than microgravity. During ISS operations, 24 hour urine collections and 48 hour dietary monitoring were performed early (< FD 30), mid-mission (FD30-FD100), and late (within 30 days of landing). Postflight urine and dietary monitoring were performed at approximately R+0-2, R+7 and R+14 days.

Subjects were active astronauts and cosmonauts who were certified for space flight. There were no gender specific requirements, therefore both male and female crewmembers participated in this study. This investigation was designed as a double blind study with neither the investigators nor the subjects knowing whether the subjects were ingesting potassium citrate or placebo.

RESULTS:
This investigation was successfully completed by 19 crewmembers. The majority of renal stones are composed of calcium containing salts. The risk of calcium oxalate stone formation as determined by the urinary supersaturation of calcium oxalate was observed to be lower in the potassium citrate treated group. The decreased risk was evident during the in-flight and immediate postflight assessment sessions. The risk of calcium phosphate (brushite) risk followed the same trend observed with the risk of calcium oxalate stone formation.

This study also evaluated the effect of fluid intake and urinary output on the supersaturation of the urine and the potential risk of stone formation. Regarding the correlation between 24-hr urinary volume and the risk of calcium oxalate stone development, data indicate an inverse relationship between urine volume and risk of calcium oxalate stone formation.

Approval for elimination of the double blind requirement was received from NASA in December, 2005. As a result, the participating crewmembers ingested only potassium citrate as a countermeasure to the risk of renal stone formation. Data from all the ISS missions were combined for a detailed analysis involving statistical analysis and evaluation of the pharmacologic countermeasure to reduce the risk of stone formation.

Potassium citrate-treated crew members had decreased urinary calcium excretion and maintained the calcium oxalate supersaturation risk at preflight levels compared to that in controls. Increased urinary pH in the treatment group decreased the risk of uric acid stones. Results from this investigation suggest that supplementation with potassium citrate may decrease the risk of renal stone formation during and immediately after spaceflight.

experiment_title: Metabolic Response to Exercise
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Both space flight and ground simulation of microgravity result in hemodynamic and biochemical changes in metabolites, enzymes and blood plasma hormones that correlate with deteriorated physical performance. Biochemical characterization of energy supply at rest does not provide full information on the body reserves, specifically the ability to maintain performance (i.e. during exercise). The study of the effects of graded exercise on these parameters during long-term bed rest has shown inadequate metabolic response to exercise and proved to be highly effective for assessment of applied countermeasures.

The primary objective of this experiment was to study directly the effect of long duration space flight on metabolic function during graded exercise on a bicycle ergometer, based on the levels of energy substrates and metabolites in the venous blood, enzyme activities and hormone levels regulating energy metabolism. This experiment was performed in conjunction with and to enhance another experiment entitled, “Aerobic Capacity using Graded Bicycle Ergometry” (3.2.1).

APPROACH:
A baseline blood sample was to be taken 10 minutes prior to aerobic exercise by bicycle ergometry. Crewmembers had a light breakfast before the test and recorded in detail food and fluid intakes. Aerobic exercise was to be performed as detailed in Experiment 3.2.1. Immediately following exercise and after a 20 minute rest period, repeat blood samples were supposed to have been drawn.

Blood samples were obtained preflight and were used for hematocrit measurement and determination of lactic acid, pyruvic acid, lactate dehydrogenase activity (LDH), and lipid content. Enzyme activities of ATPase, LDH, and glyceraldehyde-6-phosphate dehydrogenase were determined on sample erythrocytes. For comparison purposes these parameters were determined on other days when exercise was not performed.

RESULTS:
No results are available. This experiment was manifested on the Mir 18 mission. However, due to crew scheduling constraints, no data were obtained either preflight or inflight.

experiment_title: Bioassays of Body Fluids
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Orthostatic hypotension and weight loss were observed in the crewmembers of Gemini 3, 4, 5, and 6 immediately after flight. Scientists were concerned that space flight might affect the balance of body fluid and electrolytes since fluid losses can contribute to both of these symptoms. This led to a series of ground-based studies to simulate some of the conditions of space flight. An attempt was made to define the physiological parameters that would be affected by the condition of microgravity. These studies utilized bed rest and water immersion as a means of simulating microgravity.

Both the cardiovascular and musculoskeletal systems experienced changes during the ground-based studies. Changes in body fluid chemistry were found to be reflective of the status of these systems. This experiment was designed to obtain objective data concerning the effects of space flight on the human body by examining alterations in the body fluid chemistry.

APPROACH:
Preflight plasma samples were collected from all crewmembers of Gemini 7, Gemini 8, and Gemini 9 approximately 10 days and 3 days before launch. Plasma samples were not collected in flight. Gemini 7 postflight plasma samples were collected immediately after recovery, and 6 hours, 24 hours and 72 hours after flight. Gemini 9 postflight plasma specimens were collected after recovery, and 6 hours and 72 hours after flight. The Gemini 8 mission was terminated after 11 hours and no postflight data was collected for this experiment.

Urine sampling was scheduled preflight, inflight, and postflight for Gemini 7, 8, and 9. Preflight, two 48-hour urine samples were collected approximately 10 days and 3 days before launch. Inflight urine collection on Gemini 7 and 9 was accomplished by utilizing a specially designed urine transport system. The urine transport system permitted researchers to calculate the total urine volume for each void by means of tritium dilution. A 75 ml aliquot of each void was collected into a plastic sample bag and stored for return to Earth. No refrigeration was used, but benzoic acid was added as a preservative. Urine was collected continuously for 48 hours after landing. Inflight and postflight urine samples were not collected for the Gemini 8 crewmembers.

Water and fluid electrolytes were examined to determine the mechanisms associated with weight loss during flight. The concentrations of plasma sodium, potassium, and chloride ions were measured preflight and postflight, and the rates of urinary excretion of these electrolytes were determined pre-, in-, and postflight. Total plasma protein concentrations, measured preflight and postflight, were used to indicate dehydration.

Fluid intake and output were measured to determine whether weight loss was caused by sweat and insensible losses or by changes in renal function. Fluid intake was ad lib, but the quantities ingested during the pre- and postflight phases were recorded. The majority of the fluid intake was obtained with the diet. Inflight intake was estimated from a water dispensing device on board the space craft. The information was not sufficiently precise to perform calculation of fluid balance data.

To complement the water measurements and electrolyte-balance measurements, both urinary antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and aldosterone were measured. The production of ADH is responsive to thoracic blood volume changes, and it was postulated that microgravity would decrease ADH secretion and result in an increase in urinary volume. Aldosterone was measured to study the mechanisms associated with sodium excretion. Increases in aldosterone secretion would result in decreased urinary excretion of sodium, and vice versa. Researchers hypothesized that aldosterone secretion would be decreased in space flight, resulting in an increased urinary excretion of sodium.

To measure the effects of stress in space, two groups of hormones were assayed. The first group assayed, 17-hydroxycorticosteroids, was indicative of long-term stress responses. The second group assayed, catecholamines, was indicative of short-term or emergency responses. These parameters provided an objective, long-term evaluation of the physiologic cost of space flight.

Bone demineralization was evaluated by measuring calcium, magnesium, phosphate, and hydroxyproline in plasma and urine both preflight and postflight and in urine collected in flight. Changes in bone mineralization were studied by calculating the ratio of bound to unbound calcium in the plasma. This ratio was approximated from an estimate of plasma protein and calcium. Hydroxyproline, an amino acid unique to collagen, was measured in urine to study bone and collagen breakdown. It was presumed that an increased excretion of hydroxyproline accompanying bone demineralization resulted from dissolution of bone matrix.

Urinary urea concentration was measured to study protein intake and tissue metabolism. Creatinine excretion was measured to study muscle protein metabolism. Decreases of creatinine excretion are associated with loss of muscle tone and activity.

RESULTS:
When the preflight and postflight plasma samples were analyzed for Gemini 7, by far the longest Gemini flight, electrophoretic patterns were normal. All values were in the normal range, except for an anticipated increase in 17-hydroxycorticosteroids in the first sample taken after recovery. These values decreased to preflight values within 6 hours following recovery. Hydroxyproline did not change significantly. Plasma uric acid was reduced. The cause of the reduction was unknown, but presumed to be dietary. Plasma ADH was significantly elevated in the first postflight plasma sample of one subject of Gemini 7, but returned within normal range as urine output returned to normal. It was concluded that 14 days of orbital space flight did not result in any gross aberrations of plasma electrolytes.

During the first 24-hours after Gemini 7, there was marked water retention for both subjects. The output for each subject was approximately 1 liter less than the preflight 24-hour volume. In addition, there was marked retention of chloride, sodium, and potassium. The water retention and the rapid weight gain after flight were consistent with the hypothesis that weight loss during flight was the result of fluid loss. Electrolyte and water retentions observed immediately postflight in the Gemini 7 subjects were consistent with bed rest studies that showed an increased ADH secretion contributed to decreased urinary volume.

During Gemini 9, inflight urine volumes based on the tritium dilution were as great as 12 liters per urination. This great variation in urine volumes was indicative of an anomaly. Therefore, no further attempt was made to analyze or interpret the urine samples collected in flight. The Gemini 9 subjects experienced significant postflight retention of water. This was accompanied by retention of sodium, potassium, and chloride. Urinary calcium decreased slightly immediately postflight. The excretion of 17-hydroxycorticosteroids was increased immediately postflight. This was probably caused by the stress of re-entry. Postflight, the increase of plasma protein and a slightly smaller increase of plasma electrolytes were consistent with an inflight water and electrolyte loss that resulted in dehydration followed by the retention of water and electrolytes. It was not known whether the losses resulted from diuresis during flight or from sweat.

experiment_title: Bisphosphonates As A Countermeasure To Space Flight Induced Bone Loss
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this combined research study is to determine whether bisphosphonates, in conjunction with the routine in-flight exercise program, will protect International Space Station (ISS) crewmembers from the regional decreases in bone mineral density documented on previous ISS flights. Two dosing regimens will be tested: (1) an oral dose of 70 mg of alendronate taken weekly during flight and (2) an intravenous (IV) dose of zoledronic acid 4 mg, administered just once approximately 45 days before flight. The crewmember has a choice between taking oral alendronate or IV administered zoledronic acid. The rationale for including both alendronate and zoledronic acid is that two dosing options will: maximize crew participation, increase the countermeasure options available to crew surgeons, increase scientific opportunities, and minimize the effects of operational and logistical constraints. Operational and logistical constraints may favor one option versus the other; however, the purpose of this study is not to compare the two dosing options. Rather, the intent is to show that bisphosphonates plus exercise will have a measurable effect versus exercise alone in preventing space flight induced bone loss.

If shown to be an effective countermeasure to space flight-induced bone loss, bisphosphonates could prevent or ameliorate several potential bone-related problems identified in NASA’s Bioastronautics Roadmap. In addition, if bisphosphonates improve the efficiency of in-flight exercise to maintain bone mass, then more crew time could be made available to improve other problem areas.

Primary Objective:

Determine the treatment effect of bisphosphonates [alendronate or zoledronic acid plus in-flight exercise (AL+EX, ZO+EX)] versus in-flight exercise alone (EX) on space flight induced bone loss. Measurements required: Percent change in femoral Quantitative Computed Tomography (QCT) values (volumetric trabecular Bone Mineral Density (BMD) of total hip, pre-flight versus R+5).

Secondary Objectives:

  • Determine treatment effect on Dual Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DXA) BMD of the hip, spine, pelvis and heel.
  • Determine treatment effect on QCT femur neck, hip trochanter trabecular BMD, and strength indices of the hip.
  • Determine treatment effect on Peripheral Quantitative Computed Tomography (pQCT) trabecular BMD and strength-strain-index of the tibia and wrist.
  • Determine the time course of changes to bone and bone regulatory systems in crewmembers taking alendronate/zoledronic acid (pre-flight, in-flight, and post-flight). Measurements will include pre- and post-flight serum markers of bone metabolism; pre-, in- and post-flight urinary markers of bone metabolism; pre and post-flight BMD.
  • Attempt to understand the underlying mechanism of changes to bone and bone regulatory systems caused by taking alendronate/zoledronic acid in microgravity. Measurements will include pre- and post-flight serum markers of bone metabolism; pre-, in- and post-flight urinary markers of bone metabolism.

APPROACH:
This experiment requires the participation of 10 long-duration crewmembers. Subjects will complete DXA scans (L-45, R+5, R+180, and R+360), pQCT scans (L-45, R+5, R+180, and R+360, R+720, and R+1080), High Resolution QCT scans (L-45, R+5, R+360), 24-hour urine collections (4 to 8 weeks prior to bisphosphonate administration, L-10, R+0, R+14, R+30, R+180, R+360), and blood draws (four to eight weeks prior to bisphosphonate administration, L-10, R+0, R+14, R+30, and R+180 R+360). Alendronate subjects will complete an Alendronate Tolerance Test around L-180, and they will take Alendronate on L-17, L-10, and L-3. Zoledronic Acid subjects will be administered the bisphosphonate on L-45 and will conduct one or more additional blood draws for post-infusion health monitoring. In addition, preflight and postflight abdominal/retroperitoneal ultrasound scans will be obtained.

While on the ISS, Alendronate subjects will ingest a pill weekly. All subjects will conduct three urine collection sessions (early, mid, and late mission). Crewmembers will also take a daily Vitamin D supplement during the duration of the mission.

The Bisphosphonates experiment urine samples will be obtained using the Urine Collection Kit (UCK). The Urine Collection Kit (UCK) is a Nomex pouch containing polyethylene Urine Collection Devices (UCDs) with male or female adapters, biocide wipes, and gauze. Each UCD contains one mL of lithium chloride as a volume marker and a sample port for sample retrieval. The Urine Containment Bag (UCB) is a large Nomex container with absorbent material and a sealing zipper for disposal of filled UCDs. The Sample Tube Dispenser is a metal and plastic rack designed to secure 60 plastic 10 mL syringes. Each syringe has a barcode label and a capped tip designed to provide an interface to connect the syringe with the UCD for sample removal. The Inventory Management System (IMS) Barcode Reader (BCR) or Personal Digital Assistant (PDA) will be used to record samples. All samples will be frozen in the Minus Eighty Laboratory Freezer on ISS (MELFI) for preservation until return to the PI for analysis.

An interim review of the data for this study indicated that it was necessary to add a new control group whose results could be compared to those of crewmembers who have taken bisphosphonates. The original historical control group (14 crewmembers from early ISS flights) exercised using the Interim Resistive Exercise Device (IRED), while the bisphosphonate subject group (7 subjects, now complete) exercised on the newer Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED). The new control group will help distinguish the relative effects of bisphosphonates versus the confounder of ARED. The control subjects will participate in essentially the same data collection protocol as the bisphosphonate group, but not take the oral or intravenous bisphosphonate.

RESULTS:
This study is still in progress. However, some preliminary results are available from a publication available in Osteoporosis International.

In addition to pre- and post-flight measurements, the investigators compared their results to 18 astronauts who flew ISS missions and who exercised using an early model resistance exercise device, called the interim resistance exercise device, and to 11 ISS astronauts who exercised using the newer advanced resistance exercise device (ARED). Their findings indicate that the ARED provided significant attenuation of bone loss compared with the older device although post-flight decreases in the femur neck and hip remained. The combination of the ARED and bisphosphonate attenuated the expected decline in essentially all indices of altered bone physiology during space flight including: DXA-determined losses in bone mineral density of the spine, hip, and pelvis, QCT-determined compartmental losses in trabecular and cortical bone mass in the hip, calculated measures of fall and stance computed bone strength of the hip, elevated levels of bone resorption markers, and urinary excretion of calcium.

experiment_title: Renal Stone Risk Assessment During Long-Term Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Exposure to the microgravity environment of space alters human physiology. A number of these changes are expected to contribute to an altered urinary function that will in turn influence the potential for renal stone formation. Studies conducted in the Space Shuttle program have shown that, immediately postflight, the urine of most crewmembers is saturated with stone-forming salts. These astronauts are at an increased risk for developing calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate and uric acid stones. Also, there was a difference in the values of astronauts flying on short missions (up to six days in space) and those with a longer exposure to microgravity (7 to 14 days), which led to the hypothesis that the risk of calcium oxalate stones increases as the length of the mission increases.

The most obvious changes observed in astronauts are the increased excretion of calcium and the negative calcium balance thought to be the result of bone loss. Other demonstrated changes include decreased urinary output, urinary pH, magnesium, and citrate concentrations and increased urinary phosphate. All of these changes would be expected to increase the urinary supersaturation of stone-forming salts.

For this experiment, three objectives were formulated:
1. To quantitate the risk of renal stone formation associated with extended duration space flight.
2. To assess the risk factors which are affected by flight duration.
3. To estimate the contribution of dietary and environmental factors to the risk of renal stone formation.

APPROACH:
To assess the renal stone-forming potential, 24-hour urine collections were taken preflight, inflight and postflight. During the inflight period, individual urine voids were collected over a 24-hour period into urine collection devices containing 1 ml 2.5 M lithium chloride as a volume marker. From each urine void, two 7 ml urine aliquots were withdrawn into syringe tubes containing 0.05% thymol or 0.1% thimerosal, mixed well and stored at ambient temperature until return to Earth for analyses.

Following the return of the samples, urine volumes were determined from the diluted lithium concentration. The urine samples were analyzed for calcium, phosphorus, uric acid, sodium, potassium, magnesium, creatinine, pH, citrate, oxalate, and sulfate. Uric acid was always determined by analyzing the thymol preserved sample, while citrate and pH were determined from the thimerosal preserved sample. Other analytes were not restricted to a specific sample.

During the NASA 6 and NASA 7 missions, an additional 14 ml of urine from each void was collected into the Dried Urine Chemistry device. The device sampled urine on a card, which was dried at ambient temperatures and stored under controlled environmental conditions until analysis. For analysis, the urine cards were rehydrated and standard assays were performed. The urinary data from the Dried Urine Chemistry cards were compared to the liquid samples and the efficiency of this new technology was assessed.

Pre- and postflight, the subjects collected 24-hour urine pools. After total volume and pH were recorded, two 10 ml aliquots were removed for biochemical analysis. The first sample was analyzed for creatinine, magnesium, phosphorus, potassium, sodium and uric acid. The second 10 ml aliquot was acidified with 6M hydrochloric acid (HCl) and analyzed for calcium, magnesium, citrate, oxalate and sulfate. All samples were processed immediately or stored at -20 degrees Celsius until analysis.

From the determined urinary levels of calcium, sodium, phosphorus, uric acid, oxalate and sulfate, the urine’s supersaturation with stone-forming salts, such as calcium oxalate, brushite (calcium phosphate), struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate), sodium urate, and uric acid, was determined and the renal stone risk was estimated.

In addition, detailed diet logs were maintained by the crewmembers for 24 hours prior to and during the 24-hour urine collection period in order to assess the effect of dietary factors on the potential for renal stone formation.

RESULTS:
This investigation continued to support previous data from both short-term Shuttle and long duration Mir missions that crewmembers exposed to the microgravity environment of space flight increase their risk of renal stone formation. The crewmember provided excellent compliance with the objectives of this investigation with the exception of the effects of flight duration. Due to scheduling difficulties, no early in-flight session was performed so the effects of mission duration could not be evaluated. Theses data will be combined with data obtained from other long duration missions and the potential for renal stone development assessed.

experiment_title: Fluid Electrolyte Metabolism
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Our previous experiments have revealed that an adult organism may well remain functional and a developing fetus may also develop normal functions in a space environment. However, changes were also observed in space-flown fetuses and animals. In this experiment it is assumed that a longer flight and exposure to microgravity may aggravate these changes. The purpose of this experiment is to accumulate new data concerning the metabolism of water and electrolytes in the placentas and fetuses that developed during spaceflight.

Approach:

Animals were laparotomized on the 8th gestational day to measure implantation rate, and on the 20th gestational day to remove one uterine horn containing fetuses. Animals were flown from the 9th through the 20th gestational day. One fetus and placenta from the flight, laporatimized viviarium controls, and synchronous groups were analyzed. Fetus organs were dissected and dried to a constant weight at 105 degrees Celsius to measure content, and then ashed in concentrated nitric acid at 90 degrees Celsius. Sodium and potassium were measured in air propane flames using a Corning-410 photometer. Calcium, copper, iron, and magnesium were measured in air-acetylene flame using a Hitachi atomic absorption spectrophotometer. Placentas were also analyzed for the same parameters.

Results:

In placentas of the flight dams, water, sodium, potassium, magnesium, and iron did not differ from those in synchronous and vivarium dams. Calcium in the placenta of the flight dams was lower than in synchronous dams and identical to that in vivarium controls, whereas copper in the placentas of the flight dams was higher than in the vivarium controls and very similar to that in synchronous dams. In fetuses of the flight group, water, sodium, and magnesium in fetuses of the flight group did not differ significantly from those in the synchronous controls and were lower than in the vivarium controls. Potassium, calcium, and copper in fetuses of the three groups were identical. Iron in the fetuses of the flight group was higher than in the synchronous group and identical to that in the vivarium controls. The data obtained allow the conclusion that no changes in water, sodium, potassium, iron or copper in the fetuses and placentas were observed that can attributed to the effect of microgravity. Minor changes seen in the flight fetuses and placents were also observed in the synchronous group.

experiment_title: Bioavailability of Nutrients in Food
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
NASA is planning for long-duration missions beyond low Earth orbit. In order to ensure sustainment of crew health and performance, adequate nutrition must be delivered by the food system and efficiently absorbed by crewmembers to prevent micronutrient deficiency. No collective source of literature on nutrient bioavailability in processed foods is available. The purpose of this task is to conduct a literature review of nutrient bioavailability taking into account the form of food ingredient interactions and processing conditions. The review will identify where information is inadequate and be used to propose formulation and processing suggestions for the development of food products with improved bioavailability.

The Specific Aims were:

  1. Review current scientific literature on bioavailability of nutrients and how it is affected by form, ingredient interactions and processing conditions.
  2. Characterize the conditions that reduce or improve bioavailability of nutrients for future food development.
APPROACH:
The methodology isn’t available.

RESULTS:
Supplemental forms of vitamins and minerals generally are better absorbed by the body than the natural forms of the micronutrient though this phenomena is not always the case. The bioavailability of vitamin E and riboflavin is higher from natural sources as compared to their synthetic counterparts. Additionally, natural forms of vitamin C, biotin, calcium, magnesium, potassium, and zinc were shown to achieve equal serum concentrations as the supplements after consumption of like amounts in controlled test scenarios. Hence, as necessary, food fortification can occur with many of the micronutrients without adverse consequence to the physiological delivery provided that adequate stability of supplemental micronutrients can be achieved.

Many ingredient interactions and matrix effects occur with micronutrients that impact nutrient absorption. One ingredient interaction which occurs during the absorption phase is the competitive absorption of similar compounds in the body. For example, beta-carotene competes with other carotenoids for intestinal absorption. Likewise, zinc limits iron absorption when the two are consumed simultaneously. Another interaction affecting bioavailability is the inhibitory nature of phytate and phytic acid, naturally occurring compounds in plants, with the mineral absorption of calcium, chromium, iron, magnesium, phosphorus, and zinc. Some vitamins, such as vitamins A and E, have increased bioavailability if some fat is consumed simultaneously. Vitamin A, riboflavin, and vitamin C show increased absorption if more dietary fiber is present at consumption so that the vitamins have a longer gastrointestinal residence time for absorption. Processing impacts to the bioavailability of micronutrients were very limited. Vitamin concentrations in foods are commonly affected by heat, water leaching, or oxidation. However only two vitamins actually had documentation of bioavailability differences that was dependent on the processing method. Vitamin A provitamins, because of their placement in the microstructure of plants, often become more bioavailable after cooking or pureeing. The niacin in grains must be released by acid or alkali extraction to allow significant absorption.

Future work with regards to nutrient bioavailability in the space food system should focus on ensuring that micronutrients are provided in an optimal matrix within many food items. Both vitamin and mineral absorption in many instances was dose-dependent, meaning that percent absorption was higher at lower doses, up to a physiological nutrient saturation level, but overconsumption of micronutrients did not result in absorption at the same rate above saturation. Hence, micronutrients should be spread across many food items to ensure continued nutrient delivery at each meal occasion. Competing nutrients should be staggered in their consumption. Additionally, fortification efforts must take into account the data here in terms of surrounding food matrix and form of the supplemental micronutrient used.

experiment_title: Bone Resorption in Rats During Spaceflight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Calcium metabolism is altered in weightlessness. In humans, bone loss occurs and urinary calcium output is increased. Experiments on previous Cosmos flights have shown that bone formation in the tibia is depressed in young, growing rats, but no direct information has been obtained about bone resorption, or any of the other calcium metabolic parameters such as excretion, absorption, or net calcium balance. The basis of the present study was to determine the response of calcium homeostasis and bone to weightlessness.

Approach:

Calcium tracer kinetic methods were used in this study. In the normal situation, both bone and dietary calcium are made up of natural calcium, and thus are labeled with stable isotopic tracers such as 48Ca. If one removes 48Ca from the diet, however, then dietary calcium is distinguished from bone calcium by lack of this tracer. This is done by replacing natural dietary calcium with isotopically- separated ~100% 40Ca. As calcium is excreted from the serum, it is replaced by calcium coming from both bone and diet. As the only source of 48Ca is the bone, the amount found in serum represents the fraction of calcium turnover coming directly from bone. Animals were started on the tracer diet at the time of loading into flight hardware. Specimens received from the Soviets following flight were the rib cage (left and right) from each animal and approximately 50% of each two-day excreta collection from each animal. The muscle from each rib cage was used as an indicator of tracer activity in the serum.

Results:

Bone resorption expressed as the fraction of exchangeable calcium pool coming from bone was 0.690 ± 0.089 in the flight animals versus 0.675 ± 0.085 in synchronous controls, measured at the end of the flight period. Bone resorption rate at the end of the flight period was 15.7 mg Ca/day in flight rats and 20.2 mg Ca/day in the controls. It is significant that resorption normalized by calcium turnover does not decrease during flight, so that the decrease seen in the bone resorption rate is probably secondary to a decrease in total calcium turnover. Of particular interest may be the fact that while bone resorption rate decreased during flight, it was still 75-80% of normal at the end of the flight. This may indicate that bone loss on even longer flights will continue. The continual imbalance of bone formation and breakdown, and the large excretion of other minerals (sodium, potassium) from the body indicate that mineral homeostasis does not adapt to weightlessness.

experiment_title: Effects of Skeletal Unloading and Vitamin E on Bone in Mature Rats
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Bone loss is a critical concern for crewmembers in space. Free radicals have been shown to affect bone in vivo and in vitro by stimulating osteoclasts and increasing the rate of bone resorption. In space, increased exposure to radiation increases the possibility of oxidative damage to bone, and antioxidant nutrients may protect the skeletal tissue.

Rodent hindlimb unloading (HLU) is an alternative method to space flight for investigating microgravity-induced physiological changes. HLU produces a deficit in bone formation, lowers the number of osteoblasts, and has been used as a model for examining bone changes in simulated weightlessness.

This ground-based study evaluated the potential of vitamin E for preventing bone loss associated with weightlessness in the HLU rat model. The long-term goal was to identify an optimal dose of vitamin E to reduce the risk of bone loss and fractures under conditions of weightlessness. The hypothesis was that the dietary antioxidant vitamin E would reduce deterioration of bone in a dose-dependent manner when the bone loss was due to weightlessness and, possibly, oxidative stress. There were two specific aims. One was to investigate whether vitamin E prevents the loss of bone mineral density and deterioration of biomechanical properties in the HLU rat model in a dose-dependent manner. The other specific aim was to examine some of the underlying mechanisms by which vitamin E exerts bone-protective effects using histomorphometric, biomechanical and biochemical analyses.

APPROACH:
Eight and one-half-month-old rats were assigned to one of three diets containing 15, 75 or 500 International Units (IU) of dl-alpha tocopherol, a form of vitamin E. These amounts were low, recommended or high for this vitamin intake. The rats were assigned to either ambulatory (AMB) or HLU conditions. Diets began nine weeks prior to the start of the hindlimb unloading period and the rats were either HLU or AMB for four weeks. At eight days and at one day prior to necropsy, rats were injected with calcein for dynamic bone histomorphometric analysis. They were scanned using a small animal software package prior to unloading and at the end of the treatment period. Rats were anesthetized for scanning and blood was drained by cardiac puncture. Serum was then analyzed for various markers. Age at necropsy was approximately eleven months.

Mechanical strength of the femur was assessed with three-point bending. The femur was placed on two rods spaced 20 mm apart and force was delivered to the mid-shaft. The fourth lumbar vertebral body (L4) was prepared with parallel flat ends and placed on a fixed lower pressure plate while an upper plate moved downwards at a rate of three mm/min to cause compression in the front to rear direction in order to conduct compression analysis. Load displacement plots were analyzed to determine material properties. The average cross section for each vertebral body was used to calculate its ultimate stresses and Young's modulus, which is a number representing the ratio of stress divided by strain. Histomorphometric analysis of the femur produced multiple measurements.

Bone mineral area, bone mineral content, and bone mineral density (BMD) of the excised fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) and of the left femur were estimated. Femurs and the third lumbar vertebra were ashed, and the mineral residue was dissolved in concentrated nitric acid and diluted for analysis of calcium, magnesium, iron, copper and zinc.

RESULTS:
Results were divided into two parts. HLU and AMB conditions were compared and dose-dependent effects of vitamin E on bone parameters of interest under both conditions were evaluated. Significant effects of near weightlessness were seen in 11-month old rats. Both the L5 and femur BMD were significantly lowered in HLU animals compared to AMB controls. Lower BMDs in the HLU group were accompanied by reduced structural properties. The material properties of L4, ultimate stress, yield stress, and Young's modulus of elasticity were significantly decreased by HLU. Histomorphometric data indicated that HLU decreased the rate of bone formation and increased the rate of bone resorption. Serum markers indicated an increase in tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase activity, a marker of bone resorption, but no change in either marker of bone formation (alkaline phosphatase activity or osteocalcin). The findings confirmed that deleterious effects on bone of older animals due to HLU were similar to the deleterious effects on younger, growing animals. However, alterations in bone metabolism that result in bone loss of mature animals appeared to more closely mimic the metabolic bone changes occurring in crewmembers in space.

Dietary treatments were effective in creating differences in serum vitamin E concentrations even though diet was not begun until the rats were eight and one-half months old. The diet produced significant differences in ferric reducing ability of serum and strong trends for decreased malondialdehyde, a product of lipid peroxidation, in the liver. Both ferric reducing ability of serum and liver malondialdehyde are indicators of antioxidant status. In HLU animals, high intakes of vitamin E had a positive effect on material properties of vertebrae measured by increased yield stress and by Young's modulus of elasticity. The positive effects of the high vitamin E intake were not observed in AMB controls. Histomorphometry data indicated that higher doses of vitamin E produced positive effects on bone volume parameters in HLU rats. Contrary to expectations, the same doses of vitamin E had negative effects on these histomorphometric parameters in AMB controls. Serum alkaline phosphatase, a marker of bone formation, increased with increased vitamin E in the diet.

Data indicated that higher doses of vitamin E improved skeletal health. Higher bone volume and biomechanical properties in HLU animals were observed with the increased dietary vitamin E. Contrary to expectations, vitamin E at higher doses was found to be deleterious to bone in AMB control animals. Research previous to this study showed that higher doses of vitamin E were beneficial in aged mice but had no beneficial effects on the bone of younger mice. It is possible that the bone of older animals or of those in HLU conditions benefit from more vitamin E, particularly if the HLU resulted in greater oxidative damage.

Research of the mechanisms of vitamin E in mature bone is critical to understanding its role in bone health. There is the potential for vitamin E to protect against oxygen derived from free radicals. In the mature, 11-month old rats of this study, dietary vitamin E did not produce significant effects on bone mineral area, bone mineral content or BMD. Since dietary changes are cumulative over time and subtler than the bone response was to HLU, the bone mineral area, bone mineral content and BMD might not be apparent during the relatively brief time course of this experiment. Nutrition studies may require extended depletion or supplementation periods before HLU to enable differences to be observed during the relatively short HLU period. Additional data may be obtained through studies that analyze markers over time. Time series studies examining markers of bone resorption and also changes in gene expression due to HLU and nutritional or pharmacological interventions could provide insight into alterations in bone metabolism.

experiment_title: Kidneys and Fluid-Electrolyte Homeostasis
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous studies have examined the effects of spaceflight on the water, sodium, potassium, calcium, and magnesium concentrations in the skin, bone, liver, kidneys, heart and reproductive organs. However, the specific effects of microgravity could be masked by the effects of readaptation to the Earth's environment. The purpose of this experiment is to study the kidney and fluid-electrolyte homeostasis of rats dissected inflight.

Approach:

The kidney was isolated into its components (medulla, papillae, and cortex) and dried for water measurement. The dried samples were ashed using nitric acid at 80 degrees C. Sodium and potassium levels were measured using a photometer. Calcium and magnesium were measured using an atomic absorption spectrophotometer. The results were analyzed using Student's t-test.

Results:

Data analysis was difficult due to significant variations within the controls. However, the following results were obtained. Rats dissected inflight (IF) had water and sodium contents in the renal component identical to the controls. Potassium content in the medulla and cortex were identical, while in the papillae it was lower in flight rats. Calcium was decreased in the cortex, and magnesium were decreased in the cortex and papillae. Rats dissected immediately post-flight (R+0) showed a decrease in water content in the cortex and papillae. The concentrations of electrolyes were identical to those of the controls. Rats dissected 14 days post-flight (R+14), had water and electrolyte concentration unchanged in the medulla and papillae while water and electrolyte concentrations in the cortex increased.

experiment_title: Metabolism of Red Blood Cells
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Previous space flight studies revealed that exposure to microgravity causes changes in red blood cells (erythrocytes), which are manifested in changes in erythrocyte mass, a decreased osmotic stability and alterations in metabolic parameters. Changes in erythrocyte shape and plasma membrane parameters were observed during and after previous space flights in humans and animals, and can cause a deterioration in erythrocyte function. The purpose of this investigation was to determine and evaluate the dynamics of the changes in erythrocyte function during and after space flight. In particular, the parameters of (1) energy metabolism, (2) oxidation-reduction system, and (3) condition of plasma membrane were evaluated.

APPROACH:
The biochemical characteristics of erythrocytes were studied before flight (at L-60 and L-30), during flight (Mission Day (MD) 14, MD 90 and MD 108), and postflight on R+0 and R+9 (days after landing) on three astronauts. Before and after flight the studies were performed using intact and frozen erythrocytes and whole blood, whereas during flight only frozen erythrocyte samples were collected. The erythrocytes were obtained from venous blood stabilized with EDTA, which was centrifuged and then frozen at -20 degrees Celsius until analysis.

To analyze the changes in energy metabolism, oxidation-reduction system, and the condition of the plasma membrane, a series of parameters was determined:

  • Energy metabolism was determined by content of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG), glycolysis rate, activity of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and hexokinase (HK).

  • The oxidation-reduction system was determined by the content of reduced glutathione and glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity.

  • The condition of plasma membrane was evaluated based on parameters describing the lipid and phospholipid composition and the activity of the transport ATPases for sodium ions (Na+), potassium ions (K+), calcium ions (Ca++), and magnesium ions (Mg++).

    The metabolic indices were assayed using spectrophotomeric techniques. Lipid and phospholipid composition were studied with thin-layer chromatography, and the extraction was performed by the method of Bligh and Dyer. The transport ATPase activity was based on the decrease in inorganic phosphate content associated with ATP dephosphorylation in the incubation medium at +38 degrees Celsius.

    RESULTS:
    Glutathione levels and ATPase activity could not be determined for the samples taken on MD 14. Also, hexokinase activity was not determined for samples taken on MD 90, MD 108 and postflight on R+0 and R+9 due to an insufficient amount of cell material.

    The analyzed data showed that, starting from MD 14, the ATP level decreased, mainly in one subject, and the activity of glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase decreased in all three subjects. This effect, as well as a decline in the intracellular ATP content, may indicate a decrease in cellular resistance. This suggestion is also confirmed by data about plasma membrane characteristics. In particular, the activity for Na+, K+, Ca++ ATPases were declined, which may have been caused by changes in the membrane’s physical and chemical properties and in the composition of its main components, the lipids and proteins.

    The study of lipid and phospholipid composition of the membranes revealed significant changes in the cholesterol content, which was increased in all crewmembers inflight and postflight, starting on MD 14 and was still elevated on R+9 in all three crewmembers. While the phospholipid content of the membrane remained practically at the same level, the elevated cholesterol content indicated a change in the membrane’s phase state -- an increase in the membrane’s rigidity and a possible reduction of its deformability.

    Postflight, the ATP level and the glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity were increased in all three crewmembers compared to inflight data. Also, the Na+, K+, and Ca++ ATPase activity was increased. Elevated lactate levels measured on R+0 indicated the prevalence of anaerobic processes.

    On R+9 virtually all parameters were within the normal range except for cholesterol content and reduced glutathione content in two subjects. The membrane cholesterol levels of these two subjects remained elevated and the glutathione content was significantly decreased.

    Overall, the results of this investigation showed significant inflight changes in erythrocyte metabolism and membrane condition for all subjects. The observed destabilization of the cell membrane may have resulted from changes in the blood plasma, caused by shifts in hormone levels, electrolyte balance and lipid metabolism. But direct effects of space flight on the quality of erythrocytes cannot be excluded.

experiment_title: The Space Environment Causes Acceleration of Vascular Aging: Roles of Hypogravity, Nutrition and Radiation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Data indicate that many International Space Station (ISS) crewmembers experience an acceleration of changes to their veins and arteries that are similar to those of aging populations. Emerging research is pointing towards linkages among cardiovascular health risk, carotid artery aging, bone metabolism and blood biomarkers, insulin resistance and radiation. This study is expected to provide insights into the mechanisms of cardiovascular aging and diabetes development. Specific objectives are to:
  1. Identify the mechanism(s) of increased arterial stiffness
  2. Determine if insulin resistance develops during spaceflight and identify the cardio-metabolic consequences
  3. Identify the interactions between cardio-metabolic health and bone metabolism
  4. Identify the interactions between radiation and vascular health in spaceflight

APPROACH:
Testing for this experiment will include an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), blood sampling (two blood draws several days apart), 24-hr blood pressure monitoring, a 72 hour data collection using the Bio-Monitor Smart Shirt, and resting ultrasounds of the arteries.

Preflight, between 90 and 60 days (L-90 to L-60 days) prior to launch, each test will be performed once.

Inflight, each test will be performed twice, once early in the mission between 20 and 40 days (L+20 to L+40 days) after launch, and again later in the mission between 30 days and 1 day (R-30 to R-1 days) prior to return to Earth.

Postflight, the OGTT will be performed twice, once between 9 and 11 days (R+9 to R+11 days) after return to Earth and again at R+6 months. Blood sampling will be performed three times at R+0 days, between R+3 and R+4 days, and at R+6 months. 24 hour blood pressure monitoring will be done twice, once at R+5 days and again at R+6 months. Resting ultrasound will be performed twice, first at R+3 or R+4 days, and again at R+6 months.

Some sessions are identical to sessions included in the Vascular_Echo experiment. When a crewmember is enrolled in both this study and Vascular_Echo, the sessions will be performed once and shared between the two experiments.

Ultrasounds of the arteries will provide information on stiffness and aging. Blood samples will provide measurements of circulating bone biomarkers. The oral glucose tolerance test will provide information on early-onset insulin resistance. Wearable sensors will provide accompanying fitness and activity information. Data collected by other experiments and shared will include body mass, radiation, medications, and physical fitness evaluations.

RESULTS:
This experiment is in progress and results are not yet available. This is an international experiment. NASA does not currently have an agreement with international space partners to archive their data in the LSDA.

experiment_title: Evaluation of the Medical Food, Enterade-R, as a Radiation Countermeasure for Enteric Dysfunction
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Radiation-induced gastrointestinal (GI) toxicity and the corresponding symptoms of nausea and vomiting are of particular concern on a space flight of extended duration. However, research on emesis and antiemetics has been limited, partly because common laboratory animals, e.g., rats and mice, do not vomit. Pica, the eating of nonnutritive substances, is an illness-response behavior in rodents that is indicative of emesis. Previous work has focused on pica models, ion flux, and mineral loss studies to help better understand the effect of Enterade on GI responses to low-dose gamma- and proton radiation. To meet the needs of cancer patients, as well as astronauts experiencing radiation-induced nausea and vomiting, the investigator team developed Enterade—a modified elemental rehydration solution composed of nine selected amino acids. These studies have shown that Enterade, which is undergoing clinical trials in two locations, (1) increases electrolyte absorption; (2) improves the mucosal barrier mechanism; (3) decreases anion and fluid secretions; (4) decreases osmotic diarrhea; and (5) improves appetite by decreasing nausea and vomiting and controlling the symptoms of GI toxicity.

APPROACH:
To examine absorption patterns, in vivo perfusion models of the gut were used in conjunction with various mineral isotopes in the presence or absence of gamma- or proton radiation, and with or without Enterade treatment. Mineral isotope levels in the lumen perfusate and plasma were assessed. In addition, chamber studies using specific mineral isotopes were performed using non-, proton-, or gamma-irradiated ileal tissues. Furthermore, intestinal tissues from irradiated mice show radiation dose-dependent increases in the Cl- channel anoctamin 1 (ANO1), a key transporter mediating radiation-induced diarrhea. Investigators performed MS/MS analysis and validated the identity of the protein.

RESULTS:
In irradiated mice, Enterade treatment resulted in decreased kaolin intake (pica), improved fluid intake, and improved body weight with effects comparable to those of ondansetron, as well as improved radiological clearance and lung function. Proton and gamma radiation both caused anion secretion, but differed in induction of intracellular Ca2+- and cAMP-mediated chloride secretion. In preliminary studies, investigators observed radiation dose-dependent stool loss of zinc, magnesium, copper, and phosphorus with proton radiation, and Enterade reduced proton radiation-induced stool loss of zinc.

experiment_title: Microprobe Analyses of Epiphyseal Plates from Spacelab 3 Rats
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Ultrastructural studies of epiphyseal plates from young rats flown aboard Cosmos 1129 showed that production and mineralization of matrix vesicles were delayed in flight rats. Also, the matrix of metaphyseal trabeculae contained fewer collagen fibers than did the matrix of ground controls, and the collagen was less mature as shown by smaller fiber size and lack of banding. A comprehensive analysis of plate and zone height was not carried out but no apparent difference was seen in height of zones or numbers of cells per zone. This study was to determine if differences in bone matrix formation could be observed after seven days in microgravity.

Approach:

Proximal tibial epiphyseal plates were dissected from right tibias of six flight and six control rats and prepared for microprobe analysis using a freeze substitution method. Measurements of matrix composition were made in longitudinal septi of each of the four zones: resting, proliferative, hypertrophic, and calcifying. Na, Mg, P, Ca, and K distributions were among the parameters measured. Portions of these plates were also analyzed extensively by light and electron microscopy to detect differences in height and cell number per plate and zone, as well as ultrastructure of collagens, proteoglycan granule size and number per area, and matrix vesicle distribution.

Results:

In control plates, all zones had high levels of Na, and in unmineralized regions, low levels of Mg, P, and Ca. K and S levels were high and increased from the proliferative to the calcifying zones. The level of P rose in the mineralized regions of the matrix and Ca/P ratios ranged from 1.2-1.4. In contrast, flight animals had very low Na and K values; Mg levels were unaffected. S levels were less than half of control values, and Ca values were less in both unmineralized and mineralized regions, although the Ca/P ratio was similar to that of controls. These data indicate that even a short space flight can alter bone mineralization, and that the primary defect is at the level of initial matrix production. Data is consistent with other flight studies, and in contrast to the increased matrix formation seen in studies of embryonic limbs centrifuged in vitro. Less matrix formation is also consistent with analyses of growth plate height and the hypothesis that decreased gravity causes decreased differentiation.

experiment_title: Animal Studies on Spacelab-3
experiment_description:
Objectives:

NASA-Ames undertook the first of several missions using animals as model mammalian systems with which to delineate the fundamental mechanisms of physiological response to an environment; i.e., microgravity. The primary objective of the Spacelab-3 mission was to evaluate the ability of the Research Animal Holding Facility (RAHF) to maintain animals in a normal, laboratory environment in space. It also provided the opportunity to obtain preliminary data on animal health and well being in flight as well as to sample selected physiological parameters which might be the focus of future flight experiments.

Approach:

Two monkeys and two groups of twelve rats each were flown in the primate and rodent cage modules of the RAHF, respectively. It was important to select an animal that grows normally, behaves normally, and is free from chronic stress. One group of rats was composed of twelve-week-old adults and the other group was composed of juveniles about eight weeks old. Four of the large rats were implanted with a transmitter, which permitted the continuous monitoring of EKG, heart rate and deep-body temperature. Food and water consumption, activity, and intermittent photographic records were obtained automatically and temperature, humidity, and light cycles were all controlled via the RAHF. Animals spent one hour in the Spacelab prior to launch, and rodents were not sacrificed until twelve hours following recovery. More extensive studies were performed by various investigators on the rats, following biosample distribution.

Results:

Data indicate that the RAHF was able to maintain both rats and monkeys in a relatively normal condition suitable for their use as experimental animals. Both monkeys ate less food and were less active in space than on the ground. One animal appeared to maintain relatively normal eating behavior throughout the mission, while the other showed abnormally low food consumption for the first four days followed by substantial recovery during the last three days. Videotape records were consistent with the conclusion that the latter animal may have suffered from space motion sickness. Heart rate monitored in flight rats was lower at all times, but its circadian rhythm was unchanged from that of preflight. Mean body temperature was not changed; however, its rhythm was increased inflight, suggesting that microgravity may cause body-temperature rhythm to become free-running. Growth parameters and several indices of chronic stress suggested that changes in bone and muscle were a result of exposure to microgravity per se and not an artifact resulting from adverse housing conditions. It is apparent that microgravity induces a wide range of physiological changes.

experiment_title: Lower Body Negative Pressure - Countermeasure Against Postflight Orthostatic Intolerance
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
During space flight, astronauts experience a headward fluid shift due to the absence of gravity. This fluid redistribution is associated with many physiological changes, such as cardiovascular deconditioning and reduced blood volume. These changes have the potential to cause problems when astronauts return to Earth's 1-G environment, such as orthostatic hypotension when standing, which may result in presyncopal or syncopal symptoms.

Previous studies have shown that after 1-2 weeks of bed rest, ingestion of a 1-liter salt water solution during 4 hours of continuous exposure to 30 mmHg lower body negative pressure (LBNP) will protect orthostatic function and blood volume for up to 24 hours. It was hypothesized that a similar countermeasure would reduce the effects of fluid loss induced by headward fluid shift during space flight. The inflight countermeasure, LBNP combined with salt and fluid ingestion, is intended as a single application, end-of-mission treatment to pre-adapt the cardiovascular system to orthostatic stress exposure during and after reentry, landing and cabin egress. The objective of this experiment was to evaluate the efficacy of the proposed countermeasure in reversing the effects of microgravity in the cardiovascular system. This investigation also documented additional cardiovascular responses to graded simulated orthostasis in space flight, including leg volume and total peripheral resistance changes.

APPROACH:
Four crewmembers participated in the study; they were divided into two groups, countermeasure and control. Preflight and postflight collection sessions were performed in the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Cardiovascular Laboratory, and landing day collection occurred at Edwards Air Force Base. Medical monitoring and sample collection were provided by members of the investigative team.

Flight simulation baseline data collection sessions, at 6 and 3 months preflight, consisted of two 3-day repetitive sessions in which inflight LBNP procedures were followed. During these sessions, subjects performed the complete inflight experiment. No blood or urine collection occurred during these sessions.

The preflight supplemental baseline data collection occurs at L-30, L-10, and L-5. This required all participating subjects to undergo a single response test on each specified day. For each test, subjects provided a 24-hour urine specimen for analysis of electrolytes (Na, K, Cl) and hormones (ADH, aldosterone, epinephrine, norepinephrine) important in fluid regulation. Additionally, a blood sample was drawn, pre- and post- ramp for blood volume (hematocrit, hemoglobin), electrolyte, and hormone level determinations.

Inflight, LBNP permitted both testing and countermeasure protocols to be employed. A collapsible LBNP device (LBNPD) was used for all inflight decompressions. The American Flight Echocardiograph (AFE) was used to obtain and electrocardiogram (ECG) and generate a 2-dimensional image of the heart using ultrasound. The Automatic Blood Pressure System (ABPS) measured heart rate and blood pressure and provided output consisting of ECG, Korotoff sounds, cuff pressure, and the vacuum signal from the LBNP controller. The Central Venous Pressure Device (CVPD), an ultrasound probe which is pressed lightly over the jugular vein, was used to document blood flow and estimate central venous pressure. Calf measurements were obtained during LBNP using the Ultrasonic Limb Plethysmograph in which electrodes are attached to the crewmember's leg. The Stocking (Leg) Plethysmograph was used to determine leg circumference that was later calculated into leg volume.

LBNP response tests or "ramps", were conducted three times inflight over four flight days (4,5,6, and 7) for each subject. The control subjects performed a single ramp (flight day 4). During this test, 6 minutes of baseline data were collected, after which the pressure was decreased in 10 mmHg steps every 3 minutes until a pressure of -50 mmHg was attained. After 3 minutes at -50 mmHg, the vacuum was released and 3 minutes of recovery data were collected. ECG, cardiac dimensions, and calf dimensions were monitored continuously, and BP was taken every minute of the ramp. Leg volume was measured immediately before and after each ramp.

The LBNP countermeasure protocol, called "soak", was conducted once inflight ( on either flight day 4 or 5) for each participating crewmember. After 6 minutes of baseline data collection, the pressure was decreased in 10 mmHg steps every 3 minutes until -50 mmHg was attained. The vacuum was then reduced to -30 mmHg for the soak period and maintained for 225 minutes. During the first hour, the subjects ingested salt tablets (8 grams total) and four beverage containers of water (128 ounces total). ECG and BP were continuously monitored for 10 minutes at scheduled times every hour. In addition, one BP measurement was taken every 15 minutes throughout the soak. After the 4-hour treatment, the pressure was reduced in 10 mmHg steps every 3 minutes until -50 mmHg was attained. After 3 minutes at this pressure, the vacuum was released and 6 minutes of recovery data was collected. ECG, cardiac dimensions and calf dimensions were monitored continuously; BP measurements were made every minute.

Postflight data collection occurred at R+0 (landing day), R+1, R+3, and R+5 days. Each collection session included one ramp test on both inflight countermeasure subjects and the two control subjects. Urine and blood sample collection on participating subjects followed the same protocol as the preflight supplemental data collection.

RESULTS:
The results present a summary of 12 subjects from six shuttle missions (STS-32, STS-43, STS-44, STS-42, STS-50, and STS-47). Valuable data on the time course of the loss of orthostatic tolerance were collected on almost all crewmembers. However, data applicable to the evaluation of the countermeasure were obtained on only 4 (including both Spacelab -J participants) on the 12 subjects.

HR increased significantly between preflight and early inflight ramp tests, but remained unchanged between the early inflight and pretreatment tests. One day after treatment, HR was significantly decreased compared to the pretreatment test and not significantly different from the preflight value. Two days after treatment, HR was returning toward the pretreatment value, but significantly different from the preflight value.

In conclusion, LBNP treatment restored heart rate responses to simulated orthostatic stress one day after treatment toward preflight values. Increased leg volume after treatment was no greater than after the brief LBNP tests, indication that fluid retention in the legs was probably not a major contributor to the treatment's effectiveness. Partial cardiovascular protection was still present two days after the treatment. Incomplete treatments (LBNP without fluid loading, or fluid loading without four hours of LBNP) are not effective (confirming bed rest findings).
