experiment_title: Solid Tumor Risk Estimation: Incorporating Intercellular Interaction Effects
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Under this NSCOR grant, investigators made a number of findings that help provide a mechanistic framework for biologically-based risk models. Investigators requested and received a cost extension to finish off experimental characterization of proton and iron irradiation studies to address angiogenesis processes that are important in radiation carcinogenesis and can be viewed as bottlenecks to carcinogenesis advancement. The significance of this in the carcinogenesis risk context lies in the challenge it presents to the standard radiogenic cancer paradigm. This paradigm holds that cancer may be understood as an autonomous expansion of an initiated cell clone, followed by the chance genetic creation of a cancer cell in that clone that then inevitably expands to become a diagnosed cancer. At the basis of these events is thought to be the DNA lesion. Investigators argue that essential population-level and tumor-environmental dynamics can alter this picture dramatically, either promoting cancer development or slowing the course of existing cancers. Their basis extends beyond DNA damage to include the familiar “hallmarks” of cancer that constitute “bottlenecks” to tumor advancement – population-level logistic growth effects, acquisition of angiogenic potential, and competency for invasion, to name three. Investigators have shown that radiation can progress or limit cancers by modifying these bottlenecks. Because these bottlenecks may be significant enough to increase the likelihood of transforming an initiated cell, or to change the likelihood an existing cancer advances to clinical detection over a lifetime, they must be included in the overall assessment of radiogenic cancer risk. It follows that existing models that fail to include such bottleneck effects are inherently flawed in that they do not include all radiation actions bearing on the development of manifest cancer disease.

APPROACH:
Proton-induced gene regulation was investigated in a number of human cell types that actively contribute to carcinogenesis progression, including not only cancer cells but also primary non- transformed stromal and microvascular endothelial cells. A baseline was obtained by analysis of the proton-induced global gene expression signature in the primary human non-transformed cells. Both human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLMVEC) and normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHDF) were irradiated (0Gy and 2Gy) and genome-wide array analysis was performed on RNA isolated six hours after proton exposure.

RESULTS:
Investigations to this end show that cancer-progression-modifying tumor-host interactions indeed occur at a number of levels, including: 1) reduction of angiogenesis by protons, with enhancement by 56Fe (similar to gamma); 2) reduction in the ability of both targeted and non-targeted cells to invade following proton exposures; in contrast with 3) augmentation in ability of tumor and host stromal cells to follow chemotactic stimuli following exposure to 56Fe ions; 4) Reduction in support for tumor proliferation and survival following proton radiation; effects opposite to 5) the stimulation of support for tumor proliferation and survival observed with 56Fe (and gamma). In addition, 6) mouse age generally, as differentially modified by radiation, was found to have a significant effect on cancer progression. Lastly, investigating the potential influence of intercellular interactions within the tumor on radiation modulation of cancer progression, investigators found that 7) cell-cell interactions among the cancer stem cell (CSC) and non-stem tumor compartments, known to be differentially affected by radiation, can critically affect carcinogenesis course.

1) Reduction of angiogenesis by protons, with enhancement by 56Fe (similar to gamma):
Using pan-genomic arrays, expression of key pro-angiogenic and inflammation-associated genes including VEGF-1A, C-MYC, IL-8, and IL-6, were found generally to be downregulated by protons (1GeV). RT-PCR reconfirmed this down-regulatory trend for a number of specific angiogenesis-regulating genes, including VEGF, IL-8, HIF-1A, and IL-6, c-MYC, FGFR1 and ANGPT1, in human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLMVEC), normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHCF), and A549 lung carcinoma 6 hours after receiving doses of sizes 0.5, 1 and 2Gy. In contrast, when the fibroblast, endothelial and tumor cells were gamma-irradiated at the same doses, the expressions of VEGF, IL-8, HIF-1A and IL-6, were upregulated in a dose-dependent manner relative to control (0Gy) 6hr post-irradiation.

Having established the proton-induced downregulation of these angiogenic genes (6 hours post-irradiation), regulation of the corresponding proteins was examined. ELISA assays specific for VEGF and IL-8 were performed after irradiation of endothelial (HLMVEC), fibroblast (NHDF) and tumor (A549) cultures. At 24h hours post-irradiation, levels of secreted IL-8 in the culture supernatants were reduced by 31% and 50% in endothelium and tumor cells respectively. Secreted VEGF was also significantly reduced in proton-irradiated fibroblast (17%) and tumor cells (34%) versus sham-irradiated controls (although results with endothelial cells were indeterminate). These findings indicate a dose-dependent downregulation of important angiogenic genes and, for the most part, a significant reduction in protein levels following proton irradiation.

For comparison, 56Fe-induced gene regulation was investigated in the same cell types as for protons. Again, a baseline was obtained by analysis of the iron ion-induced global gene expression signature in the primary human non-transformed cells. Both human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLMVEC) and normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHDF) were irradiated (0, 0.2, 0.4, and 1Gy) and genome-wide array analysis was performed on RNA isolated 6 hours after radiation (or sham) exposure. Expression of key pro-angiogenic and inflammation-associated genes including, VEGF-1A, C-MYC, IL-8, and IL-6, were found to be upregulated. The expression patterns of a number of the angiogenesis-regulating genes, including: VEGF, IL-8, HIF-1A, IL-6, c-MYC, FGFR1 and ANGPT1 were again investigated using quantitative RT-PCR. Results from the quantitative assessment of a number of these genes are shown. Significant upregulation of expression was observed for these genes in both the irradiated HLMVEC and NHDF cells, compared to sham-irradiated controls (p<0.05). To further investigate the ability of 56Fe ion irradiation to upregulate specific pro-angiogenic genes, expression levels were also investigated in human lung adenocarcinoma (A549). Just as for primary human fibroblast and endothelial cells, these cancer cells also showed upregulation of VEGF, IL-8, IL-6 and HIF-1A, at 6hr post-irradiation.

2) Reduction in the ability of both targeted and non-targeted cells to invade following proton exposures:
Beyond the suppression of genes critical in angiogenesis, investigators determined that proton irradiation could also suppress the ability of cells to invade under chemoattractant conditions in vitro. The invasion of the proton-irradiated endothelial, fibroblast, and tumor cells was investigated using a matrigel invasion assay. Compared with untreated controls, proton-irradiated cells (2Gy) showed significantly reduced invasion through the matrigel extracellular matrix. Quantification of the results demonstrated that following proton irradiation, the invasive capacity of A549, NHDF and HLMVEC cells was reduced, by 46, 15 and 14% respectively.

Next, the invasion/migration of endothelial (HLMVEC) in response to soluble factors produced by either proton-irradiated fibroblast (NHDF) or proton-irradiated tumor cells (A549) was analyzed. In an effort to mimic the crosstalk that occurs under in vivo conditions between fibroblast, cancer cells and microvascular endothelial cells, a co-culture transwell chamber system was used. Irradiated or sham-irradiated tumor or fibroblast cells were seeded in the lower chamber. The upper chamber used was an invasion chamber in which untreated endothelial cells were seeded. Since it is known that both fibroblast and cancer cells produce angiogenic factors (e.g. VEGF) that chemoattract endothelial cells, investigators studied how proton irradiation would alter this paracrine interaction. Compared to the matched sham-irradiated cell populations, both the 2-Gy proton-irradiated fibroblasts and tumor cells were less effective (19% and 16% respectively) at inducing endothelial cells to invade and traverse to the underside of the membrane. They propose that the reduced invasion of endothelial cells was, in part, a direct consequence of the demonstrated reduced secretion of angiogenic factors from the proton-irradiated cells. Indeed, addition of either recombinant VEGF or IL-8 to the irradiated compartment counteracted the anti-migratory effect of proton irradiation.

3) Augmentation in ability of tumor and host stromal cells to follow chemotactic stimuli following exposure to 56Fe ions:
Extending the finding of increased expression of genes critical in angiogenesis, investigators determined that iron ion irradiation could also augment the ability of cells to invade under chemoattractant conditions in vitro. Thus far, the invasion of the iron ion-irradiated fibroblast (NHDF) and tumor (A549) cells has been investigated using a matrigel invasion assay. Compared with untreated controls, iron ion-irradiated cells (0.2Gy) showed significantly increased invasion through the matrigel extracellular matrix; even more so than 1Gy. Quantification of the results demonstrated that, following 0.2Gy iron ion irradiation, the invasive capacity of A549 and NHDF cells was increased by 47% and 18% respectively.

Investigators next analyzed the invasion/migration of HLMVEC in response to soluble factors produced by either iron ion-irradiated A549 or iron ion-irradiated NHDF cells. In an effort to mimic the crosstalk which occurs under in vivo conditions between fibroblast, cancer cells and micro-vascular endothelial cells, a co-culture transwell chamber system was used. Irradiated or sham-irradiated A549 or NHDF cells were seeded in the lower chamber. The upper chamber used was an invasion chamber in which untreated HLMVEC cells were seeded. Since it is known that both fibroblast and cancer cells produce angiogenic factors (e.g. VEGF) that are chemoattractant to endothelial cells, investigators studied how iron-ion irradiation would alter this paracrine interaction. They found that, compared to the matched sham-irradiated cell populations, both the 0.2-Gy iron-irradiated fibroblast and tumor cells were more effective at inducing endothelial cells to traverse to the underside of the membrane.

Investigators hypothesized in this case that increased secretion of angiogenic factors from the iron ion-irradiated cells was responsible for the increased invasion of endothelial cells. Addition of small molecule inhibitor of VEGF, SU11248 to the irradiated compartment counteracted the pro-migratory effect of iron ion irradiation.

Invasion of tumor (A549), fibroblast (NHDF) and human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLVMEC) towards conditioned media from 56Fe-exposed cells was also analyzed. A dose-dependent upregulation in invasion was observed. Interestingly, breaking this trend was a dramatic upregulation of invasion of fibroblast cells towards CM from tumor cells irradiated at 0.2Gy, and a downregulation of tumor cells towards CM from LMEC cells irradiated at 0.2Gy. As a matter deserving further investigation, an upward deviation in the vicinity of 0.2Gy from linearity has been consistently noted for the pro-progression effect of 56Fe radiation.

4) Reduction in support for tumor proliferation and survival following proton radiation:
To investigate the modulation of additional aspects of tumor progression by proton radiation, the ability of endothelial (HLMVEC) cells to proliferate was examined in a transwell co-culture assay with proton-irradiated or sham-irradiated tumor (A549) or fibroblast (NHDF) cells. Cancer cells are already known to secrete pro-angiogenic factors e.g. VEGF and IL-8 that can recruit endothelial cells and stimulate their proliferation. Decreased cell proliferation was observed for endothelial cells sharing media with proton-irradiated fibroblasts or proton-irradiated cancer cells, but not for endothelial cells sharing media with the sham-irradiated matched controls. In contrast, when this same assay was conducted using photon-irradiated fibroblast or tumor cells, an increased, rather than a decreased, proliferation of endothelial cells was observed.

Next examined was the degree to which proton-irradiated cells (cancer, fibroblast, or endothelial), plated in the upper chambers of transwell plates modulates the proliferation of fibroblast or endothelial cells in the lower chambers. A measurable reduction in proliferation of both fibroblasts and endothelial cells associated with proton-irradiated cancer cells was detected compared to that of controls. Investigators further investigated whether addition of the angiogenic factors VEGF or IL-8 could restore the original proliferation capacity. The proton radiation-induced reduction in responding cell proliferation was partially ameliorated by the addition of VEGF (20ng/ml) or IL-8 (20ng/ml) to the irradiated cell compartment (normalized to sham-irradiated controls). The data suggests that proton-induced suppression of these specific angiogenic factors may well play a direct role in inhibiting adjacent cell proliferation. Such proton-induced suppression of cell proliferation could well have ramifications for treatment optimization. The reduction in proliferation/survival was most pronounced for the NHDF stromal fibroblasts that shared media with 2Gy-irradiated tumor cells. Proliferation levels of the fibroblast cells that shared media through transwells with proton-irradiated tumor cells were less than 50% of their matched fibroblast controls that shared media with sham-irradiated tumor cells. In line with other growth factor rescue experiments, addition of recombinant VEGF or IL-8 partially restored the proliferation levels to 71% and 90% respectively. Similar results were observed for the other cell combinations.

To ascertain the dose dependence of survival of endothelial (HLMVEC), fibroblast (NHDF), or tumor (A549) cells, and whether proton-irradiation induced inhibition of IL-8 might actually contribute to the radiation sensitivity of these cells, clonogenic assays were performed with or without the addition of recombinant human IL-8 (20ng/ml). Cells were irradiated at 1, 2 and 4Gy of protons. It was found that treatment of cells with recombinant IL-8 significantly spared the 2-Gy proton irradiated cells from clonogenic inhibition. The SF2 (survival fraction after 2Gy) of proton and photon/gamma (results not shown) was found to be 0.68 and 0.78 respectively, with the cell killing effect of proton being slightly higher than that of photon radiation.

5) Stimulation of support for tumor proliferation and survival observed with 56Fe (and gamma):
The ability of the HLMVEC cells to proliferate was examined in a transwell co-culture assay with iron ion irradiated or sham-irradiated A549 tumor (or NHDF fibroblast) cells. Contrary to protons, increased cell proliferation was observed for endothelial cells sharing media with iron ion-irradiated fibroblasts or iron ion-irradiated cancer cells, but not for endothelial cells sharing media with the sham-irradiated matched controls.

6) Mouse age generally, as differentially modified by radiation, and was found to have a significant effect on cancer progression:
Tumor progression dynamics for young (Y) and middle-aged (MA) mice, with or without iron irradiation at 1GeV/u, were studied for LLC implanted in syngeneic C57BL/6 mice with and without 5x0.2Gy of iron irradiation. Progression was gauged in terms of two quantities: tumor growth rates after approximately exponential growth starts, and “effective” initial tumor volumes, which is proposed to account for differential tumor/stromal “reorganization” times following injection and before growth of the tumor mass.

To do this, the two quantitative aspects of tumor development just mentioned were taken to be the growth rate c and the “effective initial tumor volume” b, obtained by extrapolating the fitted exponential curve backwards to time zero and interpreted as mainly a measure of either stromal incorporation into the tumor, or how supportive the microenvironment was prior to the near exponential growth phase. Growth data were fitted to V = b*exp(ct), with b the geometric mean of the b’s for individual mouse fits, and c the arithmetic mean of the c’s for individual mouse fits.

The data show generally that tumor growth rates are dependent on host age, and that there was a statistically significant decrease in average growth rates c for the unirradiated middle age (MA) as compared to the unirradiated young (Y) hosts, with only a modest increase in the effective initial volume. As regards perturbation by irradiation, the following results were found: i) the effective initial volume b was very significantly decreased by irradiation in both young (Y) and middle-aged (MA) mice; ii) the overall progression decrease by irradiation in the young (Y) mice was due exclusively to a dramatic decrease in effective initial volume; while iii) the more modest decrease in progression by irradiation in middle-aged (MA) mice was due to a slight increase in growth rate compensating for a substantial decrease in effective initial volume; and iv) modest decreases in both average growth rates and effective initial volumes were noted for irradiated middle-aged (MA) mice compared to irradiated young (Y) mice.

To gain some molecular-level understanding, protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks were constructed from the gene array data. Demonstrated were highly regulated protein interactions for tumors of the young (Y) iron-irradiated mice compared with those of the unirradiated groups and of the middle-aged (MA) iron-irradiated compared with those of the unirradiated groups. Overall, the network based on data from tumors growing in irradiated versus unirradiated young (Y) mice demonstrated more regulation of activity than did the network based on data from tumors growing in the irradiated versus unirradiated middle-aged (MA) mice. The general directions of the significantly regulated proteins due to irradiation also coincided with the direction of regulations of genes; mostly down in young (Y) hosts, and a slight bias upward in the middle-aged (MA) hosts. As was also true for the gene regulations, iron irradiation induced a greater genetic response overall in young (Y) compared to middle-aged (MA) hosts.

Interestingly, two central network hubs, FASN (fatty acid synthase) and AKT1 genes, were found to be downregulated within the tumors of young (Y) mice in response to iron-irradiation. FASN is a key metabolic enzyme responsible for lipogenesis and it plays a central role in energy homeostasis. It has been shown that FASN can be highly expressed in aggressive and metastatic tumors. AKT1 is one of three homologous isoforms of the AKT (PKB) protein kinase family that control a wide variety of cellular functions including proliferation, survival, and metabolism. Given the wide range of pro-growth cellular functions AKT1 modulates, it is not surprising it is also implicated in tumor progression and metastases.

Using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) software, specific pathways were constructed around FASN and AKT1 that included those genes directly or indirectly up or down regulated for tumor samples from young (Y) or middle-age (MA) mice with and without iron irradiation. Comparisons between groups were done by calculating the log2-fold change, with increasing levels of up- (red) or down- (green) regulation indicated by the darker shades of the respective color and with grey indicating genes present in the network without a 2-fold change under the perturbation studied. In the case of young (Y) unirradiated versus irradiated mice, FASN is seen to be downregulated. By contrast, no FASN regulation was detected between the tumors from the middle-aged (MA) irradiated and unirradiated groups, consistent with the reduced degree of suppression of progression by irradiation noted for these hosts.

7) Cell-cell interactions among the cancer stem cell (CSC) and non-stem tumor compartments, known to be differentially affected by radiation, can critically affect carcinogenesis course:
In recent years cancer stem cells (CSCs) have been hypothesized to comprise only a minor subpopulation in solid tumors that drives tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis; the so-called "cancer stem cell hypothesis." While a seemingly trivial statement about numbers, much is put at stake. If true, the conclusions of many studies of cancer cell populations could be challenged, as the bulk assay methods upon which they depend have, by, and large, taken for granted the notion that a "typical" cell of the population possesses the attributes of a cell capable of perpetuating the cancer, i.e., a CSC. In support of the CSC hypothesis, populations enriched for so-called "tumor-initiating" cells have demonstrated a corresponding increase in tumorigenicity as measured by dilution assay, although estimates have varied widely as to what the fractional contribution of tumor-initiating cells is in any given population. Some have taken this variability to suggest the CSC fraction may be nearly 100% after all, countering the CSC hypothesis, and that there are simply assay-dependent error rates in the ability to "reconfirm" CSC status at the cell level. To explore this controversy more quantitatively, investigators developed a simple cellular automaton model of CSC-driven tumor growth dynamics. Assuming CSC and non-stem cancer cells (CC) subpopulations coexist to some degree, we evaluated the impact of an environmentally dependent CSC symmetric division probability and a CC proliferation capacity on tumor progression and morphology. Their model predicts, as expected, that the frequency of CSC divisions that are symmetric highly influences the frequency of CSCs in the population, but goes on to predict the two frequencies can be widely divergent, and that spatial constraints will tend to increase the CSC fraction over time. Further, tumor progression times show a marked dependence on both the frequency of CSC divisions that are symmetric and on the proliferation capacities of CC. Together, these findings can explain, within the CSC hypothesis, the widely varying measures of stem cell fractions observed. In particular, although the CSC fraction is influenced by the (environmentally modifiable) CSC symmetric division probability, with the former converging to unity as the latter nears 100%, the CSC fraction becomes quite small even for symmetric division probabilities modestly lower than 100%. In the latter case, the tumor exhibits a clustered morphology and the CSC fraction steadily increases with time; more so on both counts when the death rate of CCs is higher. Such variations in CSC fraction and morphology are not only consistent with the CSC hypothesis, but lend support to it as one expected byproduct of the dynamical interactions that are predicted to take place among a relatively small CSC population, its CC counterpart, and the host compartment over time.

Overall conclusions:
Cell-cell interactions between the tumor and host, and between tumor cell subcompartments, affect radiation-induced cancer progression, and thus cancer risk, in a highly radiation-quality-dependent fashion. Investigators focused on two radiation types, 56Fe and protons, and found them to generally encourage and discourage, respectively, a number of molecular and functional indicators of progression. This fact must be considered alongside the risks of cancer cell creation when making conclusions as to astronaut safety during long-term space flight. Closer to home, the favorable tumor-host dynamical effects noted for proton radiation in space may work to supplement its well-established physical attributes as a therapeutic modality.

experiment_title: Biochemical Changes in the Developing Wheat Seedling
experiment_description:
Objectives:

This experiment was designed to: 1) correlate changes in metabolism and energetics with the reorientation of plant organs during weightlessness; 2) to study the key enzymes associated with these processes; and 3) to determine if weightlessness retards any growth of the root and shoot because of a modification of protein synthesis and the incorporation of carbohydrates into cell wall constituents of endosperm of the wheat seedling.

Approach:

Seventy-eight wheat seedlings (38-39 mg) were surface sterilized in a 0.05% Hg Cl2 and soaked for three hours at 95 °F. The seedlings were then placed in polycarbonate stalks containing wet vermiculite. Gas samples were taken and lids were sealed. To determine the extent of root displacement and coleoptile curvature, pictures were taken postflight before the seedlings were divided for analysis. Tissue slices were analyzed for six enzymes, protein content, oxygen consumption, amino acids, and ethylene production. Growth on the clinostat simulated growth in the weightless environment; however only auxin-mediated reactions were simulated on the horizontal clinostat.

Results:

The growth of wheat seedlings appeared normal. Increased glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, glyceralderhyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, and peroxidase was noted. The increased enzyme activity was found to be physiologic and not due to structural changes in enzymes while in the weightless state. No significant differences were found in the carbohydrate distribution, starch, sucrose, glucose, total or protein nitrogen in endosperms. It was postulated that the orbital flight was not of sufficient duration to elicit a response. If weightlessness did show an effect on metabolism of the endosperm, it would theoretically be one of decreased starch and increased glucose and sucrose; a change in pattern of amino acids would occur, as demonstrated by either an increase or decrease in concentration. The data of these studies indicate that there is a change in the metabolic products of the wheat seedlings, but the altered distribution of these materials over time could not be detected in response to changes in gravitational alterations.

experiment_title: Monitoring Bone Health by Daily Load Stimulus Measurement during Lunar Missions
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
One of the key questions that remain unanswered as we prepare to send humans to other planetary surfaces is the degree to which living and exercising in these reduced gravity environments will provide an osteoprotective stimulus to prevent the loss of bone mineral density (BMD) that has been observed in microgravity. The concept of daily load stimulus is useful in this regard since it has the potential to estimate the "dose" of load to the lower extremities that will maintain skeletal integrity even in the setting of concurrent therapeutic drug and exercise countermeasures. Most observers believe that some form of supplementary exercise will be required activity on the moon, Mars, or nearby asteroid, but this will need to be optimized to provide the most efficient use of crew time. Given the continued loss of BMD observed in crewmembers after long-duration flights, this amount of loaded exercise is likely not enough to preserve an acceptable amount of bone strength.

The Specific Aims of the project were to:
1) Develop hardware based on Micro Electro Mechanical Systems (MEMS) technology that can unobtrusively monitor the accelerations applied to the body and interface with an ambulatory monitor.
2) Extend the Daily Load Stimulus Algorithm to account for recent developments in bone mechanobiology, to incorporate accelerometric signals, and to write software to perform this analysis in real-time.
3) Demonstrate the feasibility and validity of the approach in 1g, in 1/6g in the eZLS, and in another analog.
4) Integrate the hardware and software into a package suitable for flight development.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the Results below.

RESULTS:
Key Findings:
1) COMPLETE DATA COLLECTION IN eZLS FACILITY: The largest human study to date has been completed in the Exercise Countermeasures Laboratory utilizing the eZLS facility at NASA Glenn Research Center. The activity monitoring system was tested at 1g, 3/8g, and 1/6g gravity loads in the eZLS during a variety of locomotor activities and functional tasks, including walking, running, loping, hopping, ladder climb, platform jump down, rock carry, obstacle course, static hopping, and squat exercise.

2) DEPLOY SOFTWARE UPDATES AND INCREASE DATA THROUGHPUT: A comprehensive analysis of the wireless communication protocol and software configuration was conducted. Software updates have resulted in more reliable communication and more consistent data logging.

3) COMPLETE DATA COLLECTION IN PARABOLIC FLIGHT: Data was successfully collected on nine subjects during parabolic flight campaigns in October 2012 and April 2013. However, neither campaign yielded a complete and successful data set. The investigators are tentatively approved for another flight campaign in 2014 where they hope they can get a full complement of parabolas and activities/configurations with all data components.

4) CONTINUED DATA ANALYSIS: Data analysis has been an on-going effort over the life of the project. Analysis of the data continues to suggest that the partial gravity environments of the moon or Mars will not alone be osteoprotective. Exercise will remain a necessary countermeasure in these environments. It is unclear what amount of loaded exercise is necessary to maintain optimal bone health. On-going work in this study will utilize the enhanced Daily Load Stimulus theory to help answer this question. It is certain that running in reduced gravity will still benefit from use of a subject load device to increase impact during locomotor exercises. Enhancements have been made to the activity programs to allow real-time reporting of daily activity and progress toward individual daily load stimulus target goals. NASA Glenn's Integrated Medical Model (IMM) team is exploring input of the jump down data into their bone fracture risk model, and with Joern Rittweger of the German Aerospace Association to explore the energy losses experienced during static, stiff-legged hopping in 1g, 3/8g, and 1/6g environments.

5) FLIGHT READINESS: The system performed well during parabolic flight testing. The sensors have successfully been interfaced with the Smartphone platform which can be used as a portable data logging system. Currently one sensor communicates with the phone at a time, and the feasibility of connecting two Bluetooth devices to one phone is being explored.

experiment_title: First Clinical Test of Feasibility of Ultrasound to Reposition Kidney Stones
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Ultrasonic propulsion is a new technology investigators have developed that uses focused ultrasound energy to transcutaneously reposition kidney stones. On Earth and in space, the use is to expel small stones from the kidney so they will pass naturally before requiring surgery or to prevent large stones in the kidney from obstructing and causing pain or requiring urgent surgery. On Earth, the technology could also be used to expel fragments remaining after surgery that may grow to cause recurrent symptoms.

APPROACH:
This study was funded by the National Space Biomedical Research Institute (NSBRI) without commercial involvement. Thirteen awake, non-anesthetized subjects were studied without restriction of patient body habitus, stone size, or stone location. Ultrasound imaging and a pain questionnaire were completed before, during, and following propulsion. An additional two subjects underwent stone repositioning during ureteroscopy (URS). All subjects were followed weekly for three weeks.

Investigative Procedures included: a) Prior to the ultrasound study, participants completed a baseline pain questionnaire. b) Participants underwent a diagnostic ultrasound examination by a certified sonographer. This verified the stone was visible on ultrasound and near the location identified on the most recent diagnostic imaging. c) A video of the ultrasound exam screen was recorded. Select images of the kidney anatomy and stone were also captured. d) Participants underwent stone pushing with the investigational device. The operator began with 50-V output and increased to 90-V as necessary. Patient feedback on discomfort was recorded after each of the first three pushes and when noted otherwise. e) A second video of the ultrasound image from the first frame of the Push to 15 frames after the Push, and listing of the system settings, including the target location and Push power, were recorded automatically to the system hard drive. The patient position, stone position, and result of the Push burst were recorded manually. There were three potential types of motion for each push pulse, 1) no motion, 2) moved but trapped within a confined space, such as a calyx, 3) translation of the stone to a new location. A fourth option was (U) unintended Push. The IDE limited a maximum of 40 push pulses in a single session. f) Participants underwent a second diagnostic ultrasound exam to confirm the location of the stone after treatment. A video of the exam was recorded, and select images of the kidney anatomy and stone were captured. g) Participants completed a second questionnaire at the completion of the exam addressing any discomfort or pain they may have felt related to the procedure. h) Research staff contacted the patients by telephone each week for three weeks and reviewed their charts weekly for 90 days to assess for acute colic events, stone passage, and/or additional intervention. i) Subjects who might pass stones were asked to screen their urine and after four weeks received a clinical ultrasound exam to assess location and number of remaining stones. Otherwise in subjects scheduled to undergo surgery following the procedure, ureteroscopy video and notes were saved relating the number, location, size, and tissue attachment of stones.

RESULTS:
Of the 15 subjects, 11 were male; average age was 56 ± 11 years; average body mass index (BMI) was 29 ± 3; and stone size range was dust to 13 mm. There were six left and 10 right kidneys treated. Two patients reported skin discomfort and sensation at depth with a few pushes. Otherwise, there was no pain or adverse effects associated with the treatment. Stones were localized with the system and repositioned in all but one subject. In total, the system targeted and repositioned stones from all parts of the kidney and ureteropelvic juncture (UPJ, kidney outflow tract) including the lower pole (20 targets), midpole (10 targets), upper pole (6 targets), and renal pelvis/UPJ (7 targets). In two subjects measurable displacement was only seen after pushes as the subjects rolled over on the table. Average skin-to-stone distance was 6.5 cm, as the probe was small enough to push under the ribs with subjects on their side; although when this was not possible, such as during URS, stones were imaged and repositioned at depths greater than 11 cm. Stones were repositioned to a new location in all six post-lithotripsy patients, while four of the six passed over 30 stone fragments within a few days of treatment. One passed two 2 mm fragments immediately after the completion of treatment. Of the two that did not pass stones, one subject felt pain consistent with passing a stone but did not observe stone passage. De novo stones and stones as large as 8 mm were repositioned in awake patients and during URS, although movement was not as great as seen with residual fragments. In four of the 15 subjects, what was noted in clinical imaging as a single, potentially unpassable stone was shown to be several passable stones upon repositioning with ultrasound.

experiment_title: In flight Assessment of Renal Stone Risk Factor
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objectives of this study were to evaluate the potential for increased risk of renal stone formation as a consequence of space flight, and to compare this stone-forming potential to that observed in normal subjects during bedrest.

APPROACH:
One male crewmember collected all of his urine voids during two 24-hour periods before flight and two 24-hour periods during flight. The Urine Collection System (UCS) was used to collect the in-flight samples. All samples were analyzed for urinary renal stone risk factors: hypercalciuria, hyperuricosuria, hyperoxaluria, and hypocitraturia.

RESULTS:
This DSO was complete after data were collected from 1 subject. It was then supplanted by DSO 610 in the Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project. Significant results were obtained in the latter study.

experiment_title: Effect of Sex on Orthostatic Intolerance and Cardiovascular Responses during Lunar Descent and Ascent
experiment_description:
Objectives
The Artemis missions to the Moon have initiated the development of the Human Landing System (HLS) to transport astronauts to and from the lunar surface. The risk of orthostatic intolerance (OI) and the cardiovascular responses experienced during lunar descent and ascent are important considerations in the development of the HLS. OI is characterized by a group of signs and symptoms that occur after assuming an upright posture, including lightheadedness, dizziness, visual changes, increased heart rate, sudden drops in systolic or diastolic blood pressure, and significant cardiac arrhythmias. Given that OI is a concern during re-exposure to normal gravity (1-G) even after short duration exposures to weightlessness and that crew may be in a standing posture in the vehicle during decent to and accent from the lunar surface, G-loads during the dynamic phases of the Artemis mission may be problematic for some individuals. OI when standing is apparent after just days of exposure to weightlessness and spaceflight analogs, and thus it is expected that OI may be a concern even during lunar descent. Furthermore, it is unlikely that the partial gravity exposure during stays on the lunar surface will be protective against OI during ascent from the surface.

There were no reports of symptoms consistent with OI during the Apollo missions. However, all the Apollo crewmembers were male with a history high performance aircraft experience, and almost all the commanders demonstrated high heart rates during sustained G-levels ranging from 0.4- to 0.6-G over ~9 min during lunar descent and ascent. The G-levels to which the Artemis astronauts will be exposed have not been defined, but it is likely that the G-levels will be greater and/or the exposures will be longer than those experienced by Apollo astronauts based upon the flight plan required to reach Gateway, which will be at a higher orbit than the Apollo Command and Service Module. Further, the proportion of women in the astronaut corps has been increasing and it has been publicly stated that the first Artemis mission to the lunar surface will include at least one woman; thus the effect of sex on the cardiovascular responses to acceleration should be considered with regard to lunar descent and ascent. In general, women have lower orthostatic tolerance and are more susceptible to post-spaceflight orthostatic intolerance when re-exposed to 1-G. However, it is unclear whether women also would be less able to the tolerate lower levels of acceleration that likely will be experienced during descent to and ascent from the lunar surface.

Lower body compression garments are one of the countermeasures that have been used to protect against OI after exposure to weightlessness. Specifically, NASA has developed the Orion Orthostatic Intolerance Garment (OIG) for the Artemis missions, but the suit's efficacy has not been demonstrated in women and men during long exposures (20 minutes) to simulated G-levels (0.5-, 0.75, 1.0-G) that astronauts may experience during lunar descent and ascent during the Artemis missions.

This study has the following aims

1. To determine whether there are differences between hypovolemic men and women in orthostatic tolerance (assessed by tilt time) and cardiovascular responses during 20 minutes of exposure to a range of gravity levels (0.50-, 0.75-, and 1.00-G) simulated by different angles of head-up tilt that Artemis astronauts might experience during descent to and ascent from the lunar surface.
2. To determine whether the Orion Orthostatic Intolerance Garment (OIG) will protect men and women against orthostatic intolerance (assessed by tilt time) and reduce the cardiovascular responses caused by exposure to the range gravity levels (0.50-, 0.75-, and 1.00-G) simulated by different angles of head-up tilt that Artemis astronauts might experience during descent to and ascent from the lunar surface.

Approach
19 men and 19 women will be recruited to complete this study. The participants will be similar to the astronaut population along important characteristics such as age, body mass index, and physical fitness. To complete the study, subjects will participate in two phases of testing.

Phase I will evaluate differences in OI between the sexes (Aim 1). During the first of two laboratory visits (1A), test operators will obtain anthropometric measurements to be used in the design and construction of an individualized Orion OIG, familiarize the subjects to the tilt test procedures, and measure the subject’s baseline plasma volume (carbon monoxide rebreathing method) and tolerance to 80° head-up tilt (1.00-G). During the second of two laboratory visits (2A), plasma volume will be measured prior to inducing hypovolemia through administration of a furosemide infusion (20 mg). Once hypovolemia is achieved, participants will be exposed to three 20-minute sessions of head-up tilt tests at 30° (0.50-G), 50° (0.75-G), and 80° (1-G) in a randomized order counterbalanced across subjects. During each tilt test, measurements that will be obtained while supine and during head-up tilt include brachial blood pressure, beat-to-beat finger blood pressure, and heart rate (ECG) and ultrasound parameters required to calculate stroke volume, cardiac output and total peripheral resistance. Hematocrit, hemoglobin, and carboxyhemoglobin will be measured from blood samples and used to calculate red blood cell volume, total blood volume, and plasma volume. Blood samples will be collected prior to each tilt test to calculate changes in plasma volume across the test day.

Phase II also will consist of two laboratory visits. During the first visit (2A), subjects will don the OIG constructed from the anthropometric measures obtained in visit 1A to ensure correct sizing. During the second visit (2B), plasma volume will be measured using the same carbon monoxide rebreathing method prior to inducing hypovolemia through administration of furosemide infusion. After hypovolemia is achieved, subjects will don the OIG, and will be assessed for orthostatic tolerance with compression garments using the same tilt test protocol as in phase I, with G-levels presented in the same order in which they were in visit 1B to avoid any potential confounding effects of order when comparing tilt results within subjects.

Results
It is expected that females will be more susceptible to OI and demonstrate a greater heart rate response when hypovolemic than males at 1-G (Phase I) and that differences between sexes (tolerance time and cardiovascular responses) will be less as simulated G-levels decrease. The findings from this phase of the study will provide additional detail to the HLS acceleration limits during the dynamic flight phases when astronauts are standing but not wearing compression garments. However, it is expected that all subjects will be able to tolerate the entire tilt duration when hypovolemic and using lower body compression garments (Phase II). The findings from this phase of the study will provide additional detail to the HLS acceleration limits during the dynamic flight phases when astronauts are standing, but wearing compression garments, particularly with regard to the duration of tolerance.

experiment_title: Hepatic Function in Rats After Spaceflight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Among the changes that have been observed during and after space flight are elevated adrenal steroid secretion and altered concentrations of various lipids and carbohydrates in blood and other tissues. Since the liver is an important site of nutrient and xenobiotic metabolism, further study of the effects of space flight on this organ appear warranted. Based on previous findings, it was proposed that several aspects of hepatic function are altered by space flight. In particular, these include key enzymes of cholesterol and sphingolipid biosynthesis and drug metabolism (e.g. cytochrome P-450). This study was to provide additional data from analyses of liver and serum samples from space-flown rats that support this hypothesis.

Approach:

To determine the possible biochemical consequences of prolonged weightlessness on liver function, tissue samples from flight and control rat were analyzed for hepatic protein, glycogen, and lipids as well as the activities of a number of key enzymes involved in metabolism of these compounds and xenobiotics.

Results:

Among the parameters measured, the major differences were elevations in the hepatic glycogen content and HMG-CoA reductase activities of the flight rats, and a decrease in the amount of microsomal cytochrome P-450 and the activity of aniline hydroxylase, a cytochrome P-450-dependent enzyme. Decreases in these two indices of the microsomal mixed-function oxidase system indicate that space flight may compromise the ability of liver to metabolize drugs and toxins. The higher HMG-CoA reductase correlated with elevated levels of serum cholesterol. Other changes included somewhat higher blood glucose, creatinine, SGOT, and much greater alkaline phosphatase and BUN. These results generally support the earlier observation of changes in these parameters. The importance of these alterations is not known; however, they have the potential to complicate long-term space flight.

experiment_title: Hepatic Enzymes of Sphingolipid and Glycerolipid Biosynthesis in Rats from Spacelab 3
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Lipid metabolism is a major function of liver, which synthesizes these molecules for membranes, bile and lipoproteins. The activity ratio of serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) and glycerol 3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT), the initial enzymes of sphingolipid and glycerolipid synthesis, is one determinant of tissue lipid composition. Since changes have been observed in some of the enzymes of lipid metabolism in livers from rats under weightless conditions aboard Cosmos, the activities of these key enzymes, SPT and GPAT, were studied in the rats of Spacelab-3.

Approach:

Microsomes from liver samples obtained from flight and control rats were assayed for SPT, GPAT, and protein. The amount of sphinogomyelin (SM) in liver was determined by extracting the phospholipids, performing thin-layer chromatography, and quantifying the phosphate in SM. Liver and body weights were considered in the analysis of hepatic metabolism.

Results:

SPT activities of flight rats were significantly lower (approximately half) than controls, whereas GPAT activities were not significantly different, nor were liver and body weights, nor weight change during the experiment. Microsomal protein for flight rats was 33% lower than controls and there were no differences observed in SM content. This may indicate that the major effects of altering the rate of long-chain base synthesis will be found in glycolipids, or that SM levels require longer to come to a new equilibrium, since this phospholipid is generally thought to have a slow turnover rate. These findings of specific changes in hepatic SM metabolism with space flight, though, suggest adjustments of cellular membranes to zero gravity. The observed decrease in flight SPT may reflect cellular adjustments to microgravity or yet unknown hormone changes that affect this pathway.

experiment_title: Red Cell Metabolism
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The use of a hyperoxic environment in the cabins of space vehicles increases the risk of toxic effects of hyperoxic exposure. Simulated and actual space-flight studies have demonstrated decreases in the red blood cell mass. However, it was not clear if these decreases were due to hyperoxia. Studies on animals and humans exposed to oxygen under high pressure indicated that hemolysis could develop due to peroxidation of unsaturated fatty acids in red blood cell membrane. The Skylab flights provided an opportunity to study the effects of hyperoxic exposure on the metabolism of red blood cells. The objective of experiment M114 was to determine the metabolic and cell membrane changes that occur in the human red blood cell as a result of exposure to weightlessness and the spacecraft environment.

APPROACH:
During the Gemini and Apollo missions, blood samples were retrieved only during the pre- and postflight periods, limiting study of the red blood cell system. In the Skylab program, blood samples were collected during all phases of the flight. The approach of Skylab experiment M114 was to analyze peroxidation of red blood cell lipids, enzymes of red blood cell metabolism, and levels of 2,3-diphosphoglyceric acid and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to determine if changes in these variables could be related to hemolysis and subsequent decrease in red blood cell mass. In addition, hemoglobin determination was made on blood samples by using the cyanmethemoglobin method.

RESULTS:
On Skylab 2, 3 and 4, no evidence of lipid peroxidation, a biochemical effect known to be associated with irreversible cell damage, was observed. In addition, changes in observed glycolytic intermediates and enzymes provided evidence of red blood cell damage. The mean data from Skylab 2 indicated an in-flight increase in hexokinase, pyruvate kinase, and glyceraldehyde phosphate dehydrogenase. Postflight there was a significant decrease of phosphofructokinase. Skylab 3 mean data indicated significant in-flight decreases of hexokinase, phosphoglyceric acid kinase, and acetylcholinesterase, and increases in pyruvate kinase. The Skylab 4 mean data indicated significant change only in phosphofructokinase during the early in-flight phase of the mission. The most consistent change noted was a decrease in phosphofructokinase, an enzyme susceptible to the effects of oxygen that is thought to be at the center of the Pasteur effect (the shift from anaerobic glycolysis to respiration, brought about by the presence of oxygen).

experiment_title: The Effects of Micro-Gravity on Bone Cell Cultures
experiment_description:
Objectives:

This experiment was a continuation of the studies begun on the NIH.C1 flight, to examine the possible effects of spaceflight and microgravity on a number of aspects of osteoblast cell growth and gene expression. Parameters to be assessed include glucose and lactate content as a measure of cell metabolism; collagen expression, accumulation, and extracellular matrix assembly; presence of non-collagenous proteins, including osteopontin, bone sialoprotein, osteocalcin, and others; and a definition of spatial and temporal events of mineralization. The studies will examine the hypothesis that unloading bone cells in spaceflight will result in altered bone matrix production and mineral formation.

Approach:

Cells were obtained from 17 day old embryonic chick calvaria, grown in Dulbecco's modified Eagle medium supplemented with 10% FBS and ultimately inoculated into hollow fiber cartridges of artificial capillary culture units (Cellco, Inc.). Unlike the protocol for NIH.C1, the cartridges were seeded with cells in the absence of microcarrier beads. After the eight day flight, cells were removed from the cartridges and analyzed, along with the synchronous controls. Basal cartridge cells, terminated at launch, were identically studied.

Results:

Measurements of the metabolic state of the flight, basal, and control cells showed that glucose was consumed completely and to the same measurable extent by all 3 groups of cells. Differences between metabolism of basal cells and that of either flight or control cells were interpreted as a possible effect induced by the feeding regime in the STL unit. Osteopontin, bone sialoprotein, and osteocalcin appeared with reduced immunoreactivity in flight compared to control and basal cells. These results were consistent with the work from NIH.C1 showing down-regulation of collagen and osteocalcin gene expression during spaceflight. Adaptation of cultured bone cells during spaceflight is mediated in part by changes in non-collagenous proteins in addition to alterations in collagen.

experiment_title: Cardiovascular Responses to Lower Body Negative Pressure Following Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Orthostatic intolerance is a significant safety concern for Shuttle crew members during return to a 1-g environment and in cases of emergency egress. Orthostatic intolerance may result from decreased body hydration, increased leg compliance, or impaired cardiac or vascular compensatory response. Lower body negative pressure (LBNP) introduces a simulated orthostatic stress in a gradual and graded manner and it was used to test the orthostatic function of crew members before and after flight.

APPROACH:
Twelve crew members on 6- to 14-day Shuttle flights completed this protocol, but data from 2 were excluded, so that the number of participants was 10. Two different protocols of LBNP were used: pre-syncopal limit (PSL) and ramp. In the PSL protocol, which was used to assess the orthostatic tolerance and presyncopal symptoms of crew members, LBNP was applied continuously in 3-minute stages of 10 to 20 millimeters of mercury (mm Hg). The ramp protocol was more gradual and consisted of consecutive 5-minute stages at -0, -10, -20, -30, -40, -50, and -60 mm Hg. Measurements were made before, during and after ramp and PSL LBNP. Heart rate (HR) was measured with Lifepak and blood pressure with a sphygmomanometer. Total peripheral resistance (TPR), cardiac output, and stroke volume were measured by echocardiography. Blood samples were drawn before, during and after LBNP to estimate changes in body hydration (hematocrit, hemoglobin, and plasma total solids) and cardiovascular autonomic response (plasma catecholamines). Leg compliance during LBNP was measured by a mercury-in-silastic strain gauge placed around the calf.

At least 2 months before flight, each subject performed 2 or 3 PSL LBNP protocols. In the 4 months before flight, each crew member performed 2 or 3 ramp protocols. The postflight LBNP ramp test was done within 4 to 6 hours of landing (R+0), and at 3 other times between R+1 and R+8.

RESULTS:
Before flight, all crew members completed the LBNP ramp test. On day R+0, 5 of 10 were unable to complete the test due to presyncopal symptoms; HR remained elevated during all recovery tests. TPR was greater after landing than before flight. Blood analysis on R+0 revealed slight hemoconcentration and augmented catecholamine levels. Catecholamine levels were also increased by LBNP between R+1 and R+8. Leg circumference decreased dramatically after space flight and the decrease persisted for 6 to 8 days after landing. This may represent an acute decrease in muscle mass, not due solely due to dehydration because blood results indicated rapid recovery of body fluids within 48 hours. In comparing postflight response to LBNP and the stand test, LBNP gave no evidence of depressed orthostatic peripheral vascular response, which may be due to the difference between these two types of orthostatic stressors.

experiment_title: Response of Crown Gall Tissue to the Space Environment: Glutamine Synthetase Activity
experiment_description:
Objectives:

In plants, glutamine synthetase (GS) is the enzyme associated with seeds and relatively undifferentiated embryonic activity. It was of interest, therefore, to determine if the specific activity of this enzyme would be affected by gravity compensation or weightlessness in crown gall tumor tissue. The data obtained would serve as an indicator not only of the comparative differences between normal and pathological material, but also whether gravity-compensation is comparable to weightlessness.

Approach:

Upper sections of carrots were cross-sectioned and inoculated with bacterial suspensions (1 x 10-8 cells/ml) of Agrobacterium tumefaciens. Upon arrival, flight, and similarly treated control material, were weighed, frozen, lyophilized, and stored at -20 °C until assayed. Assays for GS specific activity depended on the gamma- glutamyl-transferase properties of the enzyme and were performed by a sodium arsenate modification of the D. Rudnick et al. method. The specific activity was calculated as the number of micromoles of gamma-glutamyl-hydroxymate produced per hour, per mg protein.

Results:

There was a 100% difference in GS specific activity between the flight-weightless and flight-centrifuged material. At no time did the specific activity of the flight material or ground controls approach the activity of normal carrot tissue, and in all cases the activity of the rotated flight material was much lower than stationary controls. While the reasons for these differences are not apparent, a lack of cellular differentiation or hyperplasia of the cambial zone appears to be a characteristic of compensated tumors. GS activity could be expected to be a metabolic participant in neoplasmic activity. The data also indicate that gravity-compensation and true weightlessness, with respect to GS activity, are largely comparable.

experiment_title: LBNP Treadmill and Resistive Exercises during Long-term Bed Rest
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Effective exercise methods and devices for use during space flight have not yet been demonstrated. Despite performing inflight exercise during short- and long-duration space flight, crewmembers continue to return to Earth with muscle atrophy and bone loss. Current inflight exercise does appear to lessen deleterious effects on bone and muscle, but it does not inhibit it. One possible missing component in current inflight exercise is an inablity to provide a load of force on the body that is equivalent to that experienced on Earth. Previous ground-based studies have shown that lower body negative pressure (LBNP), which has historically been used in flight to maintain the cardiovascular system, produces a reaction force on the feet that can be similar to the same foot force required for the body when standing in 1-G.

The objective of this research is to develop and test load-bearing exercise within a LBNP chamber to maintain the cardiovascular and musculoskeletal systems in microgravity. It is believed that this proposed countermeasure will provide a more effective mechanical stress on the lower extremity and that it will be a sufficient and comfortable method of providing a biomechanical load to maintain the structure and function of cardiovascular and musculoskeletal tissues. It is hoped that this type of exercise device will provide a safe and economical alternative to artificial gravity in terms of power usage, mass, volume and cost.

APPROACH:
This ground-based study was designed to test the effectiveness of exercise within an LBNP chamber during simulated microgravity. Lower extremity biomechanics and motion analyses during LBNP exercise within 50 to 60 mm Hg of pressure (equivalent to standing foot pressure at 1-G) during bed rest was compared to the same parameters during upright exercise in 1-G. Groups of human subjects were exposed to 6-degree head-down tilt bed rest for 30 days. The subjects randomly alternated between exercised and non-exercised groups, and, thus, served as their own controls.

Each day, the exercise group ran while supine on a vertical treadmill for 40 minutes at 50 to 60 mm Hg of LBNP pressure. This was followed by three sets of 10 to 15 maximal leg presses at 2-3 times their body weight. This exercise protocol was developed based upon previous studies of bone and muscle maintenance as a result of the types of mechanical loads to which the lower body is exposed.

RESULTS:
Orthostatic tolerance (time to pre-syncope during tilt and graded LBNP), plasma volume, and sprint speed decreased significantly (p<0.05) after 30 days bed rest in the control group, but was relatively maintained in the exercise group. Upright VO2 peak, muscle strength of knee and spine, and endurance decreased significantly in the control group, but were preserved in the exercise group. Also, the exercise group had normal spinal compressibility with 50% BW axial load and significantly higher back muscle strength after bed rest than the control group. Urinary n-telopeptide (NTX) excretion, an index of bone resorption, was increased during bed rest in the control group, but not in the exercise subjects. However, markers of osteoblast activity were similar in the exercise and control groups.

The treadmill exercise protocol within LBNP maintains plasma volume, orthostatic responses, upright exercise capacity, muscle strength and endurance during bed rest. These results document the efficacy of the exercise countermeasure in both males and females. LBNP exercise counteracts increased osteoclast activity, but resistive exercise may be needed to increase bone formation. Future studies should include a combination of supine treadmill exercise in LBNP and flywheel resistive exercise. Treadmill exercise in LBNP may be an early, low mass, low power and efficacious form of artificial gravity for exploration missions. However, the LBNP exercise hardware must be redesigned for space flight and crew habitability.

experiment_title: Sex- and Apo E-specific Late Central Nervous System (CNS) and Cardiovascular (CV) Effects of Space Radiation
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

In order to prepare astronauts for long-term deep space missions (one year), including missions to Mars (600-900 days), the potential risks of galactic cosmic radiation (GCR) to the brain and cardiovascular (CV) system needs to be understood. Exposure to solar protons and GCR puts astronauts at risk for radiation induced effects including: a) central nervous system (CNS) damage leading to acute or late changes in cognition, motor function, behavior and/or neurological disorders and b) cardiovascular disease (CVD) and other degenerative effects.

Space radiation is primarily made up of alpha particles, protons, and high charge and energy (HZE) particles. Not all particles have the same effect, some can be shielded while HZE particles can either pass directly through the spacecraft or create showers of secondary radiation upon impact. Secondary radiation may be more damaging to the brain than primary particles. Secondary radiation is expected to impact a large proportion of brain cells during a multi-year space journey. Irradiation of HZE particles have been shown to cause hippocampal-dependent learning and memory deficits and early exposure of 56Fe particles results in impairment in cognitive function. Radiation induces CVD due to late effects such as fibrosis, vascular changes, reduction in vessels, and altered morphology. These events can result in permanently damaged tissue that can no longer work efficiently as it once did.

Previous NASA-funded research illustrates late CNS dose-dependent, sex- and genotype-specific effects of whole-body iron irradiation on cognition and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology in mice. Male mice experienced more late CNS effects of radiation than female mice. 56Fe irradiated male C57BL/6J wildtype (WT) littermate mice showed significant cognitive impairment seven to eight months post-irradiation. This experiment will build upon previous efforts by comparing data on the late CNS and CVD effects of 56Fe or proton irradiation with the late CNS and CVD effects of simulated GCR irradiation (GCRsim) and gamma irradiation.

The overall goal of the experiment is to better assess the central nervous system and CV risks to astronauts during and after deep space travel. Specifically, to determine the long-term risks of radiation from the space environment on cognition, motor abilities, fatigue resistance, anxiety, and changes in the brain and CV system. Sex and genetic differences change the way radiation damage manifests and therefore needs to be accounted for to properly understand these risks. This experiment has the following specific aims:

  1. Investigate the late CNS and CVD effects of GCRsim in male and female APP/PS1dE9 and C57BL/6J WT mice.
  2. Examine the sex- and Apolipoprotein E (Apo E)-specific late CNS effects of GCRsim in APP/PS1dE9 mice with targeted replacement of murine Apo E with human E3 or E4.
  3. Investigate acute and late CNS effects of space radiation on neuronal health, amyloid plaques, tau pathology, and epigenetics by testing two novel human three-dimensional (3D) neural organoid models of Alzheimer’s diseases. Also investigate the potential of these models for screening mitigating treatments in the future.
APPROACH:

For Aim 1, NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) GCR simulator at Brookhaven National Laboratories (BNL) will be utilized. Four-month-old male and female APP/PS1dE9 Tg and WT mice will be exposed to sham (0 Gy), 0.5 Gy or 0.75 Gy GCRsim. WT male and female mice will also be exposed to 0.75 and 2 Gy gamma radiation. The mice will undergo the 11-test battery behavioral testing at 11 months before they are euthanized. The 11-test battery includes SHIRPA, open field test, grip-strength, wire hanging test, rotarod, spatial novelty y maze, elevated plus maze, tail suspension, acoustic startle, pre-pulse inhibition of startle, and contextual fear conditioning. A subset of mice (four mice per gender, genotype, and group) will undergo pre-irradiation (four-months-old) and post-irradiation (11-months-old) Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) imaging of the brain and heart two-weeks before irradiation and again 7-8 months after irradiation at 11-12 months of age. MRI will be used to monitor longitudinal pre- and post-irradiation changes in brain ventricular volume, hippocampal and cortical structures, and microhemorrhages, as well as changes in heart structure. Brain, heart, kidney, bone marrow, and blood from all mice will be harvested at 12 months of age and analyzed for pathological and biochemical changes, including those related to Alzheimer’s disease. Blood will be collected via cardiac puncture, and then the mice will be pericardially perfused with saline.

For Aim 2, already-crossed APP NL-F KI x human floxed Apo E targeted replacement mice (APP/E3F and APP/E4F) will be obtained and bred to generate the required number of mice needed for the study. The mice will receive whole body irradiation at 9-months of age with sham (0 Gy), 0.5 Gy GCRsim or 0.75 Gy GCRsim. Non-irradiated WT male and female mice will be used for behavioral testing controls. A subset of mice (four mice per gender, genotype, and group) will undergo pre-irradiation (9 months-old) and post-irradiation (14-15 months-old) MRI imaging of the brain and heart. Mice will undergo the 11-test battery behavioral testing at 14-15 months of age, followed by euthanasia and tissue harvest at 15 months and analyzed. Human Apo E levels and cholesterol in the brain and plasma will be measured.

For Aim 3, the BNL facility will be used to irradiate the three dimensional (3D) neural organoids and undifferentiated human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). Undifferentiated iPSCs will be irradiated and the effects of radiation on cardiomyocyte differentiation efficiency, morphology, and maturation will be determined. Human neural progenitor (ReNcell)-derived 3D neural cell cultures will be cultured with and without mutant amyloid precursor protein (APP) transfection (K670N/M671L and V717I mutations). At six weeks maturation, cultures will be transported to BNL and irradiated with GCRsim or gamma radiation (same dose schemes as Aims 1 and 2). The cultures will be analyzed for markers of neurodegeneration before irradiation and one week and six weeks post-irradiation. Cultures will be grown in 96-well plates with one plate per radiation exposure/genotype combination allowing for high throughput outcome measure analysis.

Human iPSC-derived neuron/astrocyte 3D cocultures will be generated from 4 iPSC lines available from Alstem (APOE E4/4 with isogenic E3/3, E2/2, and knockout counterparts). The organoids will be transported to BNL and irradiated with GCRsim or gamma as mentioned previously. The cultures will be analyzed for markers of neurodegeneration before irradiation and after irradiation once AD-like pathology begins to develop. Cultures will be grown in 96- and 24-well plates.

A total of 468 mice will be used over the four years, including 108 APPswe/PS1dE9 mice (54 males and 54 females), 108 APP/E3 mice and 108 APP/E4 mice (54 males and 54 females per genotype), and 144 C57BL/6 WT mice (72 males and 72 females). Mice will be irradiated at four months, tested at 11 months, and euthanized at 12 months for Aim 1 and irradiated at nine months, tested at 14 months and euthanized at 15 months for Aim 2. Mice will be euthanized by carbon dioxide inhalation.

RESULTS:

The experiment is in progress. Results will be available at a later date.

experiment_title: Monitoring of Sweat Calcium Using Skin Patches
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Bone loss can occur during bed rest due to lack of limb use, and exercise has been researched as a potential countermeasure. Calcium loss in sweat from this normal exercise program has been a concern, especially if the exercise occurs at normal room temperature.

In previous bed rest studies, early changes in bone mass have been detected by measuring calcium. Past subjects have undergone a negative calcium balance due to a rapid increase in calcium excretion through the urine and feces. Most studies did not measure calcium loss in sweat, because researchers assumed that the loss had a negligible effect on calcium balance. This assumption was not tested often, partly because an accurate measurement of sweat calcium was difficult. However, one previous study showed that calcium loss through sweat was much greater during one hour of running on a treadmill at room temperature than for the entire remainder of the day. The mean value of the calcium loss was 47 mg per hour while running and 0.8 mg per hour for the rest of the day. Another earlier study also supported the conclusion that sweat calcium loss was greater during strenuous exercise than for sedentary activities. Thus, loss of calcium in sweat could indeed prove to be a significant factor in total body calcium loss, especially when the countermeasures for bone density loss are applied. Since bone density and calcium balance are important factors in health, countermeasures against their degradation need to be optimized and a simple, reliable method of calcium sweat detection should be determined.

This bed rest study had two main purposes. First, researchers tested a non-invasive sweat collection method for its ability to monitor sweat calcium loss. Second, changes in skin calcium loss were measured with and without a resistive exercise countermeasure performed at a lower environmental temperature.

APPROACH:
The subjects of this bed rest study consisted of six females (five white and 1 black) and ten males (nine white and one black). The subjects ages ranged from 22 to 48 years, and weight ranged from 60 to 97 kg. Heights ranged from 157 to 185 cm.

Subjects were divided into three groups. One group was assigned resistive exercise with a workload that increased progressively throughout the bed rest study. A second group did not exercise, but ingested a drug called alendronate (brand name of Fosamax®), which is used to strengthen bone. The third group did not exercise or ingest a drug; these subjects served as controls.

To collect sweat from the subjects, skin patches (Osteopatch®), were attached to the skin on the back, lower chest, and upper part of the arm. Initial studies involved placing two patches, one on each side of the body, on each area for a total of six patches. Later the number was reduced from two patches to one per body region. Data from the patches were collected from four different time periods: a baseline ambulatory time before bed rest and at 6, 12 and 17 weeks of bed rest. Patches were worn for 24 hours on two consecutive days.

The subjects that were assigned resistive exercise performed the exercise six days a week with no exercise performed on Sunday. The two consecutive days for exercise sweat collection occurred within this six-day period so that both days contained exercise. For this group of subjects, sweat was collected on rest days, as well as exercise days. Since there were not two consecutive days without exercise, this sweat collection occurred on two successive Sundays. The bed rest room temperature was 23 to 26°C. The room temperature during exercise was 18°C or less to minimize sweat loss.

The skin patch used to collect sweat had an absorbing area of 14 cm2 and absorbed the solid components of sweat while the fluid evaporated out. The skin was cleaned with an alcohol swab and allowed to dry before the patch was applied. After 24 hours of wear, the patch was removed and the absorption pad portion was refrigerated until analysis. During elution, the pad was placed at the top of a tube and dried for 30 minutes to remove all fluid. One milliliter of distilled water was then added to the pad. After an hour, the tube was centrifuged for ten minutes at 3000 rpm to collect the liquid at the bottom of the tube while the patch remained secured at the top. Calcium concentration was determined from the collected liquid.

RESULTS:
Baseline data, which were taken from 12 subjects, each with six different patches duplicating the three body areas, show no differences between the duplicate body measurements. Significant differences in calcium excretion were found between back versus arm sweat and back versus chest sweat. However no significant differences were found between chest versus arm calcium excretion in sweat. No significant differences were found between the two different but consecutive days. In addition, no interaction or change in the relationships between the three regions was found over the consecutive days. The most variability in the results, 58%, was attributed to body region site with only 0.3% variability attributed to the day and 10% to site by day interaction. The range of inter-individual variability during the baseline collection varied from 18 to 32% for the three regions, with arms at 20% variability, chest at 18% variability and back at 24% variability combined over the days. The inter-individual variability for the two days combined over sites was 20% and 29%.

For seven subjects who did not exercise, data collection occurred over the four time periods. No significant differences were observed between their baseline and the other collections, which occurred at 6, 12 and 17 weeks of bed rest. Some of these subjects ingested the alendronate and others were in the control group.

During the bed rest timeframe, data from five exercise subjects were taken on exercise days and on rest days. No significant differences were observed between the rest days and the exercise days or between the two consecutive exercise days for the same subject.

Total body sweat calcium for the twelve subjects during baseline data collection was averaged for the three sites and was 35 ± 4 mg/day. The mean value for the arm was 33 mg/day. The chest mean value was 35 mg/day and the back was 37 mg/day.

The patch collection method was shown to be reliable for the measurement of sweat calcium loss. This conclusion was supported by the lack of large variations among repeated measurements by day and by site. The small difference between the back calcium excretion and the arm and chest excretion agreed with another published study that found a higher evaporation rate from the back. In this investigation, dermal calcium excretion was not studied during profuse sweating, so no conclusions could be drawn about the use of the skin patch in that circumstance.

No significant differences were found between exercise and rest day values of sweat calcium loss for bed rest subjects that performed resistive exercise with a lower room temperature. In addition, no significant differences were found between baseline and bed rest calcium loss values; this room temperature was also controlled, but was not kept as low as it was during the exercise condition. Calcium excretion in sweat has been shown in other studies to increase significantly when aerobic exercise was performed at standard room temperature. In this study, no effect was observed on sweat calcium due to exercise. This observation was due to the cool environment in which the exercise was performed and also, possibly, to the fact that the exercise in this study was resistive rather than aerobic.

This bed rest study showed that the skin patch could be used to determine the amount of calcium excreted in human sweat for up to 24 hours in normal sweating conditions. Any changes in sweat calcium from bed rest, with or without exercise in a cool environment, did not significantly affect total body calcium balance.

experiment_title: Improving Kidney Stone Detection in Space Analogs (Postdoctoral Fellowship)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts are at an increased risk of forming kidney stones because of dehydration and altered bone metabolism. A stone, while innocuous in the kidney, will often pass spontaneously causing debilitating pain that will affect mission operations. Even worse, large stones can become obstructing when they attempt to pass, resulting in a serious infection or even death without surgical intervention. The goal of this proposal is to develop an ultrasound imaging protocol to detect stones before they become dangerous. Early detection will allow for planned intervention through the administration of stone-dissolving medications, scheduled transport to Earth, or an ultrasound-based stone pushing technique in development at the University of Washington. The twinkling artifact is a rapid color change that can highlight hard objects, such as kidney stones, on a grey-scale ultrasound image; however, twinkling currently appears inconsistently on clinical ultrasound machines.

APPROACH:
The investigator team recently showed that twinkling is caused by bubbles on the stone surface and bubbles will be very sensitive to the changes in gravity and pressure that occur in space. In this proposal, investigators plan to use their knowledge of bubbles and ultrasound to increase twinkling. Using modeling and experimentation in environments that mimic space, they will develop and test imaging protocols to demonstrate their ability to detect stones in astronauts before they grow large enough to become dangerous.
