experiment_title: Regulation of Blood Volume During Spaceflight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Human adaptation to space flight is accompanied by a loss of red blood cell mass (RBCM), a loss of plasma volume (PV), and a decrease in total blood volume. This leads to a decrease in gravity-dependent space below the heart. In this study, rats were examined to determine whether similar hemodynamic changes occur, making them a suitable subject for study. SLS-1 marked the first time PV and RBCM were measured before and after flight. SLS-2 allowed for repeat determinations and the first opportunity for inflight assessment of erythropoiesis. An additional inflight experiment tested the ability of the rat bone marrow to respond to a bolus of erythropoietin, the major hormone controlling erythropoiesis in animals and humans.

Approach:

Seven days prior to launch PV and RBCM were determined by isotopic dilution of 125I labeled albumin and 51Cr labeled red blood cells respectively. On flight day 6, five rats (group A) were given 125I labeled albumin and 59Fe injections. Samples were taken ten minutes later to determine PV. Samples to determine 59Fe incorporation into RBCs were taken 24 hours later and on landing day (9 days later). The remaining 10 rats (groups B and C) were given 59Fe injections on flight day 9. Group B was also given a 200-U injection of erythropoietin at this time. Upon landing, RBCM and PV were measured for all flight rats and ground controls. 59Fe incorporation into red blood cells was also determined.

Results:

RBCM showed an increase in both the spaceflight animals and ground control animals, but less of an increase in flight animals. When this increase was normalized for growth (flight animals had a lower growth rate than ground controls), a decrease was seen in the flight animals' RBCM. Plasma volume increased in both flight and ground control animals. The PV increase was greater in ground control animals although not statistically different. 59Fe incorporation was lower in flight animals but again not statistically different. Animals that received erythropoietin injections had higher levels of iron incorporation. Incorporation was not statistically significant, indicating erythropoiesis is stimulated normally under conditions of microgravity.

experiment_title: Human Sleep, Circadian Rhythms and Performance in Space
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This was the first simultaneous study of sleep, circadian rhythms, and mood in response to the microgravity environment to determine the interrelationship between sleep, circadian rhythms and mood and task performance. The function of the circadian system (or biological clock) is that of a predictive homeostasis, which ensures that the organism, in this case a human being, is prepared from both physiological and psychological standpoints, for restful sleep at certain times of the day and active wakefulness at others. The scientists conducting this experiment believed that if the whole structure of social and physical time cues found on Earth are weakened or removed, as during space flight, the result will be circadian dysfunction. Symptoms include poor sleep, greater use of sleep aids, and degraded task performance. During the experiment, sleep data were generally indicative of the night, while performance data were representative of the day, and the circadian rhythm data were the patterns that bound the two together. In some respects, the orbiting space vehicle can be likened to a continually submerged submarine, where there are well-documented tendencies towards biological clock (circadian) dysfunction.

APPROACH:
The experiment was divided into two parts: The United States investigators were concerned with sleep performance and circadian rhythms, and the French investigators studied fluid and electrolyte balance during exposure to microgravity. Four astronauts participated as subjects. One 72-hour measurement block was performed preflight, one postflight and two inflight. The two inflight measurement blocks occurred toward the middle of the mission (FD 3-6), while the other occurred toward the end (FD 13-16) of the 17-day mission. Each block ran from start of shift to start of shift (hence impacting 4 mission days, while covering only 72 hours). On each of three nights during both 72-hour blocks, data were recorded during sleep. Each subject also kept a sleep diary, which gave subjective ratings of sleep timing and quality and alertness upon awakening, as well as hypnotic and other medication use.

In addition, physical rhythms were evaluated by measuring core body temperature, which was recorded every six minutes throughout the entire 72-hour block using a rectal thermistor and recorder. This allowed 3-cycle circadian temperature rhythms to be plotted. Biochemical rhythms were measured through the analysis of urine samples. Each void during the 72-hour measurement block was collected. Samples were frozen at -20 degrees Celsius for later assay. From these samples, investigators were studying void volume and levels of melatonin sulfate and cortisol (by radioimmunoassay) and sodium and potassium (by electrolytic techniques).

Each sleep session during the 72-hour measurement block was recorded using the Medilog Sleep Research Recorder (MSRR) system. The subjects wore electroencephalograph (EEG) electrodes to record brain wave patterns, which gave investigators an idea of the type and depth of sleep. Electrooculograph (EOG) electrodes recorded eye movements and electromyograph (EMG) electrodes recorded chin muscle tone (a relaxed chin muscle is a second indication of REM sleep). The electrodes recording EEG, EOG and EMG were positioned on the subjects' head using a cap-based system. Signals were recorded on magnetic tape. After recovery, the tapes were played back in order to 1) visually classify each minute of sleep into conventionally defined sleep stages (0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and REM); and 2) run the signals through a computer-based analysis system allowing the measurement of: a) EEG spectral density, b) a count of delta waves, and c) a count of eye movements. The procedures allowed a detailed characterization of the duration, depth and architecture of the entire sleep episode.

After each sleep period during the 72-hour measurement block, each subject completed a modified computer-based version of the Pittsburgh Sleep Diary (PghSD). This brief instrument assessed the estimated timings of sleep onset and offset, recorded the number and nature of within-night awakenings, the use of sleep-inducing medications, the use of medication to alleviate space adaptaion syndrome (SAS), and concluded with visual analog scale ratings of 1) subjective sleep quality, 2) mood upon awakening (tense versus relaxed), and 3) alertness upon awakening (sleepy versus alert).

At the end of each work shift in the 72-hour measurement block, the subjects completed a brief questionnaire regarding stresses such as fatigue, equipment malfunction and changes in procedure, as well as ratings of how long the shift lasted and how satisfied they were with their work during the shift.

The study by Dr. Gharib of fluid and electrolyte balance had several steps, designed to determine the following:
1) Early (<24 hours) and delayed (>24 hours) hormonal and electrolyte modifications and to demonstrate the correlation of these modifications with space adaptation syndrome (SAS).
2) Role of sympathetic nervous system transmitters (catecholamines, 3-methoxy 4-hydroxy phenyl glycol (MHPG)) and growth hormone (GH) with cortisol as indicators of stress.
3) The role of confinement and inactivity in the changes observed during flight. The comparison of flight data with a 17-day bed-rest study and a postflight ground-based study will be of great importance in determining these. The postflight ground study will be performed under the direction of Dr. Alexander Gundel of the Institute of Aerospace Medicine, located at the German Aerospace Research Establishment (DLR) in Cologne, Germany.

RESULTS:
When careful steps are taken to ensure that the astronauts' work/rest schedule does not lead to circadian desynchrony, there is no evidence that microgravity per se will disrupt the human circadian timekeeping system, or that such rhythms will degrade over a 17d mission. In particular, there was no evidence of amplitude reduction, phase lability or "free-running" behavior. Despite the astronauts' circadian rhythms being intact, there were some effects on sleep, notably a reduction in sleep duration, and a suppression of the deepest stages of sleep (Stages 3 and 4). However, there were no other 543 consistent effects of flight in sleep architecture. The only systematic effect on mood and performance appeared to be an increase in alertness in the early flight measurement block. End of shift questionnaires revealed time line problems and equipment malfunction to be the major impacts on the astronauts' work.

experiment_title: Induction of Bystander Effects by High LET Radiation In Cells and in Tissue Models
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The mission of NASA’s space radiation biology program is to provide knowledge on the effects of high energy charged particles on biological systems at the molecular, cellular, tissue, and organism levels in order to enable better prediction of risks of carcinogenesis and damage to normal tissues from exposures of astronauts to the ionizing radiation in space. With charged particles such as alpha-particles and low energy protons, significant differences from direct DNA damage-mediated responses have been demonstrated in a number of biological systems. Occurrence of these effects, including bystander effects and genomic instability, calls into question the use of a simple linear extrapolation of cancer risks from high dose data to low doses. This is of particular relevance to NASA because the occurrence of bystander effects in cells exposed to heavy ions or energetic protons, as found in space, has not been evaluated to date. The overall goals of this study are to test the hypothesis that heavy ions and energetic protons efficiently cause bystander effects in neighboring cells not directly traversed by the radiation and to study the mechanisms involved. There were four specific aims:

1. Determine induction of bystander effects by heavy ions compared to X-rays and protons in cultured human diploid fibroblasts and keratinocytes using endpoints specific for each cell type and including production of micronuclei, apoptosis, clonogenicity and increased gene expression.
2. Test the hypothesis that heavy ion-induced bystander effects can be modified by exposure of cells to reactive oxygen species (ROS), an overlying oxidative stress.
3. Test the hypothesis that exposure to low LET radiation alters the heavy ion-induced bystander effects.
4. Begin development of 3-D tissue models for assessment of bystander effects from heavy ions and energetic protons.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this study isn’t available.

RESULTS:
The investigators have developed a novel transwell insert co-culture system in which irradiated and unirradiated cells share medium, but are physically separated, and used this approach to demonstrate medium-mediated bystander responses in AG01522 normal human fibroblasts after X-ray exposure. At the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) at Brookhaven National Laboratory they have used this co-culture system, as well as irradiating cells at low particle fluences, to study bystander responses induced by heavy ions (1 GeV/n Fe, 1 GeV/n Ti and 290 MeV/n C) and protons (1 GeV/n). They have used iron, titanium, carbon and protons because they represent particles found in space that span a range of LET values from 0.24 to about 150 keV/micrometer, thus allowing us to test the LET dependence of various bystander responses. Investigators found substantial effects in directly irradiated AG01522 fibroblasts and h-TERT immortalized human keratinocytes using endpoints including clonogenic survival, micronuclei (MN) formation and p21 expression. For example, with the clonogenic survival assay in the AG01522 cells, we have found relative biological effect (RBE) values at 10% survival are 2.5, 2.3, 1.0 and 1.2 for 1 GeV/amu Fe, 1 GeV/amu Ti, 290 MeV/amu C and 1 GeV/amu protons, respectively, compared to 250 kVp X-rays, indicating the greater effectiveness of Fe and Ti for inducing cell killing. Fe and Ti are also very effective inducers of MN in these cells, although C ions are less effective, similar to protons.

Using their insert system,investigators have demonstrated that irradiation with 1 GeV/amu Fe ions induces a 2-3 fold increase in MN formation in unirradiated bystander AG0 cells, which is similar in magnitude to that seen with X-rays. The increase in damage in bystander cells is independent of the dose to the hit cells between 0.1 and 2 Gy Fe ions, although it is somewhat lower at 0.05 Gy. The insert system allows investigators to study the timing of bystander signaling by altering the time at which the co-culture of irradiated and unirradiated cells is started or how long the two cell populations are together. Using this approach, they have shown that when irradiated and unirradiated bystander cells are combined in shared medium immediately, one hour or three hours after irradiation, a full bystander MN formation effect is observed. However, when combining the irradiated and unirradiated cells is delayed six hours after irradiation, the bystander effect is lost. Furthermore, bystander micronuclei formation is observed even when the bystander cells are co-cultured with irradiated cells for only one hour if they are combined immediately after irradiation. This suggests that the signal transduction to bystander cells from irradiated cells occurs at a short time after irradiation, and these early stage signals sent by irradiated cells are crucial to the induction of bystander effects. The results with iron ions are similar to those with X-rays, suggesting that the bystander MN formation in this system is independent of LET. Protons also induce a medium-mediated bystander effect in terms of MN production, although the magnitude is less than seen with Fe ions or X-rays.

In addition to X-irradiation, the investigators have now shown gamma-H2AX foci formation in unirradiated bystander cells that shared medium with Fe ion-irradiated cells at different time points after co-culture. The data indicate that a 2-3-fold increase in percentage of bystander cells with gamma-H2AX foci occurs as early as one hour after irradiation, and lasts at least 24 hours. Compared to the directly irradiated cells, which have a high yield of gamma-H2AX foci at early times after irradiation and return to control levels by 24 hours, bystander cells have slower kinetics of disappearance of gamma-H2AX foci. Fe ions and X-rays induce a similar pattern of gamma-H2AX foci in unirradiated bystander cells, suggesting gamma-H2AX foci induction in bystander cells is independent of LET of the radiation.

The investigators were interested in studying the effects of very low fluences of particles where only one to two percent or less of the cells would be traversed by particles. Dr. Rusek and his team of NSRL physicists have developed procedures for obtaining these very low fluences, and, most importantly, being able to accurately quantify the particle fluences, determine the beam uniformity and determine the purity of the beam. They have now demonstrated that very low fluences of energetic protons and iron ions induce bystander MN formation and 53BP1 foci (another surrogate for DNA DSBs) in non-irradiated bystander fibroblasts that share medium with irradiated cells. Results show that while there is no significant increase in MN formation in cells directly irradiated with low fluences (2e3 to 5e6 particles/cm2 for protons and 2e3 to 2.25e5 particles/cm2 for iron ions) of protons and iron ions, there is 1.5-2-fold increase in MN formation in bystander cells in the insert system. On the other hand, 53BP1 forms foci in both directly irradiated and bystander cells with low fluences of protons and iron ion, with the percentage of irradiated cells with 53BP1 foci being a little higher than that of bystander cells. It is noteworthy that within the range of low fluences used, 53BP1 foci formation is independent of dose. This suggests that the linear no-threshold hypothesis for relationship of radiation-induced damage to dose may not hold at very low doses. Furthermore, although the the typical dose response plateau pattern of irradiation-induced bystander effects, the fluence at which the threshold occurs is still unclear. At 2e3 particles/cm2, which equals 0.4 mGy of iron ions or 0.57 microGy of protons, there is bystander MN formation with iron ion irradiation but not with protons. The lowest proton fluence that induces the bystander effect is 2e5 particles/cm2, which equals 57 microGy. These data suggest that there might be a threshold for irradiation-induced bystander effects at about 60 microGy for protons and somewhere below 400 microGy for Fe ions.

With regard to aim 2 the investigators have reported previously that ROS play a significant role in transmission of signals from irradiated to bystander cells after exposure to X-rays or Fe ions. They have now begun studies to determine the effect of low levels of oxidative stress on responses of irradiated and bystander cells to subsequent irradiation. Their preliminary data show that if bystander AG0 cells are exposed to a low, non-toxic level of hydrogen peroxide before co-culturing with irradiated cells, there does not appear to be any radiation-induced bystander MN formation, but if bystander cells are oxidatively stressed after the start of co-culturing with irradiated cells, the radiation-induced bystander MN formation is not changed compared to the sham control. Further studies are needed to confirm those results.

Relevant to aim 3, the investigators have been among the pioneering groups at NSRL to investigate the effects of “mixed,”, actually sequential, irradiations with iron ions and protons. Their preliminary data suggest that in irradiated cells the induction of micronuclei is greater when the two particle exposures are separated by three or 24 hours compared to when given within five minutes. However, depending on the time between irradiations, bystander cells appear to “adapt” to the second signal, i.e., a smaller bystander response was seen when irradiated cells were “hit” twice with 3-24 hours between the hits, than when the same dose was given in a single irradiation. Clearly, these data need repeated, but the results are intriguing.

Previously, the investigators reported progress on aim 4 showing significant signaling from X-irradiated fibroblasts to unirradiated keratinocytes and vice versa (endpoints of MN formation and p21 expression). However, interestingly, after Fe exposure their data suggest that with some endpoints there is no signaling from irradiated keratinocytes to unirradiated fibroblasts or keratinocytes, and the effect is delayed from irradiated fibroblasts to unirradiated keratinocytes. Additional investigation is still underway, and they have made progress developing a 3D tissue model using these two cell types that will allow them to test the importance of microenvironment to cell-cell signaling.

experiment_title: Contributors to Long-Term Recovery of Bone Strength following Exposure to Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The project used the adult male hindlimb unloaded (HU) animal model with three specific aims and associated experiments. The first aim addressed the observed "discordant recovery dynamic" reported for astronaut data with tasks to characterize bone mass, BMD, and bone strength relationships after HU and during various periods of recovery. Additional outcome measures include bone biochemistry and gene expression. A major emphasis was to compare detailed dynamics between the animal model and astronaut data. The animal model also permits direct comparison of calculated/estimated bone strengths with measured strengths. The second aim examined multiple mission scenarios and used HU, recovery for an interim period, and then a second HU exposure with another recovery period following. The third aim also followed the two-exposure protocol but with exercise added during the recovery period.

Specific Aims:
1. To determine the precise relationships between bone mass, BMD, and bone strength during recovery from 28 days of HU. Recovery periods of 28, 56, and 84 days will be studied, representing 1, 2, and 3 times the period of HU.
2. To determine the precise relationships between bone mass, BMD, and bone strength after a second exposure to 28 days of HU, following an initial 28 days of HU plus a recovery period. Two recovery periods interposed between HU exposures will be examined, 28 and 56 days. The recovery periods may be modified, however, based upon results from the experiments for Specific Aim 1.
3. To characterize and compare the effects of resistance training and treadmill running during recovery from 28 days of HU on the relationships between bone mass, BMD, and bone strength.

APPROACH:
Three sets of experiments were conducted to address the three specific aims of the project. In all cases, adult male Sprague-Dawley rats (6-months-old) were used, and the period of initial HU was 28 days. Recovery can be characterized in three ways: (a) by comparing to age-matched, ambulatory cage control animals (no HU, but same age); (b) by comparing to values at the end of the initial 28 days of HU (day 0 of recovery); and (c) by comparing to values at baseline (day 0 before HU). The major outcome variables examined are bone mass (size, geometry, BMC), bone mineral density (total, cortical, cancellous BMD), and bone quality (strength, plus measures of tissue-level organic matrix). Tissue-level organic matrix assays quantify collagen content, cross-link maturity, and gene expression. These were being assessed for: (i) cortical bone in the mid-diaphysis (tibia and femur); (ii) mixed cortical and cancellous bone in the metaphysis (proximal tibia and distal femur); (iii) mixed cortical and cancellous bone in the femoral neck. Using these anatomic sites allowed evaluation of the response of both cortical and cancellous bone, both separately and combined (integrally).

RESULTS:
Specific Aim 1. The basic design was to determine the time course of recovery in bone outcomes following an initial period of HU (28 days). The experiments were conducted in three cohorts of 45 animals each, constituting 5 animals in each of the 9 groups. Animals were acclimated for two weeks and singly housed in a temperature-controlled room with a 12:12 hour light/dark cycle. Body weights and total vBMD of the proximal tibia metaphysis were used to assign animals to groups with the goal of having equal mean values in all groups for these two variables. All HU animals were allowed access to food and water ad libitum. During the first week of the HU period, control animals were pair-fed to the HU animals to account for the typically observed reduced food intake during the transition to HU. All animal procedures were in compliance with the Texas A&M University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee rules and regulations.

The in vivo animal portion of Experiment 2 was completed in April 2010. Based on results from Experiment 1, and also considering the need to accelerate the overall time schedule of the project, the detailed protocol for Experiment 2 was modified from that originally proposed. The 28d recovery groups were eliminated because results from Experiment 1 indicated that the vast majority of pQCT-based parameters did not recover at that point, and this was deemed inappropriate with respect to realistic crew member scenarios. A new group was added to allow assessment of recovery following the second HU exposure.

Research review meetings were held in Houston with JSC personnel in both November 2010 and November 2011. Several modifications were agreed upon to the scope and nature of the research plan as a result of these meetings. The major items were as follows:
(1) A new collaboration was agreed upon with Dr. Stefan Judex of Stony Brook University. Ex vivo specimens from the proximal tibia would be shipped to Dr. Judex for him to conduct microCT scans and analysis of the proximal tibia metaphysis.
(2) An internal collaboration was also established with muscle biologist Dr. James Fluckey of the Health & Kinesiology Department at Texas A&M University. As a result, Dr. Fluckey and/or one of his students participated in all subsequent necropsy sessions and harvested muscle specimens. The two main outcome variables from this collaboration are wet muscle weights and muscle protein fractional synthesis rates (FSR). These measures are being made on the whole posterior crural muscle complex, as well as the separate muscles (gastrocnemius, plantaris, soleus).
(3) Only one type of exercise would be used for Experiment 3. Several factors precipitated this decision. These included persisting scheduling issues, increased animal costs, additional time delays associated with the new collaborations, and logistical details involved with the exercise protocols and integrating these within a double-HU experimental scenario. The single exercise to be used would be the resistance training approach.

Experiment 3 animal procedures started during Year 3 and were completed during Year 4. The goal of this phase was to characterize the effects of resistance exercise during the recovery period on the nature and extent of recovery following the initial HU exposure, and also on the response to the second HU exposure (both loss and recovery following HU).

Major Findings for Specific Aim 1.
In Vivo pQCT at the Proximal Tibia Metaphysis and Tibia Diaphysis
• Both vBMD and BMC (total, integral) at the proximal tibia metaphysis exhibit loss and recovery patterns better matching crewmember data than do similar parameters for the femoral neck.
• Cortical bone in the cortical shell of the proximal tibia metaphysis was lost primarily endocortically and recovered mainly periosteally.
• Calculated strength indices suggested a loss in strength at the tibia diaphysis, which was not confirmed with direct testing of mechanical properties. HU had no effect on maximum fracture force at mid-tibia diaphysis.
Femoral Neck Ex Vivo pQCT and Mechanical Testing
• Bone response to disuse and reloading is site-specific, as both mass and density at the femoral neck in the rat recover after twice the duration of unloading, whereas maximum force reaches age-matched control levels after only one recovery period.
• The femoral neck experienced a significant loss of maximum force due to unloading that fully recovered after 28 days. Estimated strength indices for the femoral neck indicated a recovery period of 56 days in contrast to the 28-day recovery that was observed with mechanical testing.
• Strength values are not substantially different for axial loading versus lateral loading in the adult rat HU animal model.
• Losses due to HU in strength for axial loading were greater than those for lateral loading, however.
• Losses due to HU in strength were generally greater than losses in vBMD or BMC especially for axial loading.
• NCSI was a better predictor of strength then NBSI.

Major Findings for Specific Aim 2.
In Vivo pQCT at the Proximal Tibia Metaphysis for Double-HU
• Both vBMD and BMC (total, integral) exhibit milder losses for the second HU compared to the first HU or the age–matched single HU. This suggests a possible protective effect of the initial HU.
• Bone in the cortical shell was lost primarily endocortically and recovered mainly periosteally.
• Recovery was not complete following the initial unloading cycle, and losses due to the second unloading cycle were not significant and smaller in magnitude than those due to initial exposure to hindlimb unloading.
• Rates of recovery for total BMC, vBMD, and cortical area were slower in older animals exposed to single or double HU cycles compared to recovery of younger animals exposed to a single HU bout.
Ex Vivo Mechanical Properties and Micro-CT at the Proximal Tibia Metaphysis for Double-HU
• Losses in densitometric properties were most dramatic for the first HU and for the cancellous bone compartment.
• Trabecular number (Tb.N) was minimally affected, with the greatest effects being reductions in trabecular thickness (Tb.Th).
• Mechanical properties derived from reduced platen compression (RPC) mechanical testing of machined proximal tibia metaphysis samples followed trends generally similar to densitometric measures for the trabecular compartment but the magnitudes of the effects were greater for mechanical properties. Specifically, ultimate stress showed age-related declines for age-matched controls, along with a general decrease for pre-to-post HU. However, the only significant difference from age-matched controls (-36%) was noted after the 1st HU exposure at a young age (6 months old).
• Trabecular vBMD following the initial HU cycle at a young age was only 11% lower than control values, which is much less than the 36% decline in ultimate stress, and thus demonstrates how BMD is not always an accurate predictor of mechanical strength.

Overall and taken together, these findings indicate that initial exposure to mechanical unloading does not exacerbate bone loss during a subsequent unloading period and two cycles of unloading followed by recovery does not have a cumulative net negative effect on total bone mass and density at the proximal tibia metaphysis.

Ex Vivo Results at the Distal Femur Metaphysis for Double-HU
• Losses in densitometric properties were most dramatic for the first HU and for the cancellous bone compartment.
• Mechanical properties of the cancellous bone, as estimated by RPC testing, were affected quite dramatically by the initial HU exposure. However, the effects of both HU exposures at the older age were essentially indistinguishable from age–related declines and properties.

Major Findings for Specific Aim 3.
Adding exercise during recovery between HU exposures revealed impressive and powerful benefits for the vast majority of variables measured.
• For in vivo pQCT results, both total BMC and total vBMD showed significantly enhanced recovery with the exercise added. Values not only recovered completely to control levels, but the exercise also engendered an apparent "protective" effect, as the losses for the 2nd HU were milder.
• At the femoral neck, however, the results were slightly different. Specifically, exercise produced benefits for total BMC only, with no appreciable effect on total vBMD. For total BMC, however, the benefits were much more dramatic, as the exercise produced "super-recovery," which is defined to indicate that mean values actually exceeded control animal values at the end of the exercise+recovery period.
• As was true at the proximal tibia, both BMC and vBMD exhibited a protective effect for the 2nd HU at the femoral neck.
• Perhaps the most dramatic effects of exercise were reflected by the mechanical strength of the FN. Both axial and lateral loading cases yielded super-recovery, with the maximum force for axial loading 35% higher than age-matched controls, and the maximum force for lateral loading 20% higher. A protective effect was also generated for maximum force at the FN, as the 2nd HU had no significant effect (no statistically significant changes pre- to post-HU).
• Trabecular vBMD for the non-exercise (2HU) group showed losses after the second HU exposure, and there was also a very significant age-related decline in trabecular vBMD in the weightbearing control animals. With exercise, however, trabecular vBMD increased during the 2nd recovery period to be higher than both non-exercise 2HU and AC groups (n.s.) and, in fact, restored to essentially the same level as baseline (day 0).
• As revealed by the microCT results, the enhanced trabecular vBMD was mainly the result of significant increases in trabecular thickness (Tb.Th) the following the 1st HU. Tb.Th was significantly higher than both 2HU (24.5%) and AC9 (26.3%) at the end of exercise period, and remained higher after the second HU period (21.8% and 27.6%, respectively). Rats exposed to resistance training did not exhibit increased trabecular BV/TV, however; presumably because of the significant decrease in trabecular number (Tb.N), which contributed to an increase in trabecular separation (Tb.Sp).

experiment_title: Morphologic and Histochemical Studies of Bone Cells from SL-3 Rats
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Non-weight bearing or hypogravity conditions are known to result in skeletal loss in the long bones. The mechanism is unknown but one hypothesis suggests that the lack of mechanical force or stress on the bone results in reduced osteoblastic activity and thus reduced new bone formation. The objectives here were to investigate the cellular activity of the bone forming cells, the osteoblast, in animals exposed to seven days of microgravity.

Approach:

The osteoblasts from tibias of adult flight and control rats were studied using cytochemical methods for alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, and dipeptidyl peptidase II. In addition, electron microscopy was used in combination with morphometric techniques to measure numbers of secretory granules containing procollagen, to count lysosomes and to measure cytoplasmic areas of osteoblasts.

Results:

Measurements of alkaline and acid phosphatase, Golgi activity, secretory granule size, and lysosomal activity, all indicated very little difference between flight and flight-simulated controls. However, there was a tendency for osteoblasts in compact bone of flight animals to show a smaller cytoplasmic volume compared to non-flight controls. Thus the "processing" of protein (including procollagen) in these osteoblasts, especially the dipeptidase cleavage activity, may be operating normally but within a smaller cytoplasmic volume, and this normal proteolytic activity within a smaller volume could result in more rapid intracellular protein degradation, including procollagen, and thus less collagen secretion. This, in effect would result in less new bone formation. An alternative explanation concerns the twelve-hour postflight delay before animal sacrifice. As collagen synthesis is stimulated during cell growth, the osteoblasts could have begun to return to normal function in this period. With a longer recovery time one presumes that a return to normal cell size would also have occurred.

experiment_title: The Effect of Long-duration Spaceflight on the Biomechanics of the Proximal Femur
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Three-dimensional quantitative computed tomography (CT) was used to assess the biomechanics of the proximal femur where significant differences in the patterns of cortical and trabecular bone loss have been found in a group of astronauts. This research will provide insight into the physiological response of proximal femoral bone tissue to space flight and may result in a more sensitive method for tracking the efficacy of countermeasures aimed at preserving skeletal strength.

The overall objective of the task was to determine the extent to which hip strength is lost during space flight and whether it is recovered as the skeleton readapts to Earth gravity. The most important aspect of this task is the use of finite element analysis to analyze bone strength with respect to loads exerted by the hip in falls. The second objective was to combine the finite element analysis of the hip with inter-subject registration techniques so that it will be possible to visualize the overall response of the proximal femur at the organ level to changes in loading. The idea is to use the technique to identify regions of the hip that may be at highest risk for failure due to abnormal loading in falls or during excursion activities. The third objective was to develop an approach for assessing muscles that are of key importance for protecting hip bone strength. If these muscles are identified, then it would be possible to reduce the time burden and injury risk associated with exercise programs by finding activities that are more efficient for protecting bone strength.

APPROACH:
The methodology for this study is embedded in the Results section below.

RESULTS:
Finite element analyses
The investigators installed finite element software developed by Dr Joyce Keyak in the laboratory at UCSF. The software, which creates biomechanical models of the hip from CT scans to estimate the whole bone strength of the proximal femur in loading conditions simulating normal ambulation and a fall to the side, has been applied to pre-flight, postflight, and a subset of one year scans from the astronauts of increment 2-8. Finite element modeling of pre- and postflight scans and one year are complete for 16 subjects, and 5 one-year scans are available for data reduction as they are computing FEM-specific corrections for a scanner change that took place during the study.

After obtaining institutional review board approval and informed consent, pre- and post-flight CT scans were obtained of the hips of astronauts who participated in long-duration International Space Station (ISS) missions. Mission length ranged from 4.3 to 6.5 months. Demographic data cannot be provided due to HIPAA regulations. A four-sample calcium hydroxyapatite (CHA) calibration phantom (Image Analysis, Columbia, KY) was placed under the subjects’ hips during scanning and used to calibrate the CT scan data in terms of CHA concentration.

From the CT scan data, a finite element (FE) model of each subject’s left proximal femur was generated using methods described previously. These models employed patient-specific geometries and material properties. Ash density (rho ash, g/cm3) of each element was computed from the calibrated CT scan data (rho QCT, g/cm3), rho ash=0.0633 + 0.887 rho QCT. Mechanical properties were calculated from as densities. These properties were calibrated to result in accurate predictions of FFE.4 The models were analyzed under loading simulating single-limb stance2, and impact from a fall onto the greater trochanter. For stance loading, force was applied to the femoral head at 20 degrees to the shaft axis, within the coronal plane. For fall loading, force was applied to the femoral head at 60 degrees to the shaft axis and 25 degrres to the coronal plane, as the opposing surface of the greater trochanter was restrained in the opposite direction. FE-computed hip strength (FFE) in each loading condition was determined. A paired t-test was used to evaluate differences between pre- and post-flight values of FFE.

RESULTS: For stance loading, the average proximal femoral strength decreased significantly (p<0.001) from 13,200 N (SD=2300 N) pre-flight to 11,200 N (SD=2400 N) post-flight . The average rate of loss of hip strength for stance loading was 2.6 percent/mo (SD=1.4 percent). For fall loading, average hip strength decreased significantly (p=0.003) from 2,580 N (SD=560 N) pre-flight to 2,280 N (SD=590 N) post-flight . The average rate of strength loss for fall loading was 1.9 percent/mo (SD=1.4 percent). The preliminary one year FEM data show that for 4/5 subjects, strength is recovered in the stance loading condition, but for 4/5 subjects strength is not recovered in the fall loading condition.

DISCUSSION: This study has shown that astronauts exposed to microgravity for 4.3 to 6.5 months lose hip strength at an average rate of 2.6 percent/mo under single-limb stance loading and 1.9 percent/mo under fall loading. Previous DXA measurements of astronauts returning from the ISS indicated that aBMD decreased by 1.4 percent/mo in the neck and 1.5 percent/mo in the total femur.1 Thus, estimates of bone strength loss that are based on DXA aBMD alone will understate the reduction in hip strength. The recovery data available thus far seem to be consistent with the investigators finding in their 2006 bone recovery paper that shows that the recovery of bone mass and areal density is nearly complete at one year, but that volumetric bone density, particularly the density of trabecular bone does not recover. This seems to be driven by periosteal expansion, which increases bone volume and mass, while the recovery of volumetric bone density lags. The larger bone may be optimized for the loads incurred in normal usage but may still be at risk for fracture in pathologic conditions such as falls. Thus, recovery of bone mass may not be sufficient to gauge the recovery of bone after space flight.

Intersubject registration
The investigators obtained the Montreal Neurological Institute Animal intersubject image registration program, installed it in their laboratory, and have applied it to successfully co-register CT scans of the hip from 16 subjects with pre- and postflight image data. They have carried out voxel by voxel statistical comparisons of those models for the pre- and postflight time points, and have demonstrated a focal pattern of accelerated bone loss in the compressive trabecular band in the femoral head region.

Quantitation of muscle cross-sectional area and attenuation coefficient from Hip CT scans
Acquisition of volumetric CT scans of the hip: Analysis of proximal femoral musculature was carried out using volumetric CT scans optimized to analyze the density and structure of the proximal femur. In these studies, the patient lied supine on the imaging table, and an anteroposterior scoutview was acquired which spans the iliac crest to the mid-thigh. The operator then defined a helical scan volume between the superior limit of the left femoral head and an inferior limit 3-5 mm inferior to the lesser trochanter. The muscle analyses was carried out on images obtained with 120/80 kVp, 150 mAs, 3 mm or 1-mm section thickness (pitch=1), 48 cm field of view, reconstructed with a soft tissue filter. Images in all studies were obtained with a QCT calibration phantom (Image Analysis, Columbia, KY) positioned below the patient’s hips.

Analysis of images for muscle cross-sectional area and mean attenuation coefficient: Based on previous studies of gait, balance and muscle function, the investigators have selected four groups of muscles to quantify which are well-visualized within the field of view of the proximal femur QCT scan: these include the hip extensors (gluteus maximus), hip abductors (gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and piriformis), hip adductors (adductor magnus, adductor brevis, adductor longus, quadratus femoris, quadratus externus, pectineus) and hip flexors (rectus femoris and sartorius). These groups are easily distinguishable on almost all of the cross-sections in the field of view in CT scans of the proximal femur. Because the cross-sectional areas of these muscle groups vary differently as a function of slice location within the QCT scans, they developed a method to select individual cross-sections on which to quantify the areas and mean attenuation coefficients of these muscle groups. This involved two steps. First investigators examined annotated optical and CT images in the Visible Human data set to determine the locations in the CT scan field of view where the muscle groups are of maximal size and are optimally distinguished from the surrounding tissue, and second they developed a protocol for employing boney landmarks to calculate the locations of these cross-sections relative to the hip anatomy, so that the muscle measurements could be compared between individuals and reproduced within an individual over time. To select the slice location, a mid-coronal reformation of the image is employed to display the proximal femoral anatomy. The user marks the slice position of the superior aspect of the femoral head and the inferior aspect of the lesser trochanter to generate a metric by which the individual muscle cross-sections can be reliably located. SH is the slice position corresponding to the superior aspect of the left femoral head. D is the distance between SH and the inferior aspect of the lesser trochanter, which defines the inferior limit of the proximal femoral analysis. The cross-sections are chosen as the slice numbers corresponding to the nearest integer to the calculations. Thus three cross-sections are selected for display, one for the extensors, one for the abductors, and a third cross-section containing the adductors and flexors. Each slice is then displayed in an image window, and the user draws the boundary around the fasceal plane of the corresponding muscle group. Once the drawings have been completed, the program processes each cross-section according to the following steps:
1) The program finds the water equivalent cell of the calibration phantom. Based on the mean and standard deviation of the HU in the water equivalent cell, the program calculates HU intervals to be used for calculations of muscle and fat areas within defined tissue boundaries.
2) The program generates the outer body contour by performing a region growing operation, searching for the skin-air boundary on each section from a user-placed seed point inside one of the muscle groups. Following that, the program performs a region growing, starting from the same seed point, finding the cortical bone/muscle boundary. The region within the bone boundary is then excluded from subsequent soft tissue calculations.
3) The program then starts at the body contour, and grows inward, searching for the fat/muscle boundary. This provides mask of lean tissue.

Findings:
Astronaut study: Investigators have applied this methodology to pre- and post-flight scans of their astronaut data, including 16 subjects with pre- and postflight QCT scans. Comparison of pre- and post-flight scans showed 1-5 percent losses in total lean area and in the areas of the flexor, abductor, adductor and extensor muscle groups, with only a 5 percent loss in the adductor area being statistically significant (p=0.02) Small losses may reflect effect of inflight and postflight exercise protocols and the acquisition of CT data over 2-4 weeks post-return, allowing for some recovery of muscle area.

Hip fracture study: To test the hypothesis that hip muscle size and attenuation are associated with hip fracture, investigators compared CT scans of the contralateral hip in 45 women (mean age 74.71±5.94) imaged within 48 hours of their hip fractures to 66 age-matched control subjects (mean age 70.70±4.66). A volumetric CT scan encompassing the proximal part of the femur was analyzed for total percentage of fat tissue in the in the CT field of view and for the CSA and lean tissue Hounsfield Unit (HU) values of the hip extensor, abductor, adductor and flexor muscles. The CT scan was also analyzed to compute areal bone mineral density (aBMD) of the hip bone. Logistic regression analyses were employed to determine differences between fracture subjects and controls in body composition measures after adjustment for age, height, and BMI. Receiver-operator curve (ROC) analyses were employed to determine if combinations of aBMD and body composition were better discriminators of hip fracture than aBMD alone.

Investigators found that subjects with hip fractures were on average 5 years older (p<0.001) had 8 percent lower BMI (p<0.05), 8 percent lower percentage fat (p<0.0001) and roughly 20 percent lower extensor and adductor CSA values than controls (p<0.0001). Despite having lower total adiposity, they had higher muscle adiposity as indicated by lower lean tissue attenuation in all four muscle groups, with statistically significant differences in the adductor, abductor and flexor groups. After adjustment for age and BMI, the fracture subjects had lower total percent fat, smaller extensor and adductor CSA values, and greater adipose infiltration (lower attenuation) in the adductor (0.001 (less than) p (less than) 0.05). ROC analyses showed that models combining percent fat, muscle CSA and muscle attenuation values with aBMD had higher AUC values than models containing only aBMD (0.97 vs 0.88, p<0.001). The investigators conclude that reduced total adiposity and increased hip muscle adiposity appear to be independent correlates of hip fracture, and combination of skeletal and body composition variables appears to enhance diagnostic efficacy compared to skeletal variables alone.

experiment_title: Smart Therapeutic Ultrasound Device for Mission-Critical Medical Care
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The major goal of this effort was to utilize existing ultrasound platforms and the concept of image-guided therapy to control traumatic bleeding, ablate benign and malignant tumors, and to diagnose and reposition kidney stones. Investigators addressed (1) Lack of advanced therapeutic capability, (2) lack of capability to treat renal stones, and (3) lack of non-invasive diagnostic imaging capabilities. The original specific aims were: 1) Support ongoing leveraged efforts in Acoustic Hemostasis and HIFU Tumor Ablation by addressing fundamental scientific issues as well as to ensure NSBRI relevance. 2) Develop methods and technologies that would enable detection of renal stones with ultrasound. 3) Develop technology and perform in vitro studies of stone commination. 4) Utilizing technology and protocols developed in SAs 2 and 3, perform in vivo studies in a porcine model.

APPROACH:
Most stones are small enough to pass naturally and thus patients are encouraged, through hydration, to try to pass the stone without intervention. This natural process might take 6-8 weeks and result in considerable discomfort to the patient over this interval. With this innovative technology, a stone could potentially be cleared in the first office visit. Many stones do not clear with hydration, and thus more aggressive approaches are required. More invasive procedures are often necessary if the stone is in the lower pole because even if fragmented, the pieces are unlikely to pass from this location. The investigators’ technological approach would keep the least invasive option open for these patients. In most existing procedures, there is a significant chance stone pieces will remain behind as seeds for future stones and further surgery. This technology could help these pieces pass. In addition, stones are often recurrent; recurring-stone patients are often monitored, so that new stones can be detected early—this monitoring could be done with this precise stone imaging approach. This technology could also move these stones to the kidney exit before they are symptomatic. This technology reduces risk of surgery, complications of surgery for the patient, and the cost of surgery to the insurance companies; furthermore, the technology does not preclude any surgical options. Lastly, the algorithms to detect kidney stones alone stand to spare many patients the ionizing radiation of a CT scan, or to provide options to pregnant women or children with stones who are unlikely to receive CT. NSBRI quickly recognized the value of this technology and helped us initiate the commercialization effort that now has the full support of the UW, the Washington Research Foundation, and a commercial hardware provider, as well as the interest of several venture capitalists and ultrasound companies.

RESULTS:
The main findings and associated research productivity are:
1. Investigators have continued to advance ultrasound technology to detect and reposition kidney stones. The imaging technology provides an alternative to imaging techniques that expose the patient to ionizing radiation on earth and provides a user-friendly technique to detect even small stones in space. The repositioning technology provides an adjunctive treatment to surgery by which to facilitate the passage of residual fragments that my regrow to new stones, and provides a way to prophylactically remove small stones before they require surgery. The technology is also used to move a large obstructing stone to a non-obstructing location to delay the need for surgery.
2. Investigators contributed to the solicitation for a Flexible Ultrasound System (FUS), both as leaders in the platform and inventors of a required clinical capability (detecting and repositioning kidney stones), and an award for delivery of an FUS has now been granted.
3. Developed a method and device to characterize the acoustic output of high intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) devices. The University of Washington (UW) Center for Commercialization (C4C) has filed a provisional patent. The technique was added to the IEC TC87 62256 60601-2-62 standards document. The technology has now been demonstrated on several clinical HIFU systems. NIH funding was obtained.
4. Developed a method to accelerate and control tissue ablation with transcutaneous ultrasound. In particular, tissue was mechanically emulsified by millisecond bursts of HIFU at output levels that produce shock waves. C4C has filed a U.S. patent application. The Philips machine was modified to produce these outputs.
5. Investigators published an explanation of the mechanism of the twinkling artifact (TA) that frequently occurs during Doppler ultrasound imaging of kidney stones. These findings lead to the conclusion that bubbles cause the twinkling artifact and as such they have developed and patented several algorithms to exploit this mechanism to better detect kidney stones. Because twinkling is seen on other calcifications in the body, the result also implies bubbles may be on present throughout the body, which has significant implications for decompression sickness.
6. Due to cost and concerns for repeated ionizing radiation exposure from CT scans on Earth, ultrasound is often used for the initial evaluation and monitoring of kidney stone patients. In space ultrasound is the only option and size of the stone is critical in treatment planning. Investigators published work, submitted a patent application, and began preliminary work to measure the inaccuracy of ultrasound in sizing stones and develop improvements.

experiment_title: Skeletal Response
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Bone is a living organ that is continuously remodeling itself. When mechanical forces applied to the skeleton during normal activity in a 1-G environment are removed, bone mineral is lost because bone resorption is greater than bone formation. Bone resorption represents a danger not only because of the risk of fracture in demineralized bones, but also because the concomitant increased urinary calcium excretion might increase the risk for the formation of kidney stones.

The purpose of this experiment was to determine the effect of microgravity on the skeletal system during space flight. Studies conducted during the Gemini 4, 5, and 7, and Apollo 7 and 8 missions used x-ray densitometry to measure the amount of bone mineral present in the os calcis, radius, ulna, and phalanges. The studies revealed significant bone mineral losses in all areas measured. The degree of loss appeared excessive for such short periods in microgravity. Further evaluation of the data determined that bone mineral loses were lower than what was first measured. The overestimates were primarily due to problems inherent in the measurement techniques used. Scientists concluded that x-ray densitometry was unreliable for calculating bone mineral losses. It was not until a much more stable method of measuring bone mineral content, called photon absorptiometry, was developed that bone mineral studies continued during Apollo 14, 15, and 16.

Early reports of significant bone mineral losses in the 5- to 14-day Gemini and Apollo missions emphasized the need for correlating mineral losses observed in ground-based studies with those observed during microgravity. Ground-based studies designed to mimic the microgravity condition were used to estimate when changes were likely to occur during a mission. Bed rest served as an experimental model since the loss of bone mineral in bed rested and immobilized patients had been observed during periods of up to 36 weeks.

It was determined during these studies that the amount of initial mineral content in the os calcis could influence the rate of mineral loss. Bed rested subjects who exhibited a high mineral content at the beginning of bed rest showed the least mineral loss both in percentage and in quantity. Conversely, subjects who exhibited a low mineral content at the onset of bed rest showed a greater rate of mineral loss. The bed rest model was also used to determine what remedial measures might be used to both reduce bone mineral loss and predict bone mineral losses in the astronauts.

Thus, another goal of this study was to establish time courses for both the bed rest and flight situations so that better estimates could be obtained on the risk of prolonged space flight as translated from the ground-based bed rest studies.

APPROACH:
Bone scans using the photon absorptiometry technique were made on the crewmembers of Apollo 14 (10-day mission), Apollo 15 (12-day), and Apollo 16 (11-day) approximately one month, two weeks, and one week before flight. Each data collection session consisted of one x-ray and three bone scans of the left central os calcis, the right radius and the right ulna. Four postflight measurement sessions were conducted for each crewmember at various times. A series of control subject measurements was made in parallel with the crewmembers. Three subjects each were studied during Apollo 14 and Apollo 15, and four subjects were studied during Apollo 16.

A photon scanning device, called a rectilinear bone mineral scanner, was used during the experiment. The extremity to be measured was placed in tissue equivalent material (TEM) to compensate for the irregular thickness of tissue cover that surrounded the bone. The extremity, encased in the TEM, was placed between the photon source, Iodine-125 (125I), and a photon detector. The photon source and detector were aligned in direct opposition to each other so that a 3-millimeter source beam was directed into a 3-millimeter entrance on the detector. The absorptiometer scanned the section of bone in a series of sixteen straight, parallel lines covering the entire area. The scanner could be configured to accommodate either the upper or lower extremity. As the transmitted beam passed through the segment of bone, the detector on the opposite side measured the intensity of the radiation after it had passed through the TEM and the bone. Researchers were then able to calculate the amount of mineral content in the bone segment. The entire system was calibrated before and after each scan by making four passes over a Witt-Cameron standard.

Because of space restrictions in the quarantine facility and isolation restrictions, only a single scanner device could be used during the postflight period of Apollo 14. For this reason, arm and heel scans were performed separately using the same scanner in each of the two configurations. On the two subsequent missions, arm and heel studies were performed simultaneously both preflight and postflight, because quarantine was no longer required.

RESULTS:
Mineral losses were not observed in the os calcis, radius, or ulna in the Apollo 14 or Apollo 16 crewmembers. Only two Apollo 15 crewmembers lost mineral from the os calcis. Both crewmembers regained the bone mineral losses and were near baseline values by the end of two weeks. The magnitude of loss, when compared to the control subjects, was 5 to 6 percent. Mineral losses were not observed in radius or ulna mineral during the Apollo 15 flight.

A significant increase in fatty tissue was observed on the plantar side of the os calcis in one subject of Apollo 14 immediately postflight. This subject showed a 34 percent increase in fat equivalence when compared to immediate preflight measurements. This increase would have resulted in a 4.3 percent overestimation of bone mineral if the soft tissue contribution had not been measured. In contrast, the other two crewmembers showed between a 8.1 and 8.4 percent increase in fat equivalence with a potential 2.5 and 2.2 percent overestimation in bone mineral. No significant changes in the soft tissue composition were observed in the Apollo 15 or 16 crewmembers.

Researchers established a predictive model for bone mineral loss for the bed rested subjects. In this model, the ratio of initial bone mineral content to the initial 24-hour urinary hydroxyproline excretion was compared to observed losses. The greater the ratio, the slower and smaller the mineral losses and, conversely, the smaller the ratio, the faster and greater the mineral losses. The accurate measurement of baseline 24-hour urinary hydroxyproline excretion was therefore an essential requirement for these predictions. Unfortunately, no time course could be established for the microgravity state because of limited data. Researchers hoped that additional data collected during the Skylab missions would determine a time course of bone mineral losses that could be compared with the bed rest data. Therefore, bed rest studies could be established as a good model for the effects of weight unloading. Secondly, bed rest studies could serve as a predictive measure for longer space missions.

It was concluded that mineral losses from bone incident to periods of microgravity were comparable to that observed in bed rested subjects and that the magnitude was not severe. If these losses were allowed to continue unabated for a prolonged period of time, the consequences might be more serious because the losses were probably not confined to the bones described.

experiment_title: HZE-induced Skin Carcinoma: An in-vivo-like Multicellular Epithelial Model System for Analysis of Radiation Quality Effects and DSB Repair Processes
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Skin as a model system to study radiation-induced human epithelial cancers: Skin is one of the most complex organs of the body, consisting of multiple cell types, including epithelial keratinocytes and connective tissue (i.e. fibroblasts). Keratinocytes form a stratified squamous epithelium and are composed of one basal cell layer and several differentiated cell layers. Proliferation is limited to the basal layer, whereas differentiating cells withdraw from the cell cycle and express various differentiation markers, dependent on the stage of their differentiation. Because radiation-induced neoplasms in skin derive primarily from epithelial cells, radiobiological studies on keratinocyte monolayers (2D) provide a good first approximation for assessing cancer development processes triggered by ionizing radiation, but also by other environmental mutagens.

APPROACH:
There is considerable evidence that ionizing radiation causes non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC), and the risk for NMSC in astronauts is increased. To further assess the cancer risk for humans from space radiation, an in-vivo-like multicellular skin model system was used. Multiple different endpoints as surrogate markers for skin cancer were assessed. Persistent chromosomal damage, altered cell proliferation, and evasion from apoptosis were studied in 2D monolayer cultures of normal primary and of initiated human keratinocytes exposed to a variety of charged nuclei (Aim 1). In addition, to more realistically recapitulate the complex architecture of a tissue, an in-vivo-like skin model system, composed of fibroblasts and keratinocytes, was used to ascertain the risk of space radiation-induced cancer development processes in 3D (i.e. persistent chromosomal damage, altered cell proliferation, evasion from apoptosis, and differentiation) (Aim 2). Lastly, a surface transplantation assay of exposed 3D reconstructed human epithelia onto immunodeficient mice was carried out to test for intermediate and late events in cancer progression (cell invasion and metastasis, respectively) (Aim 3). Investigators hypothesized that, in basal cells, unfaithful DNA DSB repair will lead to persistent chromosomal damage, promoting altered cell growth and escape from tissue homeostasis. They believe that the proposed approach is highly relevant for assessing the risk of skin cancer in astronauts and for modeling space radiation-induced tumor development in other epithelial tissues.

RESULTS:
The cytokinesis-block micronucleus (MN) assay was used to assess the genotoxicity of low doses of different types of space radiation. Normal human primary keratinocytes and immortalized keratinocytes grown in 2D monolayers each were exposed to graded doses of 0.3 or 1.0 GeV/n silicon ions or similar energies of iron ions. The frequencies of induced MN were determined and compared to gamma-ray data. RBEmax values ranged from 2.0 to 3.9 for primary keratinocytes and from 2.4 to 6.3 for immortalized keratinocytes. At low radiation doses = 0.4 Gy, 0.3 GeV/n iron ions were the most effective at inducing MN in normal keratinocytes. An “over-kill effect” was observed for 0.3 GeV/n iron ions at higher doses, wherein 1.0 GeV/n iron ions were most efficient in inducing MN. In immortalized keratinocytes, 0.3 GeV/n iron ions produced MN with greater frequency than 1.0 GeV/n iron ions, except at the highest dose tested. MN formation was higher in immortalized keratinocytes than in normal keratinocytes for all doses and radiation qualities investigated.

MN induction was also assessed in human keratinocytes cultured in 3D to simulate the complex architecture of human skin. RBE values for MN formation in 3D were reduced for normal keratinocytes exposed to iron ions, but were elevated for immortalized keratinocytes. Overall, MN induction was significantly lower in keratinocytes cultured in 3D than in 2D. Together, the results suggest that tissue architecture and immortalization status modulate the genotoxic response to space radiation, perhaps via alterations in DNA repair fidelity.

Investigators also established a surface transplantation assay, which allowed them to extend their studies of the biological responses of human skin equivalents up to several months post radiation exposure. To do so, male NOD.SCID mice (obtained from Jackson Laboratory) were subjected to the skin grafting procedure at approximately 8 weeks of age and sent to BNL 4 weeks post-surgery. Cohorts of 6 mice each were exposed to 1 Gy of 300 or 1000 MeV/n Fe ions, or to 1 Gy of 137Cs gamma-rays for comparison purposes. Six mice were sham irradiated. All mice remained at BNL until necropsy at 8 weeks post radiation exposure. Tissue sections of the human skin grafts and of the undisturbed mouse skin were fixed in 10% buffered formaldehyde for 48 hours, followed by transfer and storage in 70% ethanol until processed and embedded in paraffin. Sections of 3 µm each were assessed by H&E staining for tissue architecture, by FISH using mouse and human COT1 DNA for tissue origin, and by IHC for markers of radiation exposure (53BP1 (i.e. genomic instability), Ki-67 (i.e. cell proliferation), and involucrin (i.e. keratinocyte differentiation).

Preliminary results show that 53BP1 foci are elevated and persistent in basal keratinocytes of human skin equivalents after radiation exposure. Keratinocytes with locally accumulated nuclear staining for 53BP1 are negative for Ki-67, indicative of a reinforced irreversible growth arrest of cells with persistent genomic instability. Investigators speculate that cellular senescence is accelerated in human basal cells following high LET radiation exposure to limit the proliferation of damaged cells that are at risk for neoplastic transformation, similar to the observations reported by others using low LET IR.

experiment_title: Study of the Digestive Transportation Function of the Small Intestine
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous experiments have revealed an increase in the acidic-peptic potential of the stomach and a decline of the functional capability of the pancreas. This experiment was to conduct a morphological and biochemical investigation of changes in the mucous membrane of the small intestine after spaceflight.

Approach:

The duodenum, jejunum, and ileum sections of the small intestine were removed from flight and control animals, and the mucosa was examined with an electron microscope. Enzymes involved in cavity and membrane digestion (carbohydrases, peptidases, monoglyceride lipase, alkaline phosphatase) were investigated biochemically.

Results:

The investigation of the functional status of the small intestine revealed complex changes of enzyme activities. In the system of protein membrane hydrolysis there was a shift of proximodistal gradient dipeptidase activity indicating the compensatory nature of the changes. Analysis of processes of lipid digestion revealed a number of alterations in their digestive pattern manifested as a significant decrease of nonglyceridelipase activity, and an increase of alkaline phosphatase activity in the proximal segment of the small intestine, again, reflecting the compensatory and adaptational nature of the alterations. In the carbohydrase enzymatic change no significant alterations were found. Changes of digestive/transport hydrolysis of proteins, fats, and carbohydrates were reversible and functional in nature. The adaptive nature of the rearrangements of membrane digestion is demonstrated by a self-regulatory activity of the digestive system in the distribution of enzyme activities.

experiment_title: Monitoring of Bone Loss Bio-Markers in Human Sweat: A Non-Invasive, Time Efficient Means of Monitoring Bone Resorption Markers under Micro and Partial Gravity Loading Conditions
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Loss of bone mass, density and structural integrity is a significant health risk in a variety of populations such as the elderly, post-menopausal women, young female athletes and astronauts. Such changes in overall bone quality lead to a greater risk of bone fracture and potentially a reduced rate of bone healing after injury. The ability to monitor biomarkers of bone remodeling (e.g. ionized calcium, collagen cross links) using sweat as an analytical sample provides an attractive alternative to the more invasive and costly measures presently employed, such as a bone density scans by DXA, 24-hour urine collection protocols or whole blood analyses.

The development of a non-invasive, skin-mounted monitoring device which allows the quantitation of ionized calcium and/or collagen cross links in sweat will allow bone loss to be monitored in a wide variety of terrestrial populations that to date have not easily been monitored outside of a clinical setting. This particular project focuses on validating the concept that sweat analysis can be used as a non-invasive means of monitoring bone loss in crew members during periods of mechanical unloading under altered gravitational conditions. In addition, this project is also investigating the best technical approach to collecting a sweat sample, specifically applicable to the space-flight environment, while utilizing well-accepted, clinically validated analytical methods. Development of a technology capable of real-time monitoring of biomarkers of bone loss that satisfies the criteria required for use in the space-flight environment (i.e. non-invasive/non-intrusive, passive, small, light-weight, low power) has many direct applications in various populations here on Earth.

APPROACH:
The team was tasked with validating that the rate and extent of unloading-induced bone loss in humans can be assessed by monitoring the levels of two bone resorption markers in sweat, namely ionized calcium and collagen break-down products. Initial testing was carried out in a young healthy population (at rest and during activity) and then in a clinical population undergoing active bone loss, namely spinal cord injury patients. All groups included both male and female participants. Biomarker concentration was determined in contemporaneous samples of sweat, blood, and urine collected during both short (24 hour) and long-term studies (multiple sessions over a period of months) to define the relationship between biomarker levels in the respective biological samples. Several different sweat collection techniques were investigated to determine the most appropriate and efficient means of sample collection suitable for deployment during a space flight mission. These experiments also included investigation of the most appropriate biomarker analysis techniques that allow for future deployment in micro- or partial gravity environments. This near-real-time monitoring approach also provided the information required to justify modifying an ineffective bone loss countermeasure prescription during a mission. One of the approaches tested was a novel, micro-fabricated fluid collection capillary array, known as the micro-fabricated sweat patch (MSP) device, specifically developed for use in microgravity. The MSP technology was initially developed because of its potential to become an autonomous, solid-state collection/analysis device worn on the skin of an astronaut requiring little or no crew interaction to perform its monitoring function.

RESULTS:
Initial studies indicate significant individual variation in the amount and rate of sweating observed between subjects based on: 1) the anatomical site sampled (i.e. forehead, shoulder, forearm); 2) level of activity (i.e. "active" sweating during exercise; and 3) the concentration of biomarkers relative to the onset of "active" sweating. In addition, the existing sweat collection technology previously employed to collect sweat (i.e. commercial absorptive pad) exhibited significant analytical issues based on sub-optimal analyte retention and analyte extraction efficiency. To overcome these difficulties investigators developed a standardized sweat collection protocol in which subjects performed a defined exercise protocol at a fixed level of intensity (i.e. 30 minutes of aerobic exercise at an intensity of 40 percent of their age-predicted VO2max) under similar environmental conditions and hydration status. Sweat samples were collected at the forehead using micro-fabricated polymer capillary arrays which collect sweat as an unadulterated liquid sample. This approach allows both determination of the volume of sweat produced and has the advantage of minimal residual analyte retention within the array due to its polymer construction, unlike the commercially available absorptive sweat collection technology.

Sweat samples were initially collected at discrete time intervals to determine when during exercise-induced sweating did biomarker concentration reach "steady-state" levels. These experiments indicated that biomarker concentrations (i.e. Ca2+ and T-CCL) in "active" sweat reached a "steady state" after 15 minutes of exercise regardless of the volume of sweat produced by a particular individual. In addition, analyte concentration (i.e. T-CCL) in actively produced sweat was found to be highly correlated (R = 0.92) with plasma levels of the same analyte during the period sweat was being collected. However, comparison of analyte concentration produced during actively produced sweat and 24 hour urine voids in the same individual indicated, indicated that although related in a linear fashion (R = 0.61), sweat analyte excretion during the 15 min period of exercise was not predictive of total 24hr urine analyte excretion. As 24 hour urine void collection provides an integrated value for whole body biomarker excretion rates, comparison of the amount of biomarker excreted during a 15 minute period of “active” sweating from 7.5cm of skin surface at the fore-head appears inappropriate as a means of predicting total calcium and T-CCL excreted in a 24 hour urine void.

The team investigated the accuracy of the existing commercially available absorptive patch sweat collection technology with regard to analyte concentration relative to unadulterated liquid sweat samples collected in a contemporaneous fashion at the same anatomical site. These data indicated that the cellulose matrix of the commercially available absorptive patch posed significant analytical problems. These issues were that the cellulose matrix: 1) contained significant amounts of endogenous calcium signal; 2) resulted in significant retention of sweat-derived T-CCL that could not be extracted from the matrix using the standard method (i.e. extraction in ddH2O); and 3) that extraction efficiency from the matrix was variable between identical samples. To address these analytical issues during Year 2 of these projects, investigators studied the use of two new absorptive materials, a glass fiber material and a polypropylene woven material, for the collection of sweat over a 24 hour period. Their initial experiments focused on the extraction efficiency of four bone loss biomarkers of interest, namely calcium, T-CCL, NTx and osteocalcin (OST). They also modified the extraction protocol to utilize acidified ddH2O (pH 5.0) or a Tris buffer (pH 5.0) to enhance the solubility of these biomarkers in the extraction buffer and reduce ionic interactions within the matrix of the absorptive material. Unlike the original commercially available cellulose absorptive pad technology, efficient recovery of known amounts of all analytes was achieved using our modified extraction method from both the glass fiber and woven polypropylene materials.

Glass fiber absorptive pads (7.5cm2 in area) and the modified extraction protocol were used to collect sweat samples from a total of 18 normal healthy subjects over a period of 24 hours at three separate anatomical locations: shoulder, hip and forearm. 24 hour urine voids were also collected from these subjects during the same 24 hour period. When the total amount of calcium excreted in sweat over a 24 hour period into a 7.5cm2 glass fiber absorptive pad was compared to the total amount of calcium excreted in a 24 hour urine void obtained from the same individual, results indicated that there is a near linear correlation between the two values in sweat collected from the shoulder (R = 0.90) and forearm (R=0.86) and contemporaneous 24 hour urine voids. A similar relationship between 24 hour sweat T-CCL and 24 hour urine void T-CCL levels was observed at the shoulder (R = 0.99) in a subset of these subjects (N=6) for which this analysis has been completed. Data indicate that calcium and T-CCL levels detected in 24 hour sweat samples are highly correlated with levels detected in 24 hour urine voids from healthy individuals, suggesting that bone loss biomarker concentration in the criterion sample (i.e. 24 hour urine void) can be accurately predicted from that found in a sweat sample collected over the same 24 hour period using an absorptive pad technology.

The project then focused on validating this approach to monitoring bone loss biomarkers in a terrestrial population undergoing active bone loss (a clinical population of spinal cord injured patients). In addition, the team also developed a new protocol suitable for deployment on-orbit for the extraction and collection of analytes from the absorptive sweat patch based on the Salivette technology previously validated for use on-orbit.
