experiment_title: Physiological Effects of Iodinated Water on Thyroid Function
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Iodine has been used as a potable water treatment and storage bactericidal agent by NASA for over three decades beginning with the Apollo program, and was a critical factor for the achievement of human space flight. Iodine is currently used for Space Shuttle potable water microbial control and the U.S. component of the International Space Station (ISS). The ISS U.S. water system recycles water from urine and other wastewaters for human consumption and requires long-term storage. With the proposed iodine exposure levels and the crewmembers originating from many countries including regions of low iodine intake, concerns have been raised regarding the use of iodine in ISS potable water.

Iodine is a component of the two major thyroid hormones, thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). These hormones regulate many key biochemical processes. Major target organs are the developing brain, muscle, heart, pituitary, and kidney. Most ingested iodine is reduced in the gut to iodide, which is absorbed almost completely. Once in circulation, iodide is removed primarily by the thyroid gland and kidney. The thyroid selectively concentrates iodide with the excess excreted into the urine. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), produced in the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland, regulates the release of thyroid hormones from the thyroid gland into the blood. TSH secretion from the pituitary gland increases when the levels of circulating thyroid hormones decrease. The thyroid responds to the ingestion of elevated quantities of iodine by a transient decrease in thyroid hormone synthesis, termed the acute Wolff-Chaikoff effect.

An investigation was undertaken during three ground-based, closed-chamber tests to examine thyroid function and hormone levels in chamber subjects who consumed potable water containing iodine. The purpose of this study was to document the thyroid functional biochemical measurements (n=12), urine iodine levels (n=8), and any clinical signs or symptoms of thyroid dysfunction in the 12 crewmembers who participated in the chamber studies.

APPROACH:

The chamber tests, in order of occurrence, were 30 days, Phase II; 60 days, Phase IIa; and 91 days, Phase III. Each chamber test had four crewmembers. Each crewmember was considered to be in good health and had normal thyroid function. In all three chamber tests, after the water recycling process was completed, 3.5 to 5.2 mg iodine/L was added to the water as the disinfectant. In Phase II (30 days) and Phase IIa (60 days), thyroid hormonal status (TSH and thyroid hormone levels) was assessed both in the pre- and postchamber period. In Phase III, the 91-day study, TSH, thyroid hormones, and urinary iodine levels were measured before and several times in chamber (first measurement at the 30-day mark). These were followed up with several more measurements in the postchamber period upon the subjects' exit from the chamber at the completion of the study. Subjects were monitored until all indices of iodine/thyroid status had returned to prechamber levels.

For the Phase III study (91 days), due to changes in TSH levels at the 30-day mark, iodine was removed from the potable water before consumption. This was accomplished by installing an iodine-removal device and a microbial filter (0.2 µm) at the point of use of the water on chamber day 35. This device removed the iodine (I2 and I-) from the drinking water but did not affect the iodine levels in the remainder of the water used, i.e., for hygiene activities. Urinary iodine levels were spot-checked to determine iodine exposure.

RESULTS:

While individual water consumption was not determined for Phases II and IIa crewmembers, analysis of diet records and the systematic evaluation of water usage indicates the crewmembers consumed from 4 to 10 mg total iodine/day. For Phase IIa (60 days), drinking water contained approximately 2 to 4 mg I/L and subjects excreted approximately 4.5 to 14 mg/day. Intake measurements were only completed twice during the study. The actual individual water iodine intakes and urinary losses were quantified for the Phase III, 91-day test. The total iodine in the water varied from approximately 3 to 8 mg/L with an average level for the first 35 days around 5 mg total iodine/L. Urinary iodine levels reflect recent iodine consumption. In all subjects, urinary iodine levels increased about 10-fold during the first 30 days of the Phase III chamber study, with iodine consumption levels ranging from 8 to 20 mg/day. Urinary excretion means for subjects ranged from 9.4 to 16.9 mg I/day. The variation in iodine intake between crewmembers was related to the individual volume of potable water consumed. Following installation of the iodine removal device at the galley sink, the total iodine levels measured less than 0.05 mg/L in the drinking water but remained in full concentration in the shower and wash water. Urinary iodine levels decreased 5- to 10-fold after cessation of the water iodine exposure but remained above baseline values. By the end of the 91-day study, 56 days after cessation of drinking water iodine, the urinary values continued to remain above baseline values in three of the four subjects. In three of the crewmembers, urine iodine levels fell to an average of 0.283 mg/24 hrs by three days after test completion.

Although mean TSH levels remained within normal range throughout the studies, there was a statistically significant increase in TSH levels in the Phase II and III studies. For the Phase II study, the values returned to baseline levels in all subjects within two weeks after the subjects exited the chamber. In the 60-day Phase IIa study, although not a statistically significant change, serum TSH in three of the four subjects had increased by the end of the study. One subject, who had a baseline TSH value close to the upper limit, had a decreased TSH value below the baseline value at the end of the chamber study. This subject had the highest iodine consumption and urinary levels of the four subjects in the Phase IIa test. At day 62 postchamber, this subject had a very high TSH level and was referred for medical evaluation by an endocrinologist. There were no other biochemical or clinical signs of thyroid disease, and the TSH returned to near baseline value several months later.

In the 91-day study, the mean serum TSH level in the four test subjects increased significantly above baseline values 30 days after entering the chamber. After the iodine was removed from the drinking water on day 35 (concentration < 0.05 mg/L), the TSH values gradually decreased but did not completely return to baseline during the subsequent 56 days in the chamber.

For one subject in the Phase III study, the TSH remained higher than the baseline value but within the normal reference range throughout the chamber study period, with no decrease in the level after removal of iodine from the drinking water. After one year, the TSH levels returned to prechamber baseline levels. All other measures of thyroid function remained within normal ranges. The consulting endocrinologist diagnosed the crewmember with iodine-induced subclinical hyperthyroidism.

During the Phase III study, urinary iodine levels remained at approximately 1 mg/day after iodine removal from drinking water at day 35, but returned to baseline levels within three days of exiting the chamber. One potential source of iodine contamination involved the methods for urine collection and measurement. A study was completed and found that this was not the cause of the persistence of urinary iodine levels above baseline. Other potential sources of iodine contamination were discussed and considered, however, no plausible explanation was identified.

The results from the three chamber tests demonstrated that the levels of iodine in the potable water system proposed for the ISS were too high. Since these studies were concluded, the Food and Nutrition Board has established an upper limit for iodine intakes from all sources as 1.1 mg/day. The subjects in the chamber studies exceeded this level and consequently, for two subjects, TSH levels were significantly changed by the end of the chamber test. Since food consumption provides about 0.25 mg/day, the requirement was set at a maximum of 0.25 mg of iodine/L in ISS water supplied by the United States. This would limit water consumption to a maximum of 3 L/day to maintain daily intake levels from all sources at less than the limit established by NASA of less than 1.0 mg/day of iodine. Consequently, there remains concern that the maximum level of 0.25 mg/L of iodine in the spacecraft water will not provide sufficient microbial control, thus increasing the risk to ISS crewmembers.

experiment_title: Neuroendocrine and Cardiovascular Response to Tilt (Flight Analog)
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Stand tests are used to assess the effects of prolonged weightlessness on orthostatic tolerance during upright posture. Attempts are made to identify high-risk crewmembers before their current flight and adjust their inflight countermeasures accordingly, such as varying the proportion of aerobic versus resistive exercise and adjusting end-of-mission countermeasures. Postflight data are used to guide rehabilitative measures and optimize performance on future flights. Group data are used to assess the influence of other physical and physiological factors such as countermeasures, mission duration, and heat stress.
APPROACH:
Subjects were placed on a tilt table with ECG electrodes applied to the chest and abdomen. An intravenous catheter was placed in a vein in the arm. Blood pressure cuffs were placed on the arm that does not contain the catheter. The subject rested for 20 minutes and then blood was drawn. Continuous measures of heart rate, ECG, arterial pressure, and aortic blood flow were collected for five minutes. The subject was then tilted upright at 80° for 30 minutes. A final blood draw took place at the conclusion to compare with that drawn in the supine position. If the subject could not tolerate 30 minutes of upright tilt, the tilt table was placed in the -10° head down tilt (HDT) position and blood drawn immediately if the subject stood for longer than seven minutes; otherwise, blood was drawn after one minute.
RESULTS:
During the artificial gravity (AG) pilot study it was concluded that AG can mitigate some aspects of bed rest-induced cardiovascular deconditioning, including orthostatic intolerance and aerobic power. Mechanisms of improvement were not cardiac-mediated, but likely through improved sympathetic responsiveness to orthostatic stress.

experiment_title: Retrospective Analysis of Inflight Exercise Loading and Health Outcomes
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts perform treadmill exercise during long-duration space missions to counter the harmful effects of microgravity exposure upon bone, muscle, and cardiopulmonary health. When exercising in microgravity, astronauts wear a harness and bungee system that provides forces that maintain attachment to the treadmill. Typical applied forces are less than body weight. The current exercise devices on the International Space Station (ISS) allow astronauts to complete prescriptions at higher intensities which potentially allow for greater exercise benefits with increased efficiency. However, although overall health outcomes have improved, the specific factors related to increased benefits have yet to be determined.

This study had the following specific aims:

  1. Quantify the exercise-related mechanical loading experienced by crewmembers during their mission on the ISS.
  2. Explore relationships between exercise loading variables, bone, and muscle health changes during the mission.
  3. Determine if specific mechanical loading variables are more critical than others in protecting health.
  4. Develop methodology for operational use in monitoring crew exercise programs.

APPROACH:
This retrospective analysis was conducted using data from seven crewmembers that were subjects in the Treadmill Kinematics study (Kinematics_T2). Crewmembers completed approximately six-month missions on the ISS and performed regular exercise on the T2 throughout their mission, although each subject’s specific prescription varied. Exercise logs and inflight ground reaction force data were summarized to quantify T2 mechanical loading occurring during flight. Mechanical loading variables were compared to bone mineral density changes to determine if relationships existed.

RESULTS:
Results indicate that increased time and distance jogging related to improved bone health. Further investigation revealed that in the current subject pool, those who performed exercise sessions that include both running and jogging, such as during high intensity interval training, tended to have better bone-related outcomes. More study is necessary, including increasing subject size and inclusion of resistance exercise to better assess exercise relationships to bone health.

experiment_title: Serial Changes in Site Specific Bone Density and Structure with Paralysis
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Study 1: The purpose of the first study is to investigate the effect of paralysis on bone density and structural parameters of the tibia. Study 2: The purpose of the second study was to investigate bone mass and structure in the tibia after resection of the fibula.

APPROACH:
Study 1: were two male and two female adults aged 17-32 years who had sustained a spinal cord injury at least 4 years prior to the study. Cross-sectional structural parameters including area (A), principal area moments of inertia (Imax, Imin), polar area moments of inertia (J), and major principal axis orientation of the tibia and fibula were computed every millimeter along the scan length for the three scans of the leg using the lower energy for its larger dynamic range. Study 2: Subjects who had undergone a fibular resection at least 2 years earlier were recruited (n=3). Fibular resection was carried out in all 3 men to remedy avascular necrosis in the hip. In addition to anthropomorphic data (BW, Ht, tibial length) a set of 3 scans of the tibia on right and left sides as above was done as well as a DXA scan of the right and left calcaneus to measure areal bone density, an indication of loading symmetry. Structural parameters of the tibia and fibula as enumerated above were performed on one leg and on the tibia of the other leg.

RESULTS:
Study 1: Body weights in paraplegics were greater than in controls. Two male subjects had lower values for cross-sectional areas and density as well as lower structural parameters in the midshaft, distal tibia and femoral midshaft. Data supporting bone loss in the two female paraplegics was not convincing except at the tibial midshaft where the data was not scaled to body size. In one male subject, cross sectional areas and principal moments of inertia of the tibia were not symmetrical. Conclusions of study 1: The large variation in results of just a few subjects point to the need for longitudinal studies and more subjects to definitively measure changes in structural parameters due to paralysis and unloading. Study 2: Subject 1. The cross-sectional area of the tibia on the side of the fibular resection (rt) was increased 2% at the midshaft and 33% at the distal third compared to the unaffected tibia. The principal and polar moments of inertia on the right tibia were increased 51% and 89% at the midshaft and distal third, respectively. The midshaft was also more symmetric, but not the distal section. Subject 2: The tibia on the resected side (left) showed an increase in cross-sectional area (8% at midshaft and 10% at distal third) and an increased minimum moment of inertia of 22 % in the mid and 47% in the distal third. Imax increased by 9% in both sites. Subject 3: The increases in the cross-sectional area were 32% at the mid and 27% at the distal third, compared to the unaffected left side. Imin increased by 74% and 95% at the distal third and Imax increased 15 and 24 % in the same respective regions, an indication the tibia is more symmetric. Calcaneal density was not consistent in the 3 subjects and showed R and L differences outside the 0.6% observed in normal men. Calcaneal density was less (by 5.7 and 8 %) in the affected than the unaffected limb in two subjects who also had functional problems in gait. The lower heel density may be an indication of less load on the affected limb and was not present in the subject who reported normal gait and skiing activity post surgery. Conclusions: All three subjects with fibular resection showed an increase in cross-sectional area as well as structural parameters related to stiffness and strength, an indication of increased loading of the tibia from the ipsilateral side of the fibular resection resulting in increased bone deposition. This points to a role of the fibula in driving the shape of the tibia cross-section and in load bearing.

experiment_title: Sonographic Astronaut Vertebral Examination
experiment_description:
This study provided longitudinal, real-time data regarding adaptation of the vertebral unit during long-duration space flight to enhance mission completion, countermeasure development, and astronaut health. The ability to assess the crewmember’s musculoskeletal (MSK) system is critical to guide countermeasures, provide functional data for high risk or impact activities, and assess acute injuries which may occur during exploration class space flight or return to Earth. This study had the following specific aims:
  1. Determine the accuracy of MSK ultrasound in characterizing the normal and microgravity associated changes in the vertebral unit.
  2. Investigate the human factors, level of experience, and training necessary to perform focused cervical and lumbar vertebral MSK ultrasound in microgravity with inexperienced ultrasound operators in parallel with expert operators.
  3. Determine the anatomic changes in the vertebral unit during long-duration space flight with astronaut performed vertebral ultrasound.

APPROACH:
Preflight baseline data collection (BDC) sessions consisted of a cervical and lumbosacral vertebral MRI along with a cervical and lumbosacral vertebral ultrasound. In fight, a comprehensive evaluation of the cervical and lumbosacral vertebral units to assess alterations in the intervetebral disc (IVD) spacing, ligaments, and other structural and functional relationships secondary to prolonged microgravity were performed at FD30 (±15), FD90 (±15), and FD150 (±15). Postflight BDC sessions consisted of a cervical and lumbosacral vertebral MRI, a back-pain questionnaire, and a cervical and lumbosacral vertebral ultrasound which was conducted within the R+4 (±3) timeframe.

RESULTS:
Ultrasound correlated well with preflight and post flight MRI examinations. Investigators demonstrated that ultrasound has the potential to be an accurate tool to assess acute and chronic changes to the spine during flight. They showed changes in the curvature of long-duration crewmembers, and some changes to the intervertebral disks and bodies that may lead to a higher change of spinal injury.

experiment_title: Blood Volume Changes and Red Blood Cell Life Span
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Decreased red blood cell mass has been found regularly among astronauts returning from space flight. This observation was first documented in the crew of the 8-day Gemini 5 mission and confirmed in the crewmembers of the 14-day Gemini 7 mission. In addition, it was observed that the red blood cell half- life (the time for half of the total amount of tagged red blood cells to be removed from circulation) was shortened, suggesting that hemolysis combined with bone marrow unresponsive to stimulation of red blood cell production caused the decrease in circulating red blood cells and subsequent decreased red blood cell mass.

Red blood cell half-life was not shortened on the Apollo missions, although the crews of both Apollo and Gemini missions were exposed to at least four hours of 100% oxygen prior to launch and during flight. It was not clear whether inhibition of erythropoiesis (decreased production of red blood cells) caused by hyperoxia, or hemolysis of red blood cells (increased destruction) was the causative agent for the decrease in red blood cell mass. The Skylab missions offered the opportunity to rule out the hyperoxia hypothesis while testing whether changes in red blood cell mass are progressive with longer periods of weightlessness. Skylab experiment M113 was designed to (1) determine the effect of Earth-orbital missions on plasma volume and red blood cell populations (particularly red cell mass, life span, and production and destruction rates), and (2) provide baseline data for correlation with data from other hematologic and immunologic experiments.

APPROACH:
Red cell mass measurements were made according to the following schedule. On the 28-day Skylab 2 mission, measurements were made 29 days prior to launch, on recovery (landing) day and 13, 42 and 67 days after recovery. On the 59-day Skylab 3 mission, measurements were made 20 days before launch, on recovery day, and 14 and 45 days after recovery. On the 84-day Skylab 4 mission, measurements were made 21 days and 1 day before launch, on recovery day and 14 and 31 days after recovery. All specimens were drawn in the morning after an overnight rest with the crewman fasting, except for the recovery day samples, which were drawn within 2 hours after the spacecraft landed.

Most measurements in this experiment were obtained by the tracer kinetics method. The red blood cell mass and half-life were determined using 51chromium (51Cr) as the tracer. A sample of 12.5 milliliters of blood was drawn and mixed with 2.5 milliliters of anticoagulant acid citrate dextrose (ACD) solution and 25 microcuries of 51Cr. Ten milliliters of 51Cr-tagged cells from the sample were reinfused into the bloodstream after incubating the cells for 4 minutes at room temperature and adding 50 milligrams of ascorbic acid. The red blood cell mass was determined by averaging the radioactivity of 30- and 31-minute red blood cell samples. Red blood cell chromium half-life was estimated from the measured activity profile of 51Cr. Plasma volume was measured by injecting 2 microcuries of 125iodine human serum albumin each time the red blood cell mass was determined.

To track the red blood cell lifespan, 50 microcuries of 14carbon-glycine was injected intravenously 30 days prior to launch. The 14C radioactivity was followed for 125 days on Skylab 2, 131 days on Skylab 3, and 141 days on Skylab 4. In general, blood was drawn weekly throughout this period, including the time in space. Radioactivity was determined by extracting heme, igniting the dried extract, and determining microcuries of 14C per milligram heme. Iron turnover was determined by injecting 2 microcuries of 59iron-citrate at recovery and using blood samples drawn at 30 and 31 minutes, and 2-3 hours later. Iron reappearance was obtained from blood samples drawn 1,3,7 and 14 days after recovery. Reticulocyte counts were made from weekly preflight and postflight blood samples.

RESULTS:
The recovery mean value for the red blood cell mass of all Skylab astronauts was lower (1843 milliliters) than their preflight mean (2075 milliliters) and different from the control postflight mean (2046 milliliters). While the postflight decrease in mean red blood cell mass was 232 milliliters for the Skylab crewmembers, the corresponding value for the controls was only 7 milliliters. There was no significant difference between pre- and postflight crew mean values and control mean value either for the 51Cr red blood cell half-life or for the 14C-glycine red blood cell mean life span; neither was there any statistically significant difference between the control subjects and the Skylab crews in appearance or turnover of iron, indicating that the rate of erythropoiesis was the same for both groups. However, postflight reticulocyte counts measured at recovery following each mission were low. The postflight counts were greater than preflight values in only one crewmember of the 28-day mission 2 weeks after recovery, in all three crewmembers of the 59-day mission 1 week after recovery, and in all three crewmembers of the 84-day mission 1 week or less after recovery. The control subjects, on the other hand, did not develop a change in reticulocyte count, indicating that the changes observed in the Skylab crews were not due to blood draw amounts. Inhibited bone marrow was thought to be a possible explanation for the low red blood cell masses and low postflight reticulocyte counts, and normal iron turnover was thought to be caused by a postflight rebound in the bone marrow. As for the plasma volume, the mean percent decrease was less in the Skylab 2 crew than in the crews of the longer Skylab 3 and 4 missions, but still greater than the decrease observed during Apollo missions, which suggested that the plasma volume did not return to normal even after prolonged flights.

experiment_title: Lipid Peroxidation and Antioxidant Defense System
experiment_description:
Objectives:

The system of lipid peroxidation reacts regularly to adverse effects and results in enhancement of lipid peroxidation and build-up of LPO products in blood and tissues. Cosmos experiments have suggested a short-term stress effect, rather than any long-term adverse effects, to be responsible for these changes. This experiment was to study the effect of microgravity and other spaceflight factors on the system of lipid peroxidation and antioxidant defense of tissues.

Approach:

In the liver (right lobe), kidney (left), and skeletal muscle (quadriceps femoralis), in myocardial homogenates, and in blood plasma, the content of lipid peroxidation products - dienic conjugates, malonic dialdehyde, Schiff's bases, and the main lipid antioxidant, tocopherol - were determined. Also, the plasma total antioxidant activity was measured, and in tissue homogenates the activities of antioxidant enzymes, superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione reductase, and glutathione peroxidase were determined.

Results:

It was found that the complex of spaceflight factors did not significantly influence the system of antioxidant protection and the intensity of lipid peroxidation. Changes of lipid peroxidation and antioxidant defense parameters in skeletal muscle and myocardium appeared only in rats sacrificed nine days postflight, reflecting the existence of functional tension in these tissues as a response to gravitation stress during readaptation to terrestrial conditions. There were no significant changes of investigated parameters in blood plasma; thus, whole free radical processes of rats were compensated during the postflight period.

experiment_title: Effect of the Hybrid Training Method on the Disuse Atrophy of the Musculoskeletal System of the Astronauts Staying in the International Space Station for a Long Term-initial Verification in ISS
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
It is well known that atrophy of the musculoskeletal system due to disuse occurs among astronauts. For instance, the atrophy of the muscles and bones of astronauts experiencing microgravity is evident. Such atrophy of the musculoskeletal system is considered one of the main issues regarding a longtime stay in the International Space Station (ISS).

A “hybrid training system” (HTS) was designed to maintain the musculoskeletal system of astronauts by using an electrically stimulated antagonist to resist the volitional contraction of agonist muscles in weightlessness. In other words, electrical stimulation generates a resistive force instead of gravity. This approach consists of a compact device, produces a minimum of inertial reaction forces and has the advantage of minimizing the need for external stabilization that is currently necessary during exercise in weightless conditions.

HTS has several features. These include; 1) a simple device, 2) requiring minimal external stabilization of the subjects, 3) simultaneous contractions of both agonist and antagonist musculature, 4) volitional contraction of deep layers of muscle, 5) longitudinal bone force loads. HTS, which utilizes an electrically stimulated antagonist force as a resistance to joint motion, would become a useful exercise method in weightlessness. Multiple ground-based experiments have been encouraging but, thus far, evaluation in space has not occurred.

At the first flight of the experiment, HTS will be used for one of an astronaut’s upper limbs (non-dominant arm), and its muscular strength and bulk compared to those of the non HTS side to examine its operation capability and utility in orbit. After the usefulness of HTS for orbital operation is confirmed in this first experiment, it will be used for the astronauts during a long-term stay in space, and its effect will be investigated. The long-term goal of HTS will be to effectively prevent atrophy of the musculoskeletal system in astronauts during a long term stay in the ISS without requiring undue crew time. HTS will become a useful back-up for the standard training device in the ISS, or a useful training device in the small space ship (CTV) for the exploration of the Moon and Mars.

APPROACH:
Pre- and postflight baseline data collection: Preflight the crewmembers will have a baseline measurement of their upper limb, be measured for the HTS equipment and trained in its use, and will perform two preflight HTS data collections. HTS data collections include electronic stimulation to an upper limb, with the muscle force measured by a Hand Held Dynamometer (HHD), and circumference of the upper limb measured with a measuring tape. Bone mineral density of the upper limbs obtained by Dual Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DEXA), a muscle force measurement by Biodex 4, a muscle volume measurement by Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), height and weight will also be collected through data sharing. The same testing will be performed postflight. These measurements will be conducted 2 times (pre-/post-training), and will be used to compare those of the training side and the non-training side.

Inflight data collection: Upper arm (the non-dominant arm) joint flexion and extension will be performed using HTS for four weeks. It will involve 10 sets of 10 of upper arm curls with a 1 minute rest interval between sets. It will be approximately 16 minutes of exercise a day, and is performed 3 times a week. The muscular strength and circumference of both upper limbs will be measured by an HHD and measuring tape. The data recorded will be downlinked for verification on ground.

Medication log and exercise log from 30 days prior to the first evaluation to the closeout of HTS experiment are also required.

experiment_title: Portable Quantitative Ultrasound with DXA/QCT and FEA Integration for Human Longitudinal Critical Bone Quality Assessment
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Skeletal complications, i.e., osteoporosis, induced by microgravity during extended space mission, represent a key astronaut health problem. Lack of on-board diagnosis has increased significant risk in astronauts' bone loss during long-term space flight. Early diagnosis of such disorders can lead to prompt and optimized treatment that will dramatically reduce the risk of fracture and longitudinal monitoring microgravity and countermeasure effects. Advents in quantitative ultrasound (QUS) techniques provide a method for characterizing the material properties of bone in a manner for predicting both bone mineral density (BMD) and mechanical strength. Investigators have developed a scanning confocal acoustic navigation (SCAN) system capable of generating noninvasive ultrasound images at the site of interest. Both animal and human tests indicated strong correlations between SCAN determined data and microCT determined BMD, and bone strength, as well as monitoring fracture healing with guided ultrasound. The objectives of this study are to develop a portable broadband SCAN for critical skeletal quality assessment (e.g., hip, knee, wrist, and heel), to longitudinally monitoring bone alteration in disuse osteopenia, and to integrate ultrasound with DXA, QCT, and finite element analysis (FEA) for human subject. In vivo human tests will be evaluated at Stony Brook Osteoporosis Center and the JSC/UTMB bed rest facility. Human cadaver will be used for testing feasibility of identifying bone loss, microstructural and mechanical strength properties.

Specific Aims:
1) To develop a new broadband SCAN system capable of extracting trabecular QUS parameters and backscatter images at critical skeletal sites using single crystal material transducer with minimal loss of the acoustic signal and integration with scan technology to provide direct assessment of the risk of osteoporotic bone loss and fracture in the deep tissue. The scanning time will be less than 2 minutes. The SCAN system will be non-invasive, portable, easy to use, and automatic analysis.
2) To evaluate the capability of the broadband SCAN diagnostic system in assessing trabecular bone structural and strength parameters in cadaver subjects with microCT determined microstructure and BMD determined by DXA.
3) To longitudinally assess and correlate the degree of bone loss in osteoporosis clinic, bed rest facility to determine intra-subject bone loss and the relationship to age, gender, and rational effects at critical sites using SCAN, DXA, QCT, and FEA.
4) To determine the ability of quantitative ultrasound in pre- and post-flights, as well as rehabilitation effects for astronauts.

experiment_title: Emergence of Wheat Seedlings in Zero Gravity
experiment_description:
Objectives:

This experiment was to determine whether seeds would produce normal seedlings when germinated in the absence of a significant gravitational force. As the negative geotropism of the coleoptile and the positive geotropism of the roots would be eliminated during flight, seedling organs could be expected to show alterations similar to those produced through a clinostat. Even after only three days growth, measurable differences in coleoptile and primary root orientation should appear in the absence of the even distribution of auxin in these organs by reason of the downward transport of, and equalizing action on, auxin by the force of gravity.

Approach:

Seventy-eight wheat seedlings (38-39 mg) were surface sterilized in a 0.05% Hg Cl2 and soaked for three hours at 95 °F. The seedlings were then placed in polycarbonate stalks containing wet vermiculite. Gas samples were taken and lids were sealed. All growth took place in the dark. Photography was done rapidly at recovery by means of special camera rack systems which included a 45° mirror that reflects the side view of each seedling in the row that is set to face the camera. The orientation of the seedlings was described in quantitative terms by the combination of face-view and side-view angles that are made by the intersection of a line from the tip to the base of a root or coleoptile with a vertical line through the axis of the seedling.

Results:

Growth physiology of wheat seed germination and the development of wheat seedlings in their early stages were not disturbed sufficiently by the absence of gravity as reflected in growth rates or external morphology. The stresses of launch acceleration and vibration had no measurable effects on ungerminated wheat seeds. The basic metabolic processes, which supply the energy for normal growth, were apparently undisturbed. This indicates the independence from gravitational force of certain organelles which carry key enzymes to the sites of energy release and use. Weightlessness had no measurable effects on the endogenous mechanisms for production and distribution of the growth hormone, auxin. The wheat seedling proved to be an excellent choice of a small test plant for a space flight experiment in the growth and orientation of plant organs known to be geosensitive. The development and performance of this study led to the discovery of root epinasty, previously unknown to plant physiologists, as a factor in the orientation of plagiotropic roots.

experiment_title: Cytogenetic Study of Heavy Ion-Induced Chromosomal Damage in Human Cells
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Energetic heavy ions pose a great health risk to astronauts during extended International Space Station (ISS) and future Mars missions. High-LET heavy ions are particularly effective in causing various biological effects, including cell inactivation, genetic mutations and cancer induction. Most of these biological endpoints are closely related to chromosomal damage, which can be an indicator of health risks.

The major objectives were to: 1) comparatively assess the frequencies of complex and simple, as well as interchromosomal and intrachromosomal, aberrations induced by low- and high-LET radiation, and 2) evaluate the pattern and types of heavy-ion induced chromosomal aberrations between human 2-D epithelia cells, 3-D epithelia cells, and lymphocytes.

Experimental results of this investigation may provide the knowledge for identifying the complexity of chromosomal aberrations due to space-like radiation and for assessing the radiation risks from such end-points observed in differential cell systems. The differential radiation environment encountered in space may cause deleterious effects in humans, and these effects are of special concern for prolonged space missions beyond the protective terrestrial magnetosphere. Before such missions can be undertaken, a much more detailed understanding of these effects is required to allow planning and implementation of protective countermeasures.

APPROACH:
In this study, investigators quantitatively analyzed chromosomal damage induced by energetic heavy ions in human epithelia and lymphocyte cells, by using advanced cytogenetic techniques including the multi-color fluorescence in situ hybridization (mFISH) and mBAND techniques, which allowed the analysis of chromosomal exchanges involving all human chromosomes and intrachromosomal aberrations, respectively. Human epithelia cells were cultured in both the conventional two-dimensional (2-D) and tissue-equivalent three-dimensional (3-D) platforms. The exposure of human cells to energetic heavy ions was conducted at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) at the Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL), and a gamma radiation source at the Baylor College of Medicine was used for low-LET exposures.

RESULTS:
Results of this study validated the observation of a higher incidence of inversions for high-LET radiation. However, detailed analysis of the inversion type revealed that both iron ions and gamma rays induced a low incidence of simple inversions. Half of the inversions observed in the low-LET-irradiated samples were accompanied by other types of intrachromosome aberrations, but few inversions were accompanied by interchromosome aberrations. In contrast, iron ions induced a significant fraction of inversions that involved complex rearrangements of both inter- and intrachromosome exchanges.

experiment_title: The Effect of Daily Physical Activity and Age on Bone Density and Bone Structure in Men
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of the first study is to investigate the differences in the bone density of the skeleton as well as the structural properties of the lower leg bones in three groups of age-matched men: soccer players, runners, and sedentary controls.

APPROACH:
Methodology used the same tools developed for a previous study in women (HR 202). Three groups of 20-30 year old men were recruited: 15 elite soccer players (S) 15 elite long distance runners (R) and 15 sedentary controls (C).

RESULTS:
Age, body weight, height and tibia length were similar in all 3 groups. Average values of age were S 21, R 24.2 and C 24.3 years; for body weight were S 79.4, R 67.5, C 75.7 Kg; for height were S 181.6, R 179.8, C 180.5 cm; and for tibial length were S 40.4, R 41.4, C 40.4 cm respectively. Area was scaled by normalized body weight while tibial structural parameters in midshaft and distal third were higher in S and R than C (S 3.03, R 3.36. C 2.68 cm2 for A, S 2.37, R 2.80, C 1.95 cm4 for Imax. S had higher whole body, spine, right hip, right leg and calcaneal BMD than C (p = 0.008, 0.041, <0.001, 0.019, <0.001 respectively). S also had higher right hip and spine BMD than R (p = 0.012 and p = 0.009, respectively). R had higher calcaneal BMD than C (p = 0.002). Forty percent of R had t-scores of the lumbar spine between –1 and –2.5, similar to C whose T-scores were either below –1 (34%) or lower than –2.5 (7%).

Structural parameters (scaled values of A, Imax, Imin, and J) of the tibia were increased in S and R, indicating increased stiffness and strength. The tibial cross-sections of S were generally more symmetric than in R, indicative of their wider variety of loading conditions compared to the repetitive loading in R. There was also a relationship between the tibia and the fibula and the relative distance between the two bones indicating the two bones work together as structural elements in the lower leg.

Conclusions: Playing soccer is associated with higher BMD of the skeleton at all sites measured while running is associated with higher BMD at directly loaded sites (calcaneus), but not at relatively unloaded sites (spine). Specific loading conditions, seen in ball sports or in running, play a pivotal role in skeletal adaptation.

experiment_title: Risk Assessment of Space Radiation-Enhanced Colon Tumorigenesis
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This proposal addressed the Carcinogenesis category of the Bioastronautics Roadmap by investigating carcinogenic risk of human colonic cells and tissues after low and high LET radiation exposure. The colon is a major target for the carcinogenic effects of radiation. Aberrant crypt foci are an early precursor lesion for colorectal cancer (CRC) that is characterized by trisomy 7 (present in 37% of adenomas and 80% of adenocarcinomas). The appearance of the adenomatous polyp becomes more prevalent with increased age (10% incidence at age 40 and >25% by age 60). Pre-cancerous lesions may already exist or develop in astronauts going on long-term missions, the result of which would be an increased risk for cancer development through exposure to space radiation. The key objective was to determine the probabilities for increased colonic carcinogenesis from space radiation as a result of radiation dose, quality, and dose rate. Investigators planned to expose 2D and 3D human colonic cells and human colonic biopsies to energetic protons (H), high Z and energy particles (HZE), and x-rays and analyze results using both biological assays and genome-wide systems approaches. They are comparing these results to a novel immortalized human trisomy 7 colonic epithelial cell line and will model carcinogenic risk of these cells compared to normal and immortalized diploid colonic cells. They have also initiated a small molecule screen to identify nontoxic compounds that may inhibit the trisomy 7 cells but not the normal diploid. They have also examined DNA damage sensing, signaling, and repair kinetics in normal and trisomy 7 human colonic cell lines. Finally, they have obtained a substantial amount of information about a novel oral bioavailable compound CDDO-Me (bardoxolone methyl, RTA 402) and have determined it is an effective and nontoxic countermeasure for protecting normal colonic cells from the detrimental effects of low and high LET irradiation. As part of a new project we are extending these countermeasure studies to mouse models. This research should improve the mechanistic understanding for the variability of radiation dose, quality, and dose-rate dependencies for colon cancer development and provide biological markers for modeling and risk assessment.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the results below.

RESULTS:
Summary of findings:
1. DNA damage in human colonic epithelial cells is more difficult to repair when caused by iron particles compared to protons and gamma rays.
2. Iron damage persists longer in both 2D and 3D human colonic epithelial cell cultures compared to protons and gamma rays.
3. Epithelial cells in intact human colonic tissues display more damage foci than surrounding stromal cells after both high and low LET radiations. All cells in intact colonic tissues are exposed to the same radiation dosage and are likely experiencing equal amounts of DNA double strand breaks, but location in the cell cycle may explain why the replicating epithelial cells show more pronounced DNA damage response compared to quiescent stromal cells.
4. Additional cells from another patient have been established and characterized. Investigators have an immortalized normal diploid cell line and one that is immortalized with one chromosomal change (trisomy 7). Trisomy 7 is present in about 65% of all colonic adenoma and adenocarcinomas. They have now progressed these cells partially toward tumorigenicity by reducing p53 expression (shRNA to p53), overexpressing K-ras and c- myc and expressing a truncated APC.
5. Investigators have demonstrated and published the ability to differentiate the immortalized human colonic epithelial cell lines. They showed that their human colonic epithelial cells express several gastrointestinal putative stem cell markers including CD44, CD29, BMI-1, and LGR5. This indicates that our normal diploid hTERT immortalized human colonic epithelial cells can make similar 3D differentiated structures as do primary cells from mouse small intestine. The cells are clonal, can divide long-term (are immortalized), and single cells divide to generate self-organizing structures with several differentiated cell types and architecture of crypts present in adults in the absence of a cellular niche. The cells demonstrate polarized villin staining, junction formation (ZO-1), a subset of cells express Muc2 similarly to the staining of mouse small intestinal cells, and some even express chromogranin A (a neuroendocrine marker). This also helps demonstrate that we are culturing human colonic epithelial stem cells.
6. Investigators have also passaged the cells with trisomy 7 (contain hTERT, cdk4, shRNAp53 and mutant K-ras) and observed that a subclone of these cells contain a trisomy 20 (also very common in human colon cancer). While these cells make large colonies and grow anchorage independent in soft agar they do not make tumors in nude mice. They have now expressed c-myc in these cells and these also do not make tumors. They have also introduced a key mutant version of APC into these cells. These isogenic partially progressed cell lines are extremely useful for radiation experiments to determine biological steps in cancer progression. Importantly, our results demonstrate that it requires multiple independent changes in a single cell in order to progress a normal human colonic epithelial cells into a fully malignant (lethal) cancer cell. This suggests that the exposure to the type and doses likely to be experienced by astronauts on a long-term mission into space are less likely to have a major impact on lethal cancer formation. However, more research needs to be done to confirm this speculation.
7. Biological countermeasure experiments. Investigators have conducted a significant number of experiments with methyl-2-cyano-3,12-dioxooleana-1,9(11)-dien-28-oate (BARD, also termed RTA-402, or CDDO-Me). BARD is an Nrf2 mediated phase II enzyme activator with a well understood molecular mechanism of action. Importantly, BARD is a completely synthetic compound that is nontoxic and orally available. In two completed Phase II clinical trials BARD taken orally once-daily not only mimics the body's natural mechanism for resolving inflammation but also reduces the risk of death in patients with stage 3 chronic kidney disease. While anti-oxidant inflammation modulators (AIMs) such as BARD would be expected to provide risk reduction for low-LET radiation, it is much less certain if AIMs would be effective in protecting against high-LET irradiation. In our research, we have documented that BARD is an effective biological countermeasure by reducing high-LET irradiation associated human epithelial cell transformation.

experiment_title: Gravity and Skeletal Growth: II.  Morphology and Histochemistry of Bone Cells and Vasculature of the Tibia from Cosmos 1887
experiment_description:
Objectives:

In a previous study of animals from Spacelab-3, the osteoblast appeared to be slightly smaller in size following seven days of flight. These osteoblasts were found along the endosteal surface of the diaphyseal bone and tended to have a more uniform size as compared to osteoblasts along the trabeculae in the metaphyseal region of long bones. Therefore, this study concentrated on the cells found within the diaphyseal area of long bones. The objectives here were to investigate the relationships between vascular morphology, lipid accumulation, and osteocyte and osteoblast morphology in weight-bearing long bones.

Approach:

Electron microscopy, light microscopy, and enzyme histochemistry were used to study the effects of space flight on metaphyseal and cortical bone of the rat tibia. Following fixation and decalcification, 50 micrometers thick sections were obtained with a vibratome, and sections incubated in the various media alkaline or acid phosphatase, or NADPase. Staining for lipids was carried out on frozen sections of fixed tissues and embedded vibratome sections. Morphometry was carried out on light or electron microscopy using an interactive data analysis system.

Results:

Light microscopy of trabecular and cortical bone and the included osteoblast population showed no obvious morphological differences as a result of space flight. In the diaphyseal bone from flight animals, blood vessels near the periosteal surface often showed very dense intraluminal deposits. Also, in the periosteal region, many osteocytic lacunae were found devoid of osteocytes and sometimes filled an osmiophilic substance. Flight animals contained reactive saccules which averaged 11.3±6.1 saccules per cell, and the vivarium controls averaged 14.4±3.4 saccules per cell which contained reaction product. The vasculature of the flight animals was definitely less reactive than the control groups. Results of other measurements indicate that more vascular space per area of bone existed in flight animals as compared to the simulated controls. This data suggest that a vascular change may occur during flight which would then influence the bone forming ability of the osteoblasts in weight-bearing bones.

experiment_title: Subregional Assessment of Bone Loss in the Axial  Skeleton in Long-Term Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
As evidenced by Skylab and Mir missions, bone loss, which can increase the risk of fracture by weakening the skeleton, is an established medical risk in long-duration spaceflight. Moreover, there is little information about the extent to which the lost bone is recovered after spaceflight. Almost all of the measurements of bone loss and recovery have utilized an imaging technique called Dual X-Ray Absorptimetry (DXA). DXA systems are specially calibrated x-ray devices which measure the mass of an entire bone (e.g., a hip or a vertebrae). This approach has two limitations. First, it computes the summed mass of a given bone and cannot look separately at the porous inner core of the bone (trabecular bone) and the outer sheath which surrounds the core (cortical bone). Studies of osteoporosis and other bone diseases show that cortical and trabecular bone mass may underestimate the change in one of the components. A second limitation is that DXA computes the bone mass over a large volume of bone. If the loss of bone is localized in a small sub-region, the DXA image will detect a smaller change averaged over a large volume.

With the addition of Quantitative Computed Tomography (QCT) and Quantitative Ultrasound (QUS) techniques, this study will provide the first information on spaceflight-related compartmental bone loss (magnitude and distribution) in the axial skeleton and on the extent to which lost bone is recovered in the year following return. Furthermore, this study will have implications for the frequency of assignment to long duration missions and for the health of the astronauts in older age. The results may also be of use in the design of exercise or pharmacological countermeasures to prevent bone loss.

Comparison of QCT bone mineral density (hip and spine) between astronauts and healthy normal subjects will help to improve understanding of the prevalence of osteoporosis between different race and gender sub-groups.

The objective of the experiment is to determine the compartmental and sub-regional distribution of bone loss in the spine and hip in long-duration spaceflight and to assess how bone is recovered after return. The extent to which the spaceflight-induced changes in bone distribution compare to the spread of bone mineral density (BMD) measures in healthy men and women and the validity of calcaneal Quantitative Ultrasound (QUS) will also be determined.

APPROACH:
In an earlier study, areal BMD (aBMD) measurements by DXA showed that cosmonauts making flights of 4- to 12-month duration on the Soviet/Russian MIR spacecraft lost bone at an average rate of 1% per month from the spine and 1.5% per month from the hip. However, because DXA measurements represent the sum of the cortical and trabecular compartments, there is no direct information on how these bone envelopes are affected by spaceflight. To address this, the investigators performed a study of 16 crewmembers (male and female, age range 40–55 years) on long-duration missions (4–6 months) on the International Space Station (ISS). DXA was used to obtain aBMD of the hip and spine and volumetric QCT (vQCT) to assess integral, cortical, and trabecular volumetric BMD (vBMD) in the hip and spine. In the heel, DXA was used to measure aBMD, and quantitative ultrasound (QUS)was used to measure speed of sound (SOS) and broadband ultrasound attenuation (BUA).

These techniques can examine the trabecular and cortical bone separately and can determine whether the loss is localized in a small sub-region of the bone. Bone loss in the spine and hip was determined by comparing preflight and postflight QCT measurements. Bone recovery was assessed by comparing QCT data taken immediately postflight and one year after return. The QCT results were compared with Dual X-Ray Absorptiometry (DXA) and Quantitative Ultrasound (QUS) measurements taken at these time points. These measurements include DXA of the spine, hip, and heel and QUS of the heel. Finally, to determine how the bone loss in space compares to the range of bone density values in a normal adult population, astronaut QCT measurements in the spine and hip were compared to measurements of 120 healthy normal control subjects consisting of healthy black and white males and females between ages of 35-45.

For the DXA measurements, the lumbar spine, hip and heel were scanned. Following completion of the DXA scan, the subject underwent hip and spine QCT scans, followed by a QUS scan of the heel. DXA, QCT, and QUS scans were performed once preflight in the year before launch and two times postflight. There were no inflight measurements taken.

RESULTS:
There was no compartment-specific loss of bone in the spine. Cortical bone mineral loss in the hip occurred primarily by endocortical thinning. aBMD was lost at rates of 0.9% per month at the spine (p<0.001) and 1.4–1.5% per month at the hip (p<0.001). Spinal integral vBMD was lost at a rate of 0.9% per month (p<0.001), and trabecular vBMD was lost at 0.7% per month (p<0.05). In contrast to earlier reports, these changes were generalized across the vertebrae and not focused in the posterior elements. In the hip, integral, cortical, and trabecular vBMD was lost at rates of 1.2–1.5% per month (p<0.0001), 0.4–0.5% per month (p<0.01), and 2.2–2.7% per month (p<0.001), respectively. The cortical bone loss in the hip occurred primarily by cortical thinning. Calcaneal aBMD measurements by DXA showed smaller mean losses (0.4% per month) than hip or spine measurements, with SOS and BUA showing no change. In summary, the results show that ISS crewmembers, on average, experience substantial loss of both trabecular and cortical bone in the hip and somewhat smaller losses in the spine. These results do not support the use of calcaneal aBMD or QUS measurements as surrogate measures to estimate changes in the central skeleton.

Proximal femoral bone mass was substantially recovered in the year after spaceflight, but measures of vBMD and estimated bone strength showed only partial recovery. The recovery of BMC, in the absence of a comparable increase in vBMD, was explained by increases in bone volume and CSA during the year after spaceflight. The investigator concludes that adaptation of the proximal femur to reloading entailed an increase in bone size and an incomplete recovery of vBMD. The data indicate that recovery of skeletal density after long-duration space missions may exceed 1 year and supports the evidence in the aging literature for periosteal apposition as a compensatory response for bone loss. The extent to which this compensatory effect protects against fracture remains to be seen.

experiment_title: Fracture Healing in Haversian Bone under Conditions of Simulated Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
There is a need for information regarding hard and soft tissue healing in microgravity environments, and if impaired healing exists, what countermeasures can be called upon to enhance healing. Research on fracture healing using the rodent hindlimb suspension model shows healing is impaired in simulated microgravity, while clinical research shows that moderate, early mechanical loading caused by weight bearing induces osteogenesis and aids in repair of bone fracture. Further research is needed to determine what loads, if any, should be applied during space flight to promote fracture healing.

Most ground-based microgravity models utilize rodent hindlimb suspension to simulate how reduced loading affects isolated physiologic systems. Unfortunately, results derived from these studies are difficult to directly translate to the human condition due to major anatomic and physiologic differences between rodents and humans. Specifically, the differences in rodent and human bone structures become increasingly important when studying orthopaedic issues such as bone maintenance and healing during space flight. For example, the basic microstructure of rodent bone, known as "plexiform" bone, lacks the osteons (Haversion systems) that are the main micro-architectural feature of human cortical bone. Furthermore, it is known that the osteogenic and healing potential of rodent bone far exceeds that of adult human tissue.

Due to these limitations in current ground-based microgravity models, there exists a need to develop a ground-based, large animal model of fracture healing in simulated weightlessness that more closely approximates the human condition as has been done in the first year of this study. This animal model should be capable of simulating a wide spectrum of microgravities and able to investigate exercise protocols that may aid in the optimization of the fracture healing cascade.

Four specific aims were defined to meet these goals:

  1. Develop a ground-based large animal model of bone unloading in order to simulate full weightlessness;
  2. Interrogate the effects of a simulated microgravity environment on bone fracture healing in a large animal model;
  3. Develop a computational model of weightbearing in ovine bone under different experimental conditions in order to characterize the loads experienced by the fracture site; and
  4. Develop treadmill protocols that enhance bone fracture healing in the presence of simulated microgravity.

APPROACH:
Simulated microgravity-related alterations in fracture healing were investigated in this study. The employed methodology was based on (1) in vivo experimentation on skeletally mature female ewes to interrogate fracture healing and possible therapeutic countermeasures, and (2) finite element modeling of the ovine hindlimb under simulated microgravity and Earth gravity loading conditions to characterize the micromechanical environment of healing fractures.

REUSLTS:
In Specific Aim 1, a ground-based, ovine model of skeletal unloading was developed in order to simulate a microgravity loading condition. The external fixation unloading technique utilized in this model was able to induce mechanical unloading of the metatarsus and significant alterations in the relevant radiographical, biomechanical, and histomorphometric parameters characteristic of space flight. Specifically, the newly developed ovine model captured the characteristic decrease in osteoblast numbers and increase in osteoclast activity associated with human space flight. The unloading methodology developed in Specific Aim 1 was extended to the investigation of fracture healing in a simulated microgravity loading environment in Specific Aim 2. The findings of this study revealed that the mechanical loading environment dramatically affects the fracture healing cascade and resultant mineralized tissue strength, and that animals that healed in a reduced loading environment demonstrated significant reductions in healing rate and callus mechanical competency as compared to animals healing in a 1G Earth gravitational environment.

Specific Aim 3 outlined the development of a finite element of the ovine hindlimb in order to characterize the localized mechanical environment of a healing fracture in simulated microgravity and Earth gravitational environments. External fixation componentry was modeled to mimic the experimental methodology of Specific Aim 2 and correlate model predictions to experimental outcomes. The findings indicate that simulated microgravity unloading decreases hydrostatic stress and principal strain within the callus and fracture gap, resulting in primarily intramembranous bone formation rather than the endochondral bone formation pathway characteristic of Earth-based fracture healing.

Finally, in Specific Aim 4, two therapeutic countermeasures to the inhibited fracture healing of simulated microgravity unloading were investigated. The methodology of Specific Aim 2 was replicated, and shock wave therapy and low-intensity pulsed ultrasound were administered to animals healing in simulated microgravity and Earth gravitational loading environments. While fracture mechanical competency was not significantly altered following either countermeasure, both treatments significantly elevated osteoblast numbers and bone formation rates in simulated microgravity animals. The outcome of this study suggests that shock wave therapy and low-intensity pulsed ultrasound may be beneficial in situations involving aberrant fracture healing but elicit minimal modifications to the normal healing sequelae.

No datasets exist for this study. A final report was archived.

experiment_title: Cosmic Radiation and Effects Activation Monitor
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The increasing use of heavy space vehicles and payloads means that it is no longer adequate to predict radiation effects based on primary radiation alone. Pathlengtbs can readily approach and exceed I00 gm cm•2, which is of the order of the depth at which the maximum of cosmic-ray secondaries is produced in the atmosphere. While shielding can be beneficial against radiation belt and solar flare particles of energies up to a few hundred MeV, it can be detrimental when considering the energetic cosmic rays of several GeV. Effects of concern include biological dose to astronauts, where secondary neutrons and cosmic ray fragments are important, as well as induced radioactivity and secondary particle background in sensitive space borne instrumentation.

The Mir modules, and the forth coming International Space Station, represented opportunities to explore new radiation environments in order to obtain data on different shielding levels and the effects of radiation on larger spacecraft. The Cosmic Radiation Effects and Activation Monitor (CREAM) measures the Linear Energy Transfer (LET) effects within silicon and provides information relevant to single event upsets (SEUs) on avionics equipment.

Specific Aims:

  1. Monitor the energy disposition of spectra in silicon due to primary and secondary radiation as a function of time, orbital location and shielding.
  2. Obtain collateral data on mission integrated dose, particle influences, and induced radioactivity.
  3. Improve and test space environment and radiation shielding codes used to predict single event upset rates in electronics and background rates in sensors.

APPROACH:
The CREAM was used to collect data on cosmic ray energy loss spectra, neutron fluxes and induced radioactivity as a function of geomagnetic coordinates and detector location within the orbiter. Payload hardware consisted of the active cosmic ray monitor, a passive scintillation crystal canister, two neutron spectrometers and 10 passive detector packages. The active monitor was used to obtain real-time spectral data, while the passive monitors obtained data integrated over the mission duration. An additional control passive detector package was used for obtaining background data prior to launch.

The CREAM active monitor was a box containing sensors and associated electronics and solid-state memory. The active monitor was rotated between two passive package locations throughout the mission. CREAM used three different types of passive detectors. The first was a set of scintillation crystals packaged in an aluminum canister that remained in a central location within Mir throughout the mission.

There were also passive detector packages, which contained nickel and gold activation foils, neutron bubble dosimeters and thermoluminescent dosimeters. Eight of these packages were placed in four specific locations within Mir, while the remaining two remained in the central location within Mir. The third type of passive detector was the neutron spectrometer, which consisted of three identical sets of six gel-filled test tubes. The "test tubes," or neutron bubble detectors, were designed to measure specific energy thresholds of the neutron environment within Mir.

RESULTS:
The CREAM was flown on eight Shuttle flights between September 1991 and June 1998 and two NASA Mir missions covering the full range of inclinations as well as altitudes between 220 and 570 km, while a version has flown at supersonic altitudes on Concorde between 1988 and 1992 and at subsonic altitudes on a SAS Boeing 767 between May and August 1993.

Results show that cosmic-ray secondaries increase the fluxes of particles of linear energy transfer less than 200 MeV/(gm cm-2), while the activation of the crystals is enhanced by about a factor of three due to secondary neutrons.

Predictions of CREAM count rates during Shuttle flights show that n-Si interactions have less importance than at aircraft altitudes, and even for channels 5 to 9 contribute approximately 10-20% of the measured counts. However, the secondary particle environment (predominantly neutrons) generated by cosmic-ray interactions in the heavy spacecraft structure is the major source of activation in y-ray scintillators for low altitude Shuttle missions.

experiment_title: NASA Food Technology Commercial Space Center
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The mission of the Food Technology Commercial Space Center (FTCSC) was to lead a national effort to develop foods and food-processing technologies that enhance space missions and advance commercial food products through cooperative efforts with NASA scientists and technologists, commercial companies, and academic researchers.

The objectives of this study were:
1. Development of foods for NASA 30- to 120-day space missions in support of International Space Station (ISS) missions (minimum of one-year shelf life) .
2. Development of food and food-processing technologies to support NASA human exploration and the development of long-duration space missions (up to five years) . This included stored food systems for transit vehicles as well as food-processing systems for site-grown crops .
3. Development by the commercial partners of terrestrial commercial production and marketing plans for products and processes developed for NASA’s space program.

APPROACH:
The methodology is embedded in the Results below.

RESULTS:
NASA FTCSC affiliate faculty and commercial partners worked to develop foods and food-processing technologies that benefit NASA and the public. The Center’s commercial partners developed products for space and terrestrial applications. Following is a summary of the commercial partner activities in the final year of the study:
Ajinomoto Co., Inc., after numerous tests and consultations with NASA, terminated the precooked rice product research and turned their attention to developing food products with a calcium absorption promoter. Following positive initial results from the calcium absorption promoter research, the company plans further studies of calcium solubility, intestinal absorption, and potential benefits for bone health. Furthermore, the company funded Paul Flakoll’s research project at Iowa State University which examines the metabolic interactions of glutamine supplementation with exercise and insulin resistance in humans.

American Specialty Packaging, Alcoa Flexible Packaging, LLC and KSP (Korean Special Packaging) representatives met in Ames with FTCSC Director Anthony Pometto to discuss NASA’s future plans and goals in terms of space food packaging. Since that meeting, the companies have joined FTCSC as a commercial partner and are working on improving space food packaging.

Analytik Jena AG research has resulted in the measurement of changes in antioxidant potential in stored soybeans. Additionally, Analytik Jena has measured the influence of pasteurization and sterilization doses and low pasteurization doses of irradiation on the functional, sensory, and microbial quality of soybeans for soymilk and tofu manufacture. Research also focused on measuring the influence of radiation that soybeans would be exposed to on Mars missions and determining the influence of toasting and storage of full-fat soyflakes on shelf life. In order to conduct this research, the Photochem equipment was used and it was successful in aiding the research.

Arla Foods amba received product approval from NASA for the chocolate milk powder and the thermally-stabilized yogurt and launched the yogurt on Progress 17. Since the launch, Arla has been working to implement a space yogurt production line and to build a special packaging machine.

Biosteam Technologies, Inc. and Selective Micro conducted polymer research and compatibility testing on Selectrocide® for NASA, and completed all EPA testing and approvals for use of the compound as a complete antimicrobial for food, as well as food and non-food surfaces. Also, the company continues to develop a packet towel designed to remove mold and mildew while cleaning surfaces in space vehicles.

experiment_title: Dose Rate Effects on the Mechanisms of Space Radiation Induced Delayed Genomic Instability
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Among NASA's concerns for astronaut health risk is space radiation-induced carcinogenesis. At present, there is no practical way for astronauts to avoid radiation exposure, so it is important that the best possible risk estimates be made. Recent studies have demonstrated that epigenetic mechanisms play a key role in the radiation response and carcinogenesis. Epigenetic mechanisms regulate gene expression by DNA methylation, chromatin modifications and microRNA. This project tests the hypothesis that in vitro irradiation of cells alters epigenetic profiles and that these epigenetic profiles are affected radiation quality. Using proton and iron ion radiations the delayed effects of radiation exposure will be investigated in the progeny of irradiated cells multiple cell generations after the initial exposure. Global, repeat element and specific locus DNA methylation will be measured. Further this project explores the possibility that DNA methylation or miRNA mediated gene silencing is involved in initiating or perpetuating radiation-induced genomic instability.

APPROACH:
To determine whether epigenetic aberrations affect genomic instability investigators measured DNA methylation, mRNA and microRNA (miR) levels in well characterized chromosomally stable and unstable clonally expanded single cell survivors of irradiation.

RESULTS:
Results for this experiment are found in several publications cited below.

1. The study of the DNA methylation and miRNA profiles of the GM10115 CHO cell line ~16-20 population doublings following Fe ion or x-ray exposures was completed and has been published: Aypar, U., Morgan, W.F., Baulch, J.E. (2011) Radiation-induced epigenetic alterations after low and high LET irradiations. Mutation Research, 707:24-33. This study develops the initial picture of the effect of high and low LET radiations on DNA methylation and also begins to delve into the potential role for miR in the delayed radiation response.

2. The manuscript submitted in 7/2010 to Radiation Research was accepted and has been published. Goetz, W., Morgan, M.N.M., Baulch, J.E. (2011) The effect of radiation quality on genomic DNA methylation profiles in irradiated human cell lines. Radiation Research, 175:575-587. To date, studies of radiation-induced changes in DNA methylation have focused on the low LET radiation response, using gamma- and x-rays. This study presents data demonstrating that radiation induced changes in DNA methylation are affected in a radiation quality dependent manner. This was accomplished using protons, x-rays and iron (Fe) ions. X-rays and protons are similarly low LET radiations (2 KeV/µm and 0.55 keV/µm, respectively) that differ in other ways such as energy deposition patterns or ionization density and d-ray contribution. Fe ions are a high LET particle radiation (150 keV/µm). Low LET proton and high LET Fe ions were selected for comparison to x-rays because they are the most prevalent species in space radiation. This project also tested the hypothesis for differences in the epigenetic radiation response between normal and cancer cell lines using normal human fibroblasts and colon carcinoma cells. The results demonstrate differences in basal DNA methylation profiles between normal and cancer cell lines, but similar epigenetic radiation responses that seem to be based on radiation quality.

3. Completed the epigenetic profile (DNA methylation, miR expression and mRNA levels) of cell lines that exhibit radiation induced genomic instability, as well as validation RT-PCR for the miR and mRNA data. The manuscript for these experiments is in preparation and should be submitted by the end of 2011.
