experiment_title: Cardiac and Vessel Structure and Function with Long-Duration Space Flight and Recovery
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Cardiovascular health is influenced by many factors in normal daily life on the International Space Station. The microgravity environment dramatically changes the normal head-to-foot blood pressure gradient, causing crew to experience much higher sustained blood pressure (BP) at the brain. Normal daily life on ISS involves much lower physical activity levels, and together with the BP gradient changes are responsible for microgravity-specific structural adaptations of the heart and blood vessels compared to daily life on Earth. Changes in cardiac mass have been identified with space flight as well as bed rest and there is recent evidence of functional change in cardiac contraction as well as relaxation from bed rest studies. Arterial and venous blood vessel wall architectural properties are changed with bed rest and a recent observation indicated that arteries are stiffer during and for at least 6-days after prolonged spaceflight on ISS. These observations collectively have functional significance in terms of performance of physical work tasks or return to an upright posture after 6-months on ISS, and they might also indicate long-term or permanent cardiovascular health consequences. This is particularly relevant for future interplanetary exploration as well as on Earth where many cultures are tending to adopt increasingly sedentary lifestyles. Therefore, it is essential to gain a thorough knowledge of the cardiovascular adaptations to spaceflight and of the cardiovascular risk factors associated with prolonged weightlessness in order to establish appropriate countermeasures to maintain cardiovascular function and to mitigate if not prevent the onset of overt cardiovascular disease.

The aim of this investigation is to measure and quantify cardiac and vascular structural and functional changes and to observe biomarkers during 6-months of spaceflight and up to one year of recovery. The specific goals of this study are to collect data on the following:

  1. Cardiac contractility markers to assess left ventricle (LV) contraction changes. LV wall motion, LV wall structure, LV electro-mechanical coupling at rest and when the heart is appropriately challenged using 1G posture change.
  2. Blood vessels (arteries and veins) to obtain details on cellular-level structural changes and dimensions at rest and seated (1G). Four characteristics of vascular function will be investigated.

    1. Arterial walls might be stiffer: Indices of axial and radial wall motion will be collected and analyzed to quantify stiffness.
    2. Arterial walls might not dilate in response to a high blood flow challenge: Arterial blood flow and dilation will be monitored after a 5 minute circulatory occlusion of the forearm (Flow Mediated Dilation, FMD).
    3. Blood flow response to exercise might be impaired: Femoral artery blood flow velocity will be monitored after a brief exercise challenge.
    4. Arteries and veins might not constrict appropriately to defend blood pressure and preserve blood volume distribution: Vascular properties will be monitored in response to 3 hours partial circulatory occlusion at the thigh.

  3. Circulating biochemical markers to obtain details from plasma and salivary samples that reflect cardiovascular metabolism, growth, inflammation and oxidative stress.
  4. Telomere length in leukocytes to reflect cellular mechanisms regulating the balance between breakdown and repair.
  5. 24h ambulatory blood pressure monitoring with estimate of central arterial pressure to gain an estimate of central artery stiffness during daily life including during sleep.

The extended recovery measurements up to 12-months after landing of key variables post-flight will provide new insight into possible long-term consequences of spaceflight.

APPROACH:
Sample/Data collection will be accomplished preflight, postflight, and inflight in sessions described below.

Blood and Saliva Sessions: Blood and saliva will be collected from subjects after an overnight fast and before teeth are brushed. Blood samples will be collected into standard blood collection tubes from the antecubital vein following standard clinical procedures. Saliva samples will be collected after the blood, using commercially available and clinically standard “salivettes”, which are small, sterile, single use pieces of cotton designed to be chewed then frozen until analysis. There will be two sessions preflight between L-90 (Launch minus 90 days) and L-60 at least 2 days apart, six sessions postflight at R+0 (Return to Earth plus 0 days), R+3, R+11 to R+17, R+25 to R+31, R+51 to R+63, and R+1 year, and two sessions inflight between R-30 and R-1, at least 2 days apart.

24-hr Ambulatory Monitoring Sessions: The subject will don the blood pressure cuff on the upper arm, and clip the main unit at the waist. A technician will turn on and verify that the unit is operating properly. The subject will wear the device for 24 hours while engaging in normal daily activity and then remove it. There will be one session preflight between L-90 and L-60, four sessions postflight at R+3, R+11 to R+17, R+25 to R+31, and R+1 year, and three sessions (one optional) inflight at L+20 to L+40, R-30 to R-1, L+90 to R-31 (optional).

Resting Ultrasound Sessions: The subject will complete a questionnaire or log regarding recent exercise and medication history. Instrumentation will be followed by resting ultrasound images of the heart (cardiac echosonography study) and blood vessel wall detail, splanchnic blood pooling, thyroid dimensions, inferior vena cava lumen diameter and velocity captured while in the supine position. A pulse tonometer will be placed against the skin of the neck to collect a pulse pressure signal from the carotid artery. A blood pressure cuff will be wrapped around and inflated to occlude flow to the forearm for five minutes while ultrasound measurements are taken for an additional 3 min. The subject will then move to a seated position and ultrasound images of the heart, blood vessel walls will be repeated. The measurements of ECG, continuous finger BP, brain blood flow and cardiac output will be collected. The ultrasound images will be time-aligned during this session with the digital data collection file collected simultaneously. The digital file will, itself, contain time-matched, beat-by-beat digitized signals for the following variables: pulse tonometry, ECG, and continuous finger BP, brain blood flow and cardiac output. The latter two variables will be measured by Doppler ultrasound. There will be one session preflight between L-90 and L-60, four sessions postflight (2 optional) at R+3 or R+4, R+11 to R+17, R+51 to R+63 (optional), and R+1 year (optional), and two sessions inflight at L+20 to L+40 and R-30 to R-1. The R-30 to R-1 session may include optional add-on views if resources are available.

Exercise Ultrasound Sessions: The subject will lie supine for instrumentation of a 3-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) and a finger blood pressure cuff. The subject will complete a questionnaire or log regarding recent exercise and medication history. Ultrasound probes will be placed against the skin of the thigh and fixed in place with Velcro straps. Baseline lumen diameters and blood flow velocity of the superficial femoral and tibial arteries will be collected. The subject will complete leg squat exercises that will increase blood flow velocity to meet the metabolic demands of moderate exercise. Five minutes of post-exercise ultrasound data will be collected to observe the rate of recovery as an index of arterial function followed by de-instrumentation. There will be one session preflight between L-90 and L-60, four sessions postflight (2 optional) at R+3 or R+4, R+11 to R+17, R+51 to R+63 (optional), and R+1 year (optional), and two sessions inflight at L+20 to L+40 and R-30 to R-1.

Leg Cuff Ultrasound Sessions: The subject will complete a questionnaire or log regarding recent exercise and medication history. A partial leg occlusion test will be administered to reflect the equivalent of 30 mmHg compression of the thigh. Ultrasounds will be completed as for the Resting Ultrasound Session. After donning Braslets cuffs, the subject will return after three hours, when the ultrasounds will be repeated and timed to occur just before/just after the occlusion is released. There will be one session preflight between L-90 and L-60, and if resources allow, one optional session inflight at L+60 to L+120.

experiment_title: Toxicological Assessment of Airborne Volatile Organic Compounds
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Astronauts living for an extended period of time in a closed environment, such as the Mir Space Station, are continuously exposed to pollutants in respirable air. Pollutants originate from material off-gassing, human metabolism, systems and payload leaks, and utility chemicals. If pollutant concentrations reach high levels, crewmembers may experience health problems and scientific experiments could be confounded. This experiment was designed to sample the Mir Space Station air at various locations and times in order to estimate the effects of airborne pollutants on crew health. The following were objectives of this experiment:

  • Determine if Mir air meets U.S. standards for crew health during long-term exposure to trace contaminants
  • Sample air using several types of hardware to compare similarity of sampling methods
  • Sample Mir Space Station air at multiple locations simultaneously to assess spatial variations in the Mir complex
  • Measure ethylene concentrations to determine if plant growth experiments could be affected.
  • Assess the rate of pollutant mixing after hatch opening between shuttle and Mir.

    APPROACH:
    In-flight air sampling was performed on NASA-Mir 2-7. Instantaneous air samples were obtained using grab sample containers (GSCs), and 24 hour time-averaged air samples were obtained using solid sorbent air samplers (SSASs). Formaldehyde badges were used to measure formaldehyde concentrations throughout Mir.

    The GSCs and SSASs were tested preflight at the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Toxicology Laboratory to ensure that each sampler was clean and could perform as expected. Formaldehyde badges were tested, reconfigured to fit the NASA flight configuration, and packaged for use during flight.

    During flight, GSC and SSAS samples were taken approximately every thirty days. After each sampling session, the date, time, and location were recorded. Once during each mission, a spatial variation assessment was performed by sampling multiple modules simultaneously. The formaldehyde badges were worn by the crewmembers and also placed in the individual modules.

    Upon return to Earth, the GSC samples were analyzed by gas chromatography (GC) and a modified EPA TO-14 gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (GC/MS) method. The GC analysis was used to estimate ethylene concentrations. The SSAS samples were analyzed only via the GC/MS method. The filters were removed from the formaldehyde badges and extracted with formaldehyde-free water. The aqueous extracts were then analyzed for formaldehyde using a chromotropic acid-spectrophotometric method.

    RESULTS:
    The air quality on NASA-Mir 2-7 met, and exceeded, U.S. standards for human-rated spacecraft. However, the irritant group was slightly above a toxicity index of 1 during NASA-Mir 2, 6, and 7, and the carbon dioxide toxicity index was above 1 during NASA-Mir 2 and 3. The toxicity index was calculated for each toxicological group by summing the ratios of the measured concentrations to the space maximum allowable concentrations for each contaminant in a toxicological group. The high toxicity index of the irritant group was due in part to high concentrations of formaldehyde.

    As hypothesized, spatial variations of contaminants were small within the Mir complex for both SSAS and GSC samples. The variations were most likely caused by contaminants localized in the different modules. The rate of pollutant mixing after hatch opening between Shuttle and Mir could not be established because of too few samples. A comparison of the U.S. and Russian air sampling methods showed that the Russian AK-1 sorbent system samplers, on average, measured higher concentrations than did the U.S. samplers.

    During the course of this experiment, several opportunities arose that allowed scientists to study situations that had previously been unexamined. During NASA-Mir 4, a fire was caused by the solid fuel oxygen generator (SFOG); this presented an opportunity to study the contaminants released into the Mir atmosphere due to the fire, and also assess how well the life support system scrubs contaminants from the air. The life support system worked excellent and brought the pollutants associated with the fire back to baseline concentrations within 32 hours. During NASA-Mir 4 the investigators also had the opportunity to compare the results of the formaldehyde badges to those of the formaldehyde active sampler (FAS). Because of the difficulties involved with collecting inflight formaldehyde samples, conclusive results were not obtained. However, another opportunity arose to compare these two methods during the second phase of the Lunar Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP). The results of this test verified the validity of the badges when compared to other methods.

    During NASA-Mir 5, all sampling hardware was lost due to the decompression of the Spektr module. The focus of the experiment then changed to analyzing how well the humidity control system would scrub a large concentration of ethylene glycol from the air. It was hypothesized that ethylene glycol present in Mir air due to a leak would be removed quickly. However, ethylene glycol detector tubes were used to measure ethylene concentrations, and it took one month for the concentration to drop below the 180-day SMAC level. Additionally, ethylene concentrations measured by the GSCs during the other NASA-Mir missions were determined to be high enough to affect plant growth experiments.

    The final unscheduled event occurred during a low temperature catalytic oxidizer (LTCO) burn. Improper operation of the LTCO caused dangerously high levels of carbon monoxide (CO) to be released into the Mir atmosphere. The combustion products analyzer (CPA) recorded high levels of CO, but because the crew appeared to be doing well after the incident, the high levels were thought to have been caused by hydrogen interference. Because this was such a serious toxicological incident, many steps have been taken to prevent a reoccurrence. One step, which will be used on the International Space Station (ISS), is the use of a new CPA that has much less cross sensitivity to hydrogen.

experiment_title: Arterial Remodeling and Functional Adaptations Induced by Microgravity
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:

Astronauts returning to earth may experience postflight orthostatic intolerance, a condition characterized by the tendency to become light-headed or faint upon standing. Although hypovolemia contributes to this syndrome, evidence is mounting that it may also stem from fundamental alterations in peripheral vascular resistance. The purpose of this study is to determine whether space flight diminishes the ability of peripheral resistance arteries to constrict and if so, what specific factors are involved. In particular, this investigation will evaluate the potential roles of: smooth-muscle atrophy, modified sensitivity to the neurotransmitters norepinephrine and acetylcholine, and alterations in the body's ability to produce the vasodilator, nitric oxide, in space. The general hypothesis of this investigation is that exposure to weightlessness induces adaptations in resistance artery function (resistance arteries being arteries whose flow characteristics can be modulated to adjust vascular resistance). This adaptation, while appropriate to microgravity, is inappropriate upon return to the Earth's normal gravitational field.

APPROACH:

To test this hypothesis, three groups of rats were used: one in space flight and two ground-based controls. It was planned for the soleus-plantaris-gastrocnemius muscle complex to be removed from both hindlimbs of each rat. Then, three resistance arteries were to be isolated from each pair of muscles. The first of these arterioles were to be used to conduct physiology experiments on vascular responsiveness. The second arteriole was to be frozen for gene expression studies, and the third arteriole was to be used to determine vessel morphology.

RESULTS:

The payload was not recovered.

experiment_title: The Influence of Space Flight on Erythrokinetics in Man
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
A consistent finding after exposure to microgravity has been a significant reduction in red blood cell mass. Erythropoietin was measured during the Spacelab 1 mission and was found to be decreased on the 8th day of flight and on landing. For SLS-1, erythrokinetics were studied before, during and after the exposure to microgravity. Measurements included plasma volume, red blood cell mass, red blood cell survival, iron kinetics, erythropoietin levels, ferritin levels and routine hematology parameters.

APPROACH:
Data were collected in the following sessions:
Preflight
Iron Kinetics, Red Blood Cell Mass and 51-Cr RBC T1/2, Hematology, Plasma Volume, Body Mass Measurement, Plasma Proteins
Inflight
Iron Kinetics, 51-Cr RBC T1/2, Hematology, Plasma Volume, Body Mass Measurement, Plasma Proteins
Postflight
Iron Kinetics, Red Blood Cell Mass and 51-Cr RBC T1/2, Hematology, Plasma Volume, Body Mass Measurement, Plasma Proteins

RESULTS:
During flight, each of the three subjects studied had a significant decrease in red blood cell mass and plasma volume. The decrease in plasma volume occurred during the first day of flight. Erythropoietin levels decreased during the first 24 hours and remained low throughout the mission. The rates at which labeled red blood cells were removed from the circulation were similar before and during spaceflight. The rate of dilution of the labeled cells by new red blood cells was markedly decreased during spaceflight when compared to the rate measured preflight. The rate of production of new red blood cells (measured with radioiron) within the bone marrow was similar after one day of spaceflight to the rate observed three months preflight and postflight. During spaceflight there was a reduction in the number of newly formed red blood cells in the circulation as indicated by reduced 59-Fe red blood cell incorporation and reduced reduced rate of change in the specific activity of older 51-Cr tagged red blood cells.

experiment_title: Protein Turnover During Space Flight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The objective of this experiment was to investigate the effects of space flight on whole-body protein metabolism by simultaneously assessing protein turnover and hormonal concentrations. Results from this experiment would provide crucial information for the establishment of a viable ground-based model for protein metabolism. Such a model would provide researchers the capability to test potential countermeasures and determine nutritional requirements for future extended-duration missions, as well as conferring benefits to healthy and metabolically stressed individuals on Earth.

APPROACH:
Whole-body protein turnover, including muscle protein breakdown, was assessed in two subjects before, during and after flight. Blood and urine samples were collected during all phases of the study. Hormonal and biochemical concentrations were measured to better understand neuroendocrine indices of protein metabolism during space flight. Food, fluid, drug intake, and amount and type of exercise were monitored. Body composition was assessed before and after flight. Preflight data were compared with inflight data to determine the effect of microgravity on each subject. Postflight data were used to monitor the readaptation process.

Blood: Blood samples were collected preflight, inflight and postflight during several 72-hour periods. These collection periods began 60 days before launch (L-60), L-35, on flight day 3 (FD3), FD6, 5 days after flight (R+5), and R+14. The protocol was similar for all collection sessions. Baseline specimens were drawn as soon as possible after awakening and before the first meal. Five milliliters (ml) of blood were drawn via butterfly into a serum separator (SST) VacutainerTM tube. An additional 2.7 ml blood sample was collected via monovette syringe for fasting glucose and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) determination with a commercial portable clinical blood analyzer (PCBA). After the fasting blood draw, each subject ingested 15N-alanine (approximately 333 micromole/kg) in capsule form.

Twelve hours after 15N-alanine ingestion, a second butterfly was inserted into the opposite arm from the initial blood draw. The subject was infused with 3-methyl-d3-histidine (1.3 micromole/kg to measure muscle protein breakdown. This was followed by a 5 ml flush of sterile saline to insure that all the tracer was delivered into the subject's circulatory system. Ten minutes later, a third butterfly was inserted in the contralateral arm and 5 ml of blood were drawn into a SST VacutainerTM. Additional blood draws (5 ml into SST) were collected 24, 48, and 72 hours after 15N-alanine ingestion. During these times, an additional 2.7 ml blood sample was collected via monovette syringe for fasting glucose and BUN determination by PCBA.

In flight, blood samples were centrifuged and stored frozen until returned for analysis. The time of inflight blood draws was recorded using a bar-code reader; relative time of day was also known (i.e., hours after awakening). After flight, specimens were analyzed for the 15N enrichments of urea and ammonia by gas chromatography / mass spectrometry. Muscle protein breakdown was determined by computer modeling of the concentration of 3-methyl-d3-histidine circulating in the blood. Serum cortisol and insulin were measured by radioimmunoassay to assess the endocrine regulation of protein metabolism and turnover.

Urine: Urine samples were collected as separate voids. Subjects were provided with small coolers and ice packs to store samples. Sample bottles were collected by the research team at least twice a day. Samples were logged and void volumes measured. Each sample was analyzed to determine protein turnover. Aliquots were removed from each sample and frozen. These frozen aliquots were used to construct 24-hour pools to determine total nitrogen excretion and nitrogen balance. Data collection took place over several 24-hour periods beginning with the first void prior to the 15N-alanine ingestion at L-60, L-35, R+5, and R+14.

During flight, urine voids were collected for 24-hour periods beginning on FD3 and on FD6 in specially configured urine collection bags. Each collection bag contained a known amount of lithium chloride (LiCl) as a volume marker. One aliquot was obtained from each void and stored frozen for processing after return to Earth. All urine aliquots were logged using a bar code reader. After flight, the urine volume per void was calculated via the LiCl marker and all samples were analyzed individually to determine protein turnover. The aliquots from FD3 and FD6 were used to construct separate 24-hour pools to determine total nitrogen excretion and nitrogen balance.

Urea and ammonia 15N enrichments were determined in all specimens by gas chromatography/mass spectrometry after flight. Although ammonia analysis depended on the ability to maintain frozen samples until return to Earth, it provided the added advantage of calculating protein turnover by averaging a rapid and smaller pool (ammonia) with a larger and slower (urea) pool. Total nitrogen (needed to determine body nitrogen balance) was determined from 24-hour urine pools by the Kjeldahl method.

Dietary Intake: Prepared and weighed meals were provided by certified dietitians during the 72 hour periods at L-60 to L-58, L-35 to L-33, R+5 to R+7, and R+14 to R+16 following the 15N-alanine ingestion. Three-day monitoring allowed any abrupt dietary changes that might affect protein turnover to be identified. In addition, subjects were asked to record any medications or supplements taken, duration and type of exercise, and phase of the menstrual cycle (if applicable).

During space flight, food/fluid/drug/exercise intakes were recorded and monitored by means of a bar-code reader during two 3-day periods: from awakening on FD3 to FD5 (inclusive) and, similarly, from FD6 to FD8 (inclusive). The bar code device had an integrated laser that allowed the user to scan items using only one hand. The bar-code reader logged the following information: subject ID, Mission Elapsed Time (MET), and food item (and lot number). This information was stored in the bar-code reader's internal memory to be retrieved after return to Earth.

Body Composition: Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) was used to determine body composition (lean body mass) preflight and postflight. Whole-body scans were obtained on L-60 and L-35 and again on R+2, R+5, and R+14. Leg scans were subdivided at the knee into upper and lower regions to allow preflight-to-postflight comparisons of locomotor muscles.

RESULTS:
Space flight results in a down regulation of protein turnover; however, protein breakdown exceeds protein synthesis. In addition, hormonal changes which accompany space flight are conducive to a net loss of muscle and body protein. Nutritional, exercise or pharmacological interventions which promote net protein synthesis must be considered.

experiment_title: The Effects of Micro-Gravity on In Vitro Calcification
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Earlier observations of animals flown in microgravity have produced conflicting information about the nature and amount of the mineral formed in bone during flight in microgravity. One cause for these differences was that much of the mineral had been formed on Earth, and there was no way of knowing how much new mineral formed in microgravity. Since crystals formed in vitro in microgravity are generally larger and more perfect than those formed under similar conditions on Earth, it was hypothesized that the initial mineral crystals formed under physiologic control in microgravity would also be larger. The purpose of this experiment was to evaluate the initial mineral formed in flight, and compare it to mineral formed in ground based controls. Since biologic mineralization is mediated both by the cells and the extracellular matrix, the second goal was to evaluate the effects of microgravity on the cells and matrix formed in this culture system.

Approach:

Cartilage cells were grown as micromass cultures and flown for 11 days; total time in culture was 16 or 19 days. All cells were fixed in 2 percent paraformaldehyde plus 0.5 percent glutaraldehyde in 0.05M cacodylate buffer, pH 7.4 for electron microscopy, histochemistry and immunocytochemistry.

Results:

No mineral was formed in either ground controls or flight experiment. There was increased cell proliferation inflight.

experiment_title: ANP, Pro-ANP and mRNA Distribution in Rat Heart During a Space Flight
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Previous studies show that spaceflight induces a wide variety of changes in biological systems, including the cardiovascular and neuroendocrine systems. Cardiovascular deconditioning occurs upon return to earth. The regulation of blood pressure is partially carried out by the noradrenergic cells groups of the brain. However, the involvement of these systems is still unknown. Data provided by SLS-1 experiments on central and peripheral catecholamines could be the result of acute stress occuring in the animals. The purpose of this experiment is to re-evaluate the data retrieved from SLS-1 and compare these data with those obtained in simulated microgravity experiments (hindlimb-suspended rats).

Approach:

The flight and control groups were divided into two groups, one group examined upon recovery (R+0) and the other nine days later (R+9). For the ground-based simulation experiment, the tail-suspended and control animals were divided into analogous groups. Rats were anesthetized with metofane and blood was taken through cardiocentesis. The animals were then sacrificed by decapitation. The brain, kidneys, and heart were removed and prepared for analysis. Thick serial frontal sections were taken to analyze the noradrenergic cell groups (A1, A2, A5, and A6) of the central nervous system. Brain and peripheral tissue samples were treated with perchloric acid. The brain and tissue extracts were analyzed with liquid chromatography for norepinephrine (NE) content. The protein content of peripheral tissues was measured with the Bradford method.

Results:

There was no significant difference of the norepinephrine (NE) contents in the A1, A2, A5, and A6 cell groups between the flight and vivarium control groups. In the peripheral noradrenergic system, neither the cardiac atria and ventricles nor kidneys showed significant differences after spaceflight. The tail suspended group, when compared to controls, showed similar results. In the central nervous system, there was no significant difference between the NE levels in the A1, A2, A5, and A6 groups. In the peripheral noradrenergic system, neither the cardiac atria and ventricles nor kidneys showed significant differences after tail-suspension.

experiment_title: The Effect of Daily Activity and Age on Bone Density
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The purpose of this study was to 1) develop a new method of quantifying daily activity level in terms of the daily history of ground reaction forces and 2) to clarify the relationship between musculoskeletal tissue stress (strain) histories and the material and structural properties of bone during normal daily activity and 3) to establish equivalent loading histories in space compared to baseline activity levels on Earth.

APPROACH:
Male subjects, aged 30-55 years of average weight and similar shoe size were selected. An insole sensor (1/8th inch thick) was fitted to a foot of each subject. Pressure between the foot and shoe sole caused the sensor to deform and output a voltage (2.5 Volts maximum) proportional to the applied force. A shielding wire threaded through the pant leg connects the insole sensor with a microprocessor unit that is attached to the waist for data acquisition. The sensor is calibrated to zero and one body weight by lifting the foot off the ground for 2.5 seconds and then a second reading is taken after placing the foot on the ground for 2.5 seconds. These static data points are stored to obtain a linear force voltage output calibration and compared with a set of dynamic points from a swaying subject to ensure no difference in readings greater than 5% that would indicate a defective sensor.

RESULTS:
Peak cyclic ground reaction forces (GRFz), normalized to subject body weight were recorded for three consecutive weekdays. Average daily histograms of the number of loading cycles vs cycle-magnitudes (loading histories) were obtained by averaging 24 hour periods. The total number of cycles for men were 4526 ±1187 and for women, 4744 ±1383. The total number of cycles greater than 0.8 BW were 3649 ±1139 for men and 3909 ±1259 for women. Mean cycle magnitude for all cycles greater than 0.8 BW were 1.11 ±0.07 BW for men and 1.13 ±0.09 for women. The number of cycles at the higher >0.2 BW for men were 7.3±12.5 and for women 5.4±9.5. A trend toward reduced high load activity was observed with age. These results demonstrate for the first time objective force measurements of human activity in men and women. The range in frequency and magnitude of daily loading may be an important contributor to variation in bone density in lower limb skeletal sites loaded down by internal forces supporting the ground reaction force.

OBJECTIVE :
To determine the level of calcium as measured during bed rest. This was not a hypothesis driven study.

Twenty-four hour urine pools were collected and aliquoted for determination of calcium/bone status for each subject. The subject’s urine was collected for each 24 hour period. Projected results are a possible increase in calcium levels over a 6 day period for each bed rest subject. experiment_title: Cervical spine and muscle adaptation after spaceflight and relationship to herniation risk
experiment_description:
Objectives:

Astronauts have an incidence rate of cervical intervertebral disc (IVD) herniation that is 21.4 times higher than that of control populations. Current cervical spine data on astronauts is lacking and animal models are inappropriate because of differences between quadrupeds (animal models) and bipeds (astronauts). Prolonged bedrest has also been found to be an inadequate model for spaceflight effects on cervical spine. As a result, this experiment seeks to understand factors that may be involved in cervical IVD herniations.
Specific Aim:
1. To perform a variety of investigations on the cervical spine to capture a range of possible factors that may be involved in cervical IVD herniations after spaceflight.
2. To create data which can be used as input for ground based in-vitro studies with cadaver spines in a custom-built dynamic disc loading simulator and other modelling endeavors.

Approach:

This study will require 10 participants. Data collection will occur during preflight and post-fight ONLY. Two preflight sessions and four post-flight sessions will be required for each participant. Data on cervical spine characteristics will be consist of magnetic resonance imaging, cervical spine 3d kinematics, neck muscle function tests, dual energy X-ray absorptiometry, and questionnaires.

experiment_title: Factors Contributing to Food Acceptability and Consumption, Mood, and Stress on Long-term Space Missions
experiment_description:
Objectives 

The three inter-related foci in this study explore factors that contribute to the long-term acceptability of a diet, in terms of satisfaction with and sufficient consumption of the foods, as well as associated moods and stress levels. Prolonged exposure to stress responses can have deleterious effects on overall astronaut health and consequently on mission success. One of the things that can contribute to both health and stress is diet and food preparation. Understanding the relation between preparation effort and the acceptability and consumption of the prepared food, as well as effects on moods and stress, will inform decisions on the amount of time and types of activities crewmembers should allot to meal preparation. The study had 3 specific aims:

1. To design procedures for preparing and consuming meals that maximize food acceptability and lead to increased consumption and positive mood, while decreasing stress.
2. To identify foods that trigger positive emotions and to evaluate the effect of such ‘trigger foods’ on the amount consumed, moods, and stress levels of individuals who are under stress.
3. To increase people’s appreciation of the variety in their diet (without increasing the number of menu items).

Methods

To determine whether preparing food and/or having the ability to choose the ingredients in the food would improve mood and reduce stress (aim 1), the investigators recruited 118 participants (36% male) and divided them into four treatment groups: choice/prepare, no choice/prepare, choice/no prepare, and no choice/no prepare. For each treatment group, subjects were given stress tasks to induce physiological and psychological stress. After the stress task, mood related measurements were taken, and participants were given menus (differing based on choice grouping) and then later food to eat (prepared based on prepare grouping). Physiological and psychological measures of stress were taken again after the meal.

To identify foods that trigger positive emotions and to evaluate the effect of such ‘trigger foods’ on the amount consumed, moods, and stress levels of individuals who are under stress (aim 2), the investigators recruited 100 participants, 67 females, who first completed an online questionnaire to indicate their comfort foods and a variety of comparison foods. Then, during two lab sessions a week apart from each other (and at least a week after the online questionnaire, counterbalanced in order), participants watched films that induced a negative effect. In one session, participants were served their comfort food. In the other, participants were served an equally liked non-comfort food, a neutral food, or no food. Short-term mood changes were measured to determine psychological effects of these foods, rather than biochemical effects on mood from particular food components (e.g., sugars or vitamins). 

To determine whether boredom with repeatedly eaten foods could be curbed by increasing appreciation for variety in one’s diet (aim 3), participants repeatedly consumed granola bars over a 2-week period. Half the participants were reminded to think about recently eaten foods, and half were reminded to think about music they had recently heard. 
The researchers also decided to recruit people to keep 28-day food diaries to determine the degree of food variety in the diets of free-living individuals. 

Results

Aim 1 test results showed that preparation group had little effect on reducing stress or improving mood. However, increases in heart rate and decreases in systolic blood pressure were observed for those in the No Prepare groups compared to the Prepare groups. Those in the No Choice groups showed a greater decrease in anxiety, anger, and systolic blood pressure after the meal than those in the Choice groups. After the meal, heart rate increased more for those in the Choice versus the No Choice groups. Stress and negative measures related to mood decreased post meal overall. 

Tests developed to satisfy aim 2 showed that consuming comfort food after the film was no more effective at improving mood than other foods or eating nothing after the film. 

Aim 3 results showed the first intervention of having participants think about foods they had eaten in the previous week significantly increased subsequent intake and self-reported satisfaction and decreased self-reported boredom. They also tested whether there was a difference in the curbing of boredom between a group that was asked to think of musical artists they had listened to recently and a group that was asked to think about recently eaten foods. There was no significant difference in the liking of granola bars between these two groups. There was however an observed behavioral difference in the willingness to continue eating granola bars. The participants asked to think of food they had recently eaten took significantly more granola bars home at the end of the study than did participants in the music group.

The ISS component of this study known as "Astro-Palate" was discontinued after completion of part A leaving parts B and C incomplete. 

Part A of Astro-Palate: The objective of this study was to determine the role of menu choice on meal satisfaction. This was conducted once relatively early and then again later in the flight.

Part B of Astro-Palate: The objective of this study was to determine the effects of eating situation on mood. Crewmembers completed questionnaires before and after the meals. This would have been done relatively earlier and then again later in the flight. The first subject arrived at the ISS in 2014. Other subjects had agreed to participate and were in varying stages of completing the pre-flight questionnaires.

Part C of Astro-Palate: Objectives: 1) to determine whether eating foods thought to be capable of improving mood will improve moods of astronauts in space when they are in a negative mood and 2) to determine whether eating such foods immediately prior to situations generating negative mood will ameliorate that mood. Crewmembers would have completed questionnaires before and after specific snacks and tasks.

experiment_title: Food Processing vs. Packaged Food System Trade Study
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Food Processing vs. Packaged Food System Trade Study addresses the efficiencies and adequacies of growing produce and processing baseline crops into edible ingredients as compared to the efficiencies and adequacies of the utilizing the existing prepackaged food system. Specifically, the research was parceled into four specific aims:
1. To determine the requirements on vegetable, fruit, and baseline crops growth and bulk ingredient supply in terms of the estimated pounds required.
2. To determine requirements for food preparation and/or processing equipment at the extraterrestrial habitat.
3. To provide a quantitative assessment of mass penalties and human factors impacts of each proposed menu option.
4. To provide an assessment of feasibility of implementing the proposed systems and identify associated technology gaps.

Recent AFT work to prepare for deep space surface missions identified the shortcomings of using the current prepackaged food system in long exploratory mission application. The degradation of the quality of thermostabilized products and degradation of nutritional content indicates the inadequacy of the current food system for a five-year mission.

This trade study is central to the decision process on whether to continue work on bioregenerative crop development for future space flight missions. Additionally, the trade study supports the decision process on whether to develop food preparation and food processing technologies and, if so, to what extent the development should occur. Because the food system has huge implications to the upmass considerations of the mission as well as measurable impact to the psyche of the crew members, the appropriate decision on the food system will directly relate to the adequacy of the food system for the mission.

APPROACH:
Two 10-day menus were developed in preparation for a Mars habitat mission. The first was built on the assumption, as in previous menu development efforts for closed ecological systems, that the food system would be vegetarian, whereas the second menu introduced shelf-stable, prepackaged meat and entrée items from the current International Space Station (ISS) food system.

RESULTS:
The trade study answered the key question to which it was targeted – is it better to take the food to Mars or grow the food on the surface? – with the ambiguous “yes.” While the advantages of growing the food at the surface involve a tremendous upmass savings, higher acceptability, and higher potential menu variety, it cannot be discounted that even a small addition of prepackaged food prompted a significant decrease in crew time utilization and decreased the likelihood of food scarcity. The results indicate the food system design should focus on a solution that is mixed with food sources, leveraging the advantages of both farming crops and stowing the food supply.

Five food systems were postulated based on three menu designs of equal caloric contribution. The first food system was based on meals derived from crops grown at the Martian habitat with minor dry ingredient additions. The second food system used the same meals as the first but was based on meals derived from a smaller number of crops grown at the Martian habitat, stable bulk commodities (rice, beans, wheat) shipped from Earth, and minor dry ingredient additions. The third and fourth food systems mirror the first and second system food sources, respectively, except both the third and fourth systems are supplemented with prepackaged meat products. The final food system was based solely on existing space food. Many recipes were reproduced to ascertain the amount of raw material, the necessary cookware, and time that was required to complete a meal. The equivalent system mass (ESM) and the food metric value (FMV) for each of the five food systems were then compared to determine which food system is preferable based upon resource utilization and other food system metrics.

For a crew of 6 on a 600-day habitat mission, Food System 3 had the lowest equivalent system mass at 8566 kilograms and the lowest food metric value at 176 kilograms. This food system had both the second lowest mass shipped and second lowest volume shipped but was third in active crew time hours. The ESM for food system 3 was driven primarily by the low mass of stowed ingredients and a crew time utilization that was less than food system 1 or 2. The modified food quality index was not very different between food systems 1-4, and therefore, the value impacted the final results very little.

The combination of the food processing data with the ESM calculations of other linked subsystems (e.g. biomass production, water) will present the most accurate view of the food processing cost to mission planners.

experiment_title: Development of a Multipurpose Extruder - Press Food Processing System
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This project was to develop versatile, low mass, energy efficient, and easily maintained multipurpose seed processing (MSP) equipment for food processing in space environments. Phase-1 of the project yielded a conceptual drawing for a MSP. Phase-II consisted of six main tasks. The first model MSP was manufactured, programmed and tested for ESM, function, and quality of processed product. The data was used to refine the model and design multipurpose screws for the extrusion and press components of the MSP to simplify the equipment. Several models of MSP's were fabricated and tested for versatility. The ESM criteria and functional parameters were used to evaluate the optimum MSP for NASA applications and non-NASA applications.

APPROACH:
The primary NASA application were to perform a variety of food processing operations including size reduction, cooking, oil extraction, dehydration, stabilization, texturization, and expansion. This capability will lead to dry and shelf stable food products such as soy flour, textured soy protein, soy oil, breakfast cereals, expanded snacks, and pasta products. The proposed MSP will be unique in that the heat of processing will be generated internally by friction without dependence on an external heat source such as steam. The heat process will reduce microbial hazards in the space environment and also improve the stability of products by enzyme inactivation.

experiment_title: Microgravity Effects on Standardized Cognitive Performance Measures
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Space travelers are subject to a variety of stresses during space flight. These include adapting to the microgravity environment, physical isolation, confinement, lack of privacy, fatigue and changing work/rest cycles. On Earth, both fatigue and changing work/rest cycle degrade cognitive performance and productivity. The purpose of this experiment was to determine the effects of microgravity upon cognitive skills critical to the success of operational tasks in space. Scientists have hypothesized that performance will deteriorate as a result of time in microgravity and that fatigue will increase concurrently.

APPROACH:
The subjects for the Microgravity Effects on Standardized Cognitive Performance Measures experiment were four crewmembers of the seven-person crew on Space Shuttle flight STS-78. A preflight orientation session provided subjects with background information and a demonstration of the cognitive test battery known as the NASA Performance Assessment Battery, or NASA-PAB. Data were collected from each subject during 37 experiment sessions: 24 preflight sessions, 9 inflight sessions performed approximately every other day, and 4 postflight sessions also performed every other day. A total of 1183 data sets were recorded for the experiment.

To evaluate any changes in cognitive performance and productivity, the investigators developed a test battery consisting of a questionnaire and several performance tests. Each test subject performed the battery at one sitting, meaning that no breaks were allowed once the test was started. A brief description of each performance test and its duration follows.

Mood Scale - This task consisted of 8 scales and involved pressing an arrow key to indicate the level of agreement with the mood description associated with each scale. The test took less than 1 minute to perform.
Fatigue Scale - This task required the subject to press a numbered key to indicate which statement best matches the subject's fatigue state. The task took less than 30 seconds to perform.
Tracking - One of the effects of microgravity is a disruption of visual-motor coordination. To investigate this effect, a tracking test was used. The test required the subject to maintain a target in the center of a horizontal line. The target was displaced by the computer program at a fixed difficulty rate, and the subject had to manipulate a control device to null the input disturbance.
Matrix Rotation Task - The functional deafferentation of the otolith organs that occurs in space, along with associated effects on the visual and cerebellar systems, raise serious questions about the individual's spatial oreintation. Thus, it is desirable to look for subtle effects on a subject's ability to perceive, remember and process spatial information. The Matrix Rotation task is used to evaluate the effects of microgravity on spatial information processing. The test used 100 basic patterns, each of which was a 5 x 5 matrix with five illuminated cells that had been selected at random. At the beginning of the trial, the subject saw a pattern. The subject studied the pattern and then pressed a response key. The pattern was immediately erased and a new one presented. The subject was asked to decide as quickly as possible if the new pattern was identical to the first pattern. The subject then pressed a designated key for "same" or another designated key for "different". As soon as the response was made, a third pattern appeared. Now, the subject had to compare the new pattern to the immediately preceding pattern, etc. For "same" responses, the two patterns were never presented in exactly the same orientation; the second pattern was always rotated either 90° to the left of 90° to the the right relative to the preceding pattern. Both reaction time and percentage-of-corrections-made were recorded. The self-paced test lasts about 1.5 minutes.
Sternberg Memory Search - The general Sternberg paradigm required subjects to respond as rapidly and accurately as possible to visually presented letters. At the beginning of the test, a set of letters drawn randomly from the alphabet was presented to the subject for memorization. Next, the screen was cleared and a series of single test letters were presented. If the presented letter matched one of the letters in the previously memorized positive set, the subject responded "same" (key press). If a different letter appeared (negative set), then the subject responded "different" (key press) indicating a non-matching letter was presented. The self-paced test lasts 2 minutes.
Continuous Recognition - One critical aspect of higher cognitive function is the ability to maintain attention and to carry out repetitive cognitive processes over some period of time. In many ways, such activities encompass those that were traditionally referred to as "vigilance". However, they add the dimension of active processing of information, rather than simple monitoring. One task that appears to capture the performance elements above is the Continuous Recognition Test. In this test, the subject saw two numbers, one above the other. The task was to remember the bottom number. When the next two numbers appeared, the task was to determine if the new top number was the same as the previous bottom number. However, before responding, the subject must note the new bottom number because as soon as a response was made, the numbers were replaced by a new pair. Thus, the subject must not only exercise very short-term memory, but, more importantly, must inhibit the response until the new button number ws committed to memory. The appropriate strategy was to develop a set pattern of observing, memorizing, observing, comparing and responding. This sequence was different from that required by most routine tasks in that it required constant attention allocation. Even brief lapses resulted in errors. The task could be made even more difficult by requiring the subject to remember and respond to numbers further removed (two or even three back) from the one immediately proceeding, thus imposing a much higher load on immediate memory. The self-paced test lasted about 2 minutes.
Performance Switching Task - Manikin and Mathematical Processing - Time-sharing was different from another required attention process that could be affected by microgravity. Astronauts must make rapid shifts in the attentional focus, as well as in the skills required to respond to a change in task demands. This externally-directed behavior cannot be made automatic in any true sense, since it must be flexible enough to respond to unusual demands. Thus, a test was needed to probe the subject's ability to shift attention and resource allocation in response to rapidly changing and unpredictable external demands.

In this procedure, the subject had to discrete tasks to perform. One was a spatially-based task, and the other was a mathematically-based test. Each of these appeared, trial by trial, simultaneously on the screen. However, an indicator appeared at the same time, directing the subject to the task that was "active" (i.e., must be responded to). The subject had to made an exclusive response to the active task, where reaction time and percent-correct data were obtained only for that task. The switching from task to task for each trial was random (within constraints). Therefore, the subject had to remember to watch the indicator on each trial, allocate the appropriate resources to respond to the trial, and then make the appropriate response. This paradigm provided a test of switching skills.

The two tests selected to exercise this paradigm were the manikin test and the mathematical processing test. As implemented in this microgravity experiment, a manikin "stick figure" was presented facing either forward or backward. In addition, the figure could be either upright or upside-down. The figure was also standing on a box and inside the box was either a rectangle or a circle. In the figure's two hands were a rectangle and a circle. The subject's task was to note which symbol was inside the box, and then to determine which of the manikin's hands was holding the designated symbol. The subject then presses the left or right of two keys corresponding to the manikin's left or right hand.

Exposing the astronauts to a series of manikins presented in a variety of orientations in microgravity, where the astronaut had the freedom to position his own body during work and sleep in non-traditional gravity orientations, was one of the more theoretically interesting tests of spatial processing using a human form. The effects of microgravity on whole-body orientation may give insight into whether this test was a perceptual measure of spatial transformation of mental images or involved pure spatial abilities requiring readaptation.

The Mathematical Processing test was based on similar tasks. It presented three single-digit numbers that must be added or subtracted. If the answer was greater than 5, one response was given. If the answer was less than 5, another response was required. This task had been reported to be a relatively pure index of mathematical functioning. The computer-paced test lasted 4 minutes.

Dual Tasking - Tracking and Sternberg Memory Search - One of the most critical and potentially sensitive higher cognitive functions that might be affected by microgravity is the ability of the subject to allocate attentional resources among several tasks. To investigate this, the task used the time-sharing paradigm which consisted of the Sternberg task and tracking task being presented simultaneously. In the implementation of the dual task, the tracking task was presented in the middle of the screen and the letters of the Sternberg task appeared in a fixed location directly about the center null point. The target of the compensatory tracking risk moved laterally. One memory set was used, consisting of 4 letters. Due to the nature of the dual task, the "fixed set" procedure was used, in which the same memory set letters were presented with several probe letters for each daily session. The test lasted 3 minutes.

RESULTS:
With only four subjects it is not possible to generalize results to a population of future space travelers. However, if one confines their analysis and interpretation to the four subjects tested in this 16-day mission, some tentative conclusions can be drawn. Generally, in-Qrbit subjects were able to respond to the tests without significant impairment. The mathematical processing task, a part of the Directed Attention Test, showed significantly degraded performance in two out of the four subjects. The Matrix test performance was degraded in one subject. The improvement seen in the Tracking test for one subject appeared to be the result of an improved tracking strategy developed in the last two practice sessions prior to launch.

experiment_title: Nutritional Intake of LSAH Participants
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ) was sent out in the fall of 1998 to collect nutrition data from participants in the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH). A total of 645 participants answered and returned this survey. The 116 male astronaut respondents had a mean age of 48.2 years, while the 448 male comparison participants had a slightly higher mean age of 50.8 years. The female respondents were generally younger, reporting a mean age of 39.3 and 40.5 years for astronauts (N=21) and comparison participants (N=66), respectively.

APPROACH:
To compare the LSAH participants to the U.S. general population, results of a national survey, the 1994-96 Continuing Survey of Food Intakes by Individuals (CSFII), are also presented. In particular, the findings for respondents over 20 years of age (5056 males and 4816 females) are used as comparison to those of the astronaut and comparison participants.

Measurements were total kilocalories (Kcal) typically consumed by respondents of both surveys, as well as corresponding percentages of total fat, protein, and carbohydrates in their typical diets.

RESULTS:
When compared to the results of male CSFII respondents 20 years old and over, male LSAH participants reported a lower total consumption of kilocalories. The lower consumption values hold true even when compared to the CSFII respondents in the age groups closer to the mean ages of the male comparisons and astronauts (age groups 40-49 and 50-59 years of age). Female comparison participants reported a mean value similar to that reported by female CSFII respondents 20 years and older. Female astronauts, however, had a lower mean total intake than this group of CSFII respondents. Their reported value comes closer to values for those 50-59 years of age and older.

When the caloric intake is broken down into fat, protein, and carbohydrates, LSAH astronauts and comparison participants reported values similar to those reported by the CSFII respondents.

This brief summary of nutritional intake shows that in general male LSAH astronauts and comparison participants report a lower total consumption as compared to the general population, while female astronauts show a lower intake as compared to the general population. The proportions of fat, protein, and carbohydrates of astronauts and comparisons are similar to that reported in the CSFII. Therefore, the composition of LSAH participants' diet does not substantially differ from that of the general population.

experiment_title: Thermostabilized Food Study
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is working towards future long-duration manned space flights beyond low earth orbit. The duration of these missions may be as long as 2.5 years and will likely include a stay on a lunar or planetary surface. For these long duration missions, a shelf life of 3 to 5 years for the prepackaged transit food system is required.

Of the preservation methods currently being used at NASA for the Shuttle and International Space Station (ISS) food systems, the thermostabilized items will have the longest shelf life. Currently four approved ISS thermostabilized packaged foods are undergoing accelerated shelf life testing in the Space Food Systems Laboratory (SFSL) at NASA/Johnson Space Center. The foods, bread pudding, carrot coins, tuna noodle casserole, and apricot cobbler, are being stored in controlled temperature chambers at 40 degrees F, 72 degrees F, and 95 degrees F. Analytical tests to measure color, texture, pH, and water activity will be correlated with the sensory tests to determine the changes occurring in the foods. The sensory tests will measure the difference from control (40 degrees F) as well as overall acceptability. Nutritional analysis will be completed three times during the shelf life test.

The objective of this research was to continue the shelf life determination of these four thermostabilized food items. Sensory and analytical data was collected every four months on the four food items that were stored at 40F, 72F, and 95F for approximately 3 years. The shelf life test was terminated after 3 years or whenever the product became unacceptable, if before 3 years. In addition to determining the shelf life of these foods, better understandings of the chemical and physical changes that can occur throughout their shelf life were learned.

APPROACH:
The entire nutritional profile was determined analytically for 26 new food items by a selected accredited laboratory at “zero time” after stabilization processing. The empirical data was then compared with the calculated nutrition data. While incongruities in the estimates prevented broad conclusions on vitamin stability, a detailed look at some of the food products confirmed previous study assumptions that the stabilization processing was resulting in degradation of many of the vitamins, including vitamin C, vitamin A, folic acid, and thiamin. Losses after retort processing were as high as 100% for vitamin A and vitamin C.

RESULTS:
For the fifteen food items tested during FY 2008, repeat analytical testing was conducted on the anniversary of their original stabilization processing. Vitamin A continued to diminish in the package for most products over the one year of storage. Likewise, most folic acid and thiamin levels decreased, and vitamin C levels in all products declined from original levels by 37% to 100%. This degradation is attributed to remnant oxygen in package after nitrogen flushing. The presence of oxygen, even at decreased levels, allowed oxidation reactions to progress which chemically destroyed the vitamins.

Given that the estimates highlighted the absence of nutrient dense menu items and that degradation of vitamin profiles was noted after processing and during storage, it is unlikely that vitamin levels will subsist through the necessary three year product life. Countermeasure exploration should begin parallel to this study completion. NASA must identify means for solving critical nutrition problems including, reformulation with more resilient ingredients; fortification and supplementation; and development of processing and preservation methods that have less effect on the nutritional content of the food, e.g., high pressure processing and microwave sterilization. Additionally, the process of nitrogen flushing the retort pouches should be revisited for optimization or replacement.

experiment_title: Food Acceptability, Menu Fatigue, and Aversion in ISS Missions
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
This study addresses the risks of performance decrements and crew illness due to an inadequate food system that does not provide adequate diversity to address multi-year and deep space habitat missions. Past research has indicated that menu acceptability can impact the number of calories consumed, which also affects the overall nutritional intake of food by the crew on a mission. These reductions can result in impacts to crew health and performance. Crew data has suggested that the use of a standard food menu for 6 months or longer results in the decline in food satisfaction, and for some items by as much as 50%.
The need for and the amount of variety in choices of foodstuffs can also be tied to the length of the missions. That is, as missions increase in length, so should the menu diversity. Risks associated with food variety reductions include increases in gastric cancer and other adverse health effects such as inadequate brain health, psychological function, and gut health. The current state of acceptability of the ISS food system throughout 6-month and 1-year missions needs to be determined before adequate diversity for multi-year missions can be defined. Additional research needs to account for the sensory and psychosocial acceptability of food by looking at menu diversification and the impacts imposed on food consumption by microgravity, food processing and storage, environmental noise, and eating environment. Such evaluations will help determine the necessary menu diversity to prevent menu fatigue and promote the selection of nutritional choices needed for longer space missions and deep space habitats.

APPROACH:
Surveys conducted weekly will be used to obtain crew feedback on the acceptability of the menu and any fatigue with menu components. Survey data will be collected using the Data Collection Tool (DCT) aboard ISS. A post-flight interview between the crew and the PI will obtain vital information concerning the flight data gathered and answers to follow-up questions concerning the in-flight food.

RESULTS:
Results will be available at a later date.

experiment_title: Evaluation of the ISS Food Intake Tracker App
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
The International Space Station (ISS) Food Intake Tracker (ISS FIT) iPad Application (App) is a dietary intake tracking method to provide a more efficient and accurate way to track intake during space flight. It has been designed to allow users to enter foods by either selecting food items from a list of foods, take pictures of the foods, barcodes, or labels, voice recording what was consumed, or typing the foods. It is intended for the users to record food on a daily basis during a mission. This study is a technical demonstration of the App, with data collection. Subjects participating in the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) ground analog studies at NASA or NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) missions where space foods are used will be recruited. Because the App has a database of space foods, it is best to test in an environment where space foods are used.

APPROACH:
The App data will be stored on a server and downlinked to the Nutritional Biochemistry Laboratory where the intake data will be translated into nutrient data. This will be used in ISS research (e.g., Integrated Nutrition study), and will provide an option for supporting (ISS) Medical Operations requirements testing.

Subjects will be briefed on how to use the ISS FIT App and they will be asked to record all of the dietary intake during the mission. After the mission, investigators will debrief them and ask for all feedback on how it worked, suggestions for improvements, and aspects that didn't work.

RESULTS:
This experiment is in progress. However, the data will not be analyzed statistically. The point of this study is to demonstrate that dietary intake can be tracked using the ISS FIT during a NEEMO or HERA mission, and identify areas in the App design for improvement. This experiment was on HERA Campaign 1, missions 2-4, HERA Campaign 2, all missions, and is scheduled for all missions on HERA Campaigns 3 and 4.

experiment_title: Effect of Space Radiation on the Nutrition and Quality of the Food
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
It is vital that food sent up into space for long durations maintain its nutritional and sensorial quality throughout the length of the mission. One major source of nutritional and sensorial quality loss during a long duration mission is ionizing radiation. Ionizing radiation has been used as a food safety aid for over a century now and research supports its effectiveness in reducing numbers of foodborne pathogens, extending shelf life and controlling pests. Most of these studies have used gamma rays (mostly from Cobalt-60, but also Cesium-137), high-energy electrons/electron beans or x-rays. This radiation has been applied mostly on the kiloGray doses since these levels provide the most microbial lethality. There is considerably less research available that studies the effects of low-dose radiation on the properties of food. NASA radiation experts estimate that on a 30 month mission to Mars, food will come in contact with no more than 5Gy of radiation. This objective of this study was to perform a literature search on effects of low dose radiation on food quality. Much of what is published in the literature uses doses considerably higher than 5Gy and it can be assumed if there is no significant difference of radiation at the kiloGray level, on certain components or properties of food, there will be no noted difference in these attributes at lower doses.

APPROACH:
This objective of this study was to perform a literature search on effects of low dose radiation on food quality. Much of what is published in the literature uses doses considerably higher than 5Gy and it can be assumed if there is no significant difference of radiation at the kiloGray level, on certain components or properties of food, there will be no noted difference in these attributes at lower doses.

RESULTS:
Overall, it is safe to say that radiation encountered at doses typical for a Mars mission is not prohibitively high to render the food supply inadequate given than space radiation at equivalent doses acts like gamma or electron bean radiation sources. However, research would be necessary to understand how actual space radiation, not just electron or gamma radiation, affects food in order to better predict and prepare countermeasures to these effects. Currently, there are no studies that have examined the effects of space radiation on food or how this type of radiation differs from more conventional types used for safety.

experiment_title: Astronaut's Energy Requirement for Long-Term Spaceflight
experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Loss of body mass commonly occurs during long-duration space flight. One explanation for the loss in body mass is the decrease of skeletal muscle use. It is also expected that the systematic ongoing negative energy balance observed in flight contributes significantly to such a loss. However, the reason for the imbalance between energy intake and energy output is not clear.

Additional knowledge of energy intake requirements during space flight is needed to maintain the health of long-duration crewmembers, to ensure high performances and the overall success of a mission, but also to ensure adequate, but not excessive cargo allotments for food. In this regard, the determination of energy requirements as a function of exercise load is a clear pre-requisite to any planed long-term manned space flight.

Astronaut's Energy Requirements for Long-Term Space Flight (Energy) will measure changes in energy balance after long term spaceflight, adaptations in the components of the total energy expenditure and derive an equation for the energy requirements of astronauts.

APPROACH:
Preflight data collection consists of one active measurement day, and a follow up void collection ten days later. The subject is wearing an activity monitor during the entire 10 day time period. After an overnight fast, the measurement day starts with a body weight measurement to calculate the Doubly Labeled Water (DLW) dosage given to each subject. A baseline urine collection is collected prior to the DLW ingestion. Approximately 45 minutes after DLW ingestion, the first oxygen uptake (OU) measurement is scheduled for 45 minutes, followed by a special breakfast. Over the next five hours, the crewmember is asked to perform a total of seven more OU measurements of 20 minutes each, which alternate with resting periods. After the second, fifth, and seventh OU void samples are collected.

Ten days after the measurement day, two additional void samples are requested from the subject, preferably from two consecutive voids.

The Baseline Data Collection (BDC) can be scheduled anytime between L-4 months and launch. The subjects should not have large deviations in their body mass (±5%) in the period from BDC to launch. The BDC data are valid for 6 months. It is preferable during the 11 days of the BDC to stay within the same geographical region (continent).

Energy in-flight data collection should be scheduled with crewmembers staying in orbit for four months or longer. The data collection should be scheduled no earlier than three months into the mission, and at least three weeks prior to landing. This 4-week limit is chosen to avoid confounding effects of the increased countermeasure programs at the end before landing.

The astronauts total energy expenditure will be measured by the DLW method, and by indirect calorimetry. In addition, body composition will be measured through hydrometry. The in-flight and preflight protocols will be conducted over a 10-day period, starting with the main measurement day. The day before the measurement day the experiment hardware is set up and the standardized meals will be consumed. Those meals will be of similar macronutrient composition and energy content and will be based on individual’s body mass.

At the start of the measurement day, intake of the DLW and a urine sampling are performed. During the measurement day, two sessions of 45 min and 4 hours of physical rest will be required during which OU is measured using the Pulmonary Function System (PFS). The 45-minute measurement period is scheduled approximately 45 minutes after the DLW intake. Then a standardized breakfast is consumed and the 4 hour session starts. This session contains continuous online OU measurements by the PFS, paused only by void samplings and 10 minute breaks for comfort. Over the following nine days, a series of void and water samplings are scheduled for every other day and the activity monitor is worn continuously.

RESULTS:
Results for this investigation are unavailable. This is an international experiment. NASA does not currently have an agreement with international space partners to archive their data in the LSDA.
